TI Unlocking entrepreneurial intentions: The power of educator
   characteristics and student identification
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrepreneurship; Education; EducatorCharacteristics; Student
   identification; Entrepreneurial intention
ID SOCIAL IDENTITY; PLANNED BEHAVIOR; ROLE-MODELS; SELF-EFFICACY; BRAND
   PERSONALITY; GENDER; IMPACT; BUSINESS; TEACHER; DETERMINANTS
AB This study explores the impact of entrepreneurship educators' characteristics on students' entrepreneurial intentions. Focusing on the personal, professional, and pedagogical attributes of educators, the research examines how these factors foster students' identification with them, subsequently shaping attitudes and perceived behavioural control relevant to entrepreneurship. A structured survey conducted among 670 university students enrolled in a mandatory entrepreneurship course served as the primary data source. Results derived from Structural Equation Modelling reveal that educators' professional and pedagogical characteristics significantly enhance students' identification, which, in turn, positively influences their entrepreneurial attitudes and perceived behavioural control. This study underscores the importance of targeted educational strategies that leverage educator influence to strengthen entrepreneurial mindsets in higher education. Practically, these findings suggest that improving educator training and selection based on professional and pedagogical qualities can foster entrepreneurial intention among students, providing valuable guidance for the development of policies and practices in entrepreneurship education.

TI The roles of student enjoyment of reading and teacher job satisfaction
   in socio-economic inequality in reading achievement
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Reading achievement; Reading enjoyment; Socio-economic status; Teacher
   job satisfaction
ID SELF-DETERMINATION THEORY; PARENTING STYLE; MOTIVATION; LANGUAGE
AB The current study examines the association between socio-economic status (SES) and reading achievement, and it also investigates whether student enjoyment of reading and teacher job satisfaction moderate this association. We used the PISA 2018 data, focusing on the reading domain. The participants were 2473 secondary school students (Mage = 15.76, SD = .29) and 1409 reading teachers nested in 97 schools from the United Kingdom. The results show that: (1) at the student level, reading enjoyment amplified the positive relationship between SES and reading achievement, suggesting that higher-SES students tend to benefit more from reading enjoyment in reading achievement. (2) At the school level, teacher job satisfaction neither enlarged nor weakened the relationship between school SES and school reading achievement.

TI When AI support shapes affect in L2 writing: Task-specific emotions
   across genre-based writing tasks
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-Assisted writing; L2 writing; Task-specific emotions; Affective
   learning
ID LANGUAGE; 2ND-LANGUAGE; STUDENTS; ENGAGEMENT; ENJOYMENT; ANXIETY
AB Despite growing interest in AI-assisted writing, learners' task-specific emotional experiences during AI-assisted L2 writing remain insufficiently understood, as prior work has largely examined affect at an overall or task-general level. This study investigated how AI-assisted writing influences task-specific emotions among L2 learners across different writing tasks. It examined whether AI support affects learners' enjoyment, anxiety, and boredom compared with traditional instruction and whether these effects vary by task type. Seventy university EFL students majoring in English at a large Chinese university completed four genre-based writing tasks (personal, narrative, expository, and argumentative) under either AI-assisted or traditional conditions. Emotional experiences were reported after each task, and linear mixed-effects models were used to analyze the data while controlling for baseline emotion levels. Results showed that AI-assisted writing significantly enhanced learners' enjoyment (d approximate to 0.51) but did not change anxiety or boredom overall. However, a significant Group & times; Task interaction emerged: AI-supported learners reported higher enjoyment and lower anxiety and boredom specifically during the argumentative task, indicating that AI's emotional benefits depend on task demands. These findings suggest that integrating AI tools can promote positive emotional experiences in cognitively demanding writing contexts and support greater engagement and comfort in L2 writing.

TI The paradox of instrumental visibility: A narrative inquiry into
   epistemic injustice in a STEM-dominated faculty
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic identity; Narrative inquiry; Epistemic injustice;
   Interdisciplinary marginalization; Resilience; STEM-dominated evaluation
ID IDENTITY; RANKINGS
AB This narrative inquiry illuminates identity disruption experienced by an educational technology scholar relocating from an education faculty to a STEM-dominated department in China. Situated within STEM-dominated evaluation regimes, the study identifies the paradox of instrumental visibility-a condition where a scholar's expertise is selectively mobilized for institutional prestige yet systemically devalued in formal evaluation and resource allocation. Framed by epistemic injustice and identity agency, the narrative traces a trajectory of disciplinary decentering, affective resistance, and relational reconstruction. Drawing on reflexive journals and institutional documents, the findings reveal how the scholar's pedagogical research was rendered institutionally illegible despite established achievements. Conversely, relational practices-including cross-institutional collaboration and international dialogue-functioned as micro-resistance, sustaining professional coherence under epistemic marginalization. By foregrounding the affective and structural dynamics of interdisciplinary mobility, this study contributes to critical debates on academic identity, epistemic justice, and knowledge governance in contemporary higher education.

TI Competition or synergy? Effects of task complexity and social demand on
   EFL learners' interactional pragmatic performance
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Task complexity; Social demand; Interactional pragmatic performance;
   Task-based interaction
ID DIFFICULTY
AB To deepen the understanding of task-based second language (L2) pragmatic learning and teaching, this study explored EFL learners' co-constructed pragmatic performance in interaction under the effects of task complexity and social demand. A total of 48 Chinese undergraduates in English majors were randomly allocated in dyads to finish four collaborative writing tasks with oral interaction phases. Task complexity was manipulated by [f elements] and [f reasoning demands] while social demand was operationalized by [f power] and [f social distance]. Learners' oral production during the interaction was analyzed through interactional pragmatic features. The results showed that increasing task complexity and social demand both significantly promoted learners' interactional pragmatic performance regarding organizing sequences, turns, and pragmatic actions. The meta-pragmatic awareness manifested during the interaction was enhanced by increasing social demand, while task complexity had an opposite impact. The results of interactive effects further revealed a competition between these two factors in promoting active turn allocation strategies and pragmatic actions. This study provides pedagogical insights for pragmatics-in-interaction and inspires future research integrating L2 pragmatics with taskbased language teaching (TBLT).

TI Loves that Kill: Debates on School Essentialism
SO TEORIA DE LA EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE school as technology; cultural evolution; school fetishism;
   essentialism; reflexive impotence; prefigurative cultures
AB This article analyzes the defense of the school formulated by Jan Masschelein and Maarten Simons, who conceive it as a space of non-productive free time. The hypothesis advanced is that this conception rests on a triple essentialism-nominal, rational, and affective-that fetishizes the school and obscures it as a technology that channels practices. The analysis confirms that this essentialism appeals to schol & eacute; as a myth, to the attribution of a rational capacity, and to the centrality of love as the ultimate foundation of legitimacy. This produces effects of reflexive impotence and blocks imagination in an accelerated scenario of digitalization and prefigurative cultures. The study is based on a theoretical-critical analysis that draws on history and sociology, Foucauldian notions of technology and governmentality, and research on cultural evolution. Teaching is considered as an adaptive capacity of the human species, prior to and external to the school, thereby questioning its naturalization as the exclusive habitat of education. The findings suggest that the emphasis on love as a source of legitimacy configures a normative shield which, far from empowering teachers, intensifies disappointment and impotence-particularly in a prefigurative culture where the symbolic centrality of adults is eroded, undermining the testimonial horizon of schooling. The article proposes identifying alternative ways of embedding teaching, suggesting three complementary paths: rejecting the school fetish through the historicization of schooling; mapping spaces where non-productive times emerge; and exploring couplings between school and post-school forms, assessing their effects on attention and equality of access to knowledge. It calls for opening educational imagination beyond mythologized recurrences in order to identify flows capable of sustaining education in its evolutionary, open, and contingent character.

TI Tiktonian Brain: Cognition and Learning in Algorithmic Digital Culture
SO TEORIA DE LA EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE brain; digital culture; critical pedagogy; social media; educational
   technology; TikTok
ID EDUCATION
AB The proliferation of digital platforms based on short, intense and highly stimulating videos, such as TikTok, is transforming the way young people process information, shape their attention and construct learning. This study proposes the concept of the Tiktonian brain as a critical category and operational construct for analysing the emerging cognitive configurations within algorithmic digital culture. Unlike media-driven or clinical notions framed from an alarmist or reductionist perspective, the approach developed here places the issue within its educational, critical and interdisciplinary dimension, integrating contributions from neuroeducation, critical pedagogy, and cultural and media studies. The methodology is framed within a theoretical-critical approach, grounded in literature review and conceptual analysis, with the aim of constructing an interpretative framework capable of guiding future empirical research and pedagogical practices. The findings highlight processes such as attentional fragmentation, the pursuit of instant gratification, and the reshaping of the desire to learn. The main contribution lies in offering criteria for educational application, including the integration of critical digital literacy into curricula, ongoing teacher training, and the design of learning environments that balance immediacy and reflection. Furthermore, institutional and educational policy implications are considered, such as curriculum review and the promotion of digital equity. Overall, the article proposes strategies to transform the risks of algorithmic culture into opportunities for critical and conscious learning, providing insights to inform both contemporary pedagogical debate and the design of educational policies adapted to the demands of the digital era.

TI Internationalisation at home through simulation-based learning:
   Intercultural teamwork and professional readiness in business education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Diversity simulation; Intercultural teamwork; Cross-cultural management;
   Experiential learning; International business education; Qualitative
   thematic analysis
AB Purpose: This qualitative study investigates how a diversity simulation, combined with theoretical input, shapes international business students' intercultural learning and perceived professional readiness in Thailand. Design/methodology/approach: A two-phase learning design was implemented. In Phase 1, students engaged with an online diversity simulation without prior lecture input, navigating intercultural team challenges independently. In Phase 2, they attended a lecture on diversity and intercultural communication, replayed the simulation and reflected on linking theory to practice. Data comprised 80 pre- and post-simulation reflective journals from 40 Business Administration students; a small number of interviews provided contextual background. Reflexive thematic analysis was conducted. Findings: Three themes emerged. Micro-ethical intercultural teamwork shows how students reframed scheduling, tone and participation decisions as questions of fairness, respect and voice. Conceptual sense-making captures how students used intercultural and organisational concepts, alongside simulation feedback, as interpretive tools for understanding team dynamics. Reflexive self-insight and emerging professional identity highlights how students articulated greater awareness of their relational impact and described intentions to act more inclusively in future multicultural work contexts. Originality: Situated in a Global South business programme, the study demonstrates how a structured simulation-theory-reflection sequence can function as internationalisation at home by supporting students' articulation of intercultural responsibility and workplace readiness without reliance on physical mobility. Research limitations/implications: Findings derive from a single institution and self-reported reflections; future multi-site and longitudinal studies are recommended.

TI I choose to be an entrepreneur! Exploring pathways of students'
   entrepreneurial career choice through a serial mediation model
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrepreneurial career choice; Entrepreneurial intention;
   Entrepreneurship education; Self-efficacy; Proactivity
ID INTENTIONS; BEHAVIOR
AB This study is intended to examine the influence of entrepreneurship education (EE) on entrepreneurial intention (EI) and its impact on entrepreneurial career choice (ECC) among university students in Indonesia through self-efficacy (SE) and proactivity. The data were taken from 332 university students from several educational-based universities in Indonesia. The analysis technique adopted a covariance-based structural equation modeling to confirm the proposed hypothesis. The findings of this study indicate that EE has been shown to predict of EI, proactivity, and SE. However, it cannot directly explain ECC among university students. This study also reveals that SE and proactivity can directly influence EI and indirectly play a role as mediators for EE and EI. The serial mediation occurs in the study to explain a path between EE and ECC. This study raises the implication to consider some bridges, such as SE and EI, as an effort to promote ECC for students.

TI 10th anniversary: The development, implementation, and evaluation of a
   novel peer-assisted learning (PAL) program
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Peer-assisted learning (PAL); Academic support; Student learning
   resources; Tutoring programs; Peer-led tutoring
AB Objectives: This brief report aims to elucidate the feasibility, effectiveness and sustainability of a peer-assisted learning (PAL) program, beyond traditional tutoring, as a part of the Doctor of Pharmacy curriculum. The report analyzes a PAL program, Student Educational Assistance (SEA), started ten years ago at a public school of pharmacy in the northeastern region of the United States. Methods: Researchers used administrative data to define the student population to assess. Then, they used a Qualtrics survey to collect information regarding the students' background, how they learn best, and specific questions about the SEA program. Quantitative data was analyzed using descriptive statistics. Qualitative data from the open-ended student survey were thematically analyzed by two members of the research team. Discrepancies were resolved by a faculty researcher. Results: One hundred and thirteen students out of 178 students who have used the SEA materials submitted a completed survey (63.5% response rate). Of these 113 students, 81% agreed using SEA material increased their confidence before exams. Additionally, 69% agreed using SEA material improved their assessment performance. Responses to the open-ended portion of the survey highlighted the importance of SEA materials in supplementing student's studying, especially through clarifying knowledge gaps and memorization through active recall. Conclusion: The outcomes of this report suggest that including various PAL modalities in the didactic pharmacy curriculum can increase student confidence in learning and perceived performance on assessments. The PAL program presented appears feasible, effective, and sustainable.

TI Tables to teamwork: Student canteen as a catalyst for collaborative
   learning in business education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Canteen; Collaborative; Informal learning; Business education
ID FIT INDEXES; ENGAGEMENT
AB This study investigates the role of student canteens as informal learning spaces that foster peer togetherness and collaborative learning within business education. Using a quantitative research design, survey data were collected from 430 students enrolled in internationally accredited universities across India. Stratified random sampling ensured representation by academic discipline, year of study, region, and student type. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) with bootstrapping to assess reliability, validity, and hypothesized relationships. The findings demonstrate that peer interaction frequency, group diversity, and informal learning discussions significantly strengthens collaborative learning engagement, which in turn positively impacts knowledge application and teamwork skills. The study contributes original insights by applying established theoretical perspectives to a new context such as informal canteen, by highlighting its value as an active learning environment.

TI AI-enhanced education: Exploring the impact of students' GenAI literacy
   on their psychological factors and learning performance
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI literacy; AI readiness; Confidence; Satisfaction; Learning
   performance
ID PERCEIVED SELF-EFFICACY; INFORMATION LITERACY; BEHAVIORAL INTENTIONS;
   TECHNOLOGY READINESS; SATISFACTION; ATTITUDES; VARIANCE; CHATGPT; MODEL
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming pedagogical methods across various disciplines at an increasing speed. However, limited research has examined how students' GenAI literacy influences psychological factors and learning performance. Based on social cognitive theory and information literacy theory, this study develops and validates a conceptual model to explain the impact of GenAI literacy in educational settings. Survey data from 221 undergraduate and postgraduate students were analyzed using the partial least squares (PLS) approach. The results indicate that higher GenAI literacy is associated with greater confidence, a more positive perception regarding using GenAI, and greater satisfaction with the learning experience. However, confidence does not offset negative AI readiness, suggesting that distinct mechanisms underpin students' apprehension towards GenAI. These findings emphasize the importance of cultivating GenAI literacy to enhance psychological readiness and improve learning performance. Educators are encouraged to design AI-supported learning environments that facilitate the development of GenAI literacy, address positive and negative readiness factors, and enhance learning performance. By clarifying how GenAI literacy influences key psychological factors, this study offers implications of integration of AI into the instruction design of higher education.

TI How study resources foster students' motives and perceived creativity:
   Longitudinal insights from the study demands-resources model☆
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Study resources; Psychological capital; Study engagement;
   Entrepreneurial self-efficacy; Perceived employability; Entrepreneurship
   courses
ID MEDIATING ROLE; SELF-EFFICACY; QUESTIONNAIRE; ENGAGEMENT; OPTIMISM;
   DESIGN; WORK; COLD; HOT
AB Building on the study demands-resources model, this study aims to investigate the relationships between study resources, psychological capital, students' motives, and perceived creativity. A total of 518 students completed a questionnaire at the beginning, middle, and end of an entrepreneurship course. The results of structural equation modelling showed that study resources, such as feedback from others, positively related to study engagement and entrepreneurial selfefficacy, which, in turn, positively influenced students' perceived creativity. Additionally, creativity support significantly related to study engagement, but not entrepreneurial self-efficacy. Furthermore, we examined how psychological capital, as personal resources, moderated the relationships among study resources, students' motives, and perceived creativity. The results of moderated mediation analyses showed that creativity support positively related to study engagement for students with high (vs. low) psychological capital, which subsequently influenced perceived creativity. This study contributes to the literature by providing empirical insights into the relationships between study resources, personal resources, students' motives, and perceived creativity. The findings also have practical implications for improving teaching pedagogies of entrepreneurship courses.

TI Coaching with compassion in graduate leadership education: A convergent
   mixed-methods pedagogical case study
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Coaching; Compassion; Emotional intelligence; Intentional change theory;
   Leadership education; Management pedagogy; Mixed methods
AB Purpose: This study investigates Coaching with Compassion (CwC) as a pedagogical innovation in graduate management education that cultivates emotional intelligence, reflection, and ethical leadership identity. Grounded in Intentional Change Theory (ICT), CwC emphasizes empathetic connection and sustainable behavior change through compassionate coaching relationships. Design/methodology/approach: Using a convergent mixed-methods pedagogical case design, data were collected from 29 Master of Public Administration students enrolled in a leadership and organizational behavior course. Students completed two individual CwC sessions, peer-coaching circles, reflective journals, and course debriefs. Session 1 focused on the ideal self and was followed by the VIA Character Strengths assessment; Session 2 integrated those results with coaching questions adapted from Primal Leadership. Qualitative evidence included reflective journals, Critical Incident Interviews, and participantobservation field notes, complemented by courseevaluation comments and descriptive pre/post self-ratings on emotionalintelligence competencies. Findings: Results showed consistent increases in self-awareness and relationshipmanagement confidence. Thematic analysis revealed a developmental sequence-(1) awakening authentic purpose, (2) reframing professional stress through compassion, and (3) linking personal growth to publicservice values-illustrating compassion as a catalyst for intentional change. Originality/value: This study contributes original empirical evidence by examining Coaching with Compassion as a classroom-based pedagogical intervention in graduate public administration education. While prior research on CwC has predominantly examined executive coaching, organizational leadership development, and professional well-being in corporate or managerial contexts, few studies have empirically investigated its use as a structured learning design within higher education curricula (Boyatzis, 2006; Boyatzis et al., 2013; Boyatzis et al., 2019). By embedding compassion-based coaching within a graduate leadership course, this research extends CwC scholarship into management education and public service preparation, offering a replicable, evidence-informed model for cultivating emotional intelligence and ethical leadership through experiential pedagogy (Boyatzis, 2024).

TI Human-AI collaboration or obedient and often clueless AI in instruct,
   serve, repeat dynamics?
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Human-AI collaboration; Large language models (LLMs); Generative AI;
   Transition network analysis; Human AI interaction
ID INTELLIGENCE
AB While research on human-AI collaboration exists, it mainly examined language learning and used traditional counting methods with little attention to evolution and dynamics of collaboration on cognitively demanding tasks. This study examines human-AI interactions while solving a complex problem. Student-AI interactions were qualitatively coded and analyzed with transition network analysis, sequence analysis and partial correlation networks as well as comparison of frequencies using chi-square and Pearson-residual shaded Mosaic plots to map interaction patterns, their evolution, and their relationship to problem complexity and student performance. Findings reveal a dominant Instructive pattern with interactions characterized by iterative ordering rather than collaborative negotiation. Oftentimes, students engaged in long threads that showed misalignment between their prompts and AI output that exemplified a lack of synergy that challenges the prevailing assumptions about LLMs as collaborative partners. We also found no significant correlations between assignment complexity, prompt length, and student grades suggesting a lack of cognitive depth, or effect of problem difficulty. Our study indicates that the tested LLM, optimized for instruction-following rather than cognitive partnership, compounds their capability to act as cognitively stimulating or aligned collaborators. Implications for designing AI systems that prioritize cognitive alignment and collaboration are discussed.

TI The double-edged sword effect of distributed leadership on the emergence
   of informal leadership among university faculty teams in mainland China
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Distributed leadership; Team cohesion; Informal leadership; Diffusion of
   responsibility; Team trust
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; ORGANIZATIONAL COMMITMENT; SELF-MANAGEMENT; ROLE
   AMBIGUITY; ROLE-CONFLICT; TRUST; PERFORMANCE; ANTECEDENTS; ACHIEVEMENT;
   ONTOLOGY
AB As educational environments become increasingly complex, traditional leader-centered models are insufficient to meet the diverse leadership needs of contemporary academic teams. Distributed leadership has emerged as a promising alternative, but its dual impact remains underexplored. This study examines how distributed leadership influences team cohesion, diffusion of responsibility, and the emergence of informal leadership in higher education faculty teams. Using a two-wave, multilevel survey design, data from 1031 faculty members across 162 teams were analyzed. The results show that distributed leadership enhances team cohesion while also leading to diffusion of responsibility. Notably, team trust moderates these effects, strengthening the positive outcomes and mitigating the negative ones. By positioning responsibility structuring as the mechanism linking leadership distribution to emergent influence, this study moves beyond assumptions that participation alone fosters leadership. The findings advance a structurally contingent view of distributed leadership and extend leadership emergence theory within professional organizational contexts.

AB Preserving special education (SE) teachers' wellbeing and psychological needs has become a challenge in the last decade. TI What drives and drains teachers in Taiwan? Exploring the motivational
   roots of job satisfaction through stress pathways
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher motivation; Teacher stress; Job satisfaction; Self-determination
   theory
ID WORK ENGAGEMENT; BURNOUT; RESOURCES; DEMANDS; MODEL
AB We examine how teacher motivation types are associated with job satisfaction directly and indirectly through stress-related factors. Using cross-sectional data from the 2018 Teaching and Learning International Survey in Taiwan and drawing on self-determination theory, we differentiate between personal utility, social utility, and value-based intrinsic motivation. Structural equation modeling of a sample of 3598 junior high school teachers reveals that job satisfaction is positively associated with all three motivation types and negatively associated with high perceived workload and frequent student behavior stress. Additionally, teacher motivations are indirectly associated with job satisfaction: personal utility motivation is linked to lower satisfaction through heightened student behavior stress, whereas social utility and value-based intrinsic motivations are associated with higher satisfaction through lower stressors. Overall, job stress partially mediates between motivation and satisfaction. Intrinsic and altruistic motives may relate to lower stress levels and higher job satisfaction, providing insights for supporting teacher well-being and retention.

TI Are business simulation games just entertainment? Examining the links
   between instructional configurations, perceived instructional breadth,
   and students' flow experience
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Business simulation games; Instructional configuration; Flow experience;
   Perceived instructional breadth; Teachers' role
ID INTENTION; COMPUTER; IMPACT; TEACHERS; TAIWAN
AB As entrepreneurship education increasingly values experiential learning, business simulation games (BSGs) are widely used in higher education. However, when games overemphasize game elements, students may perceive a shallow integration of underlying knowledge. Drawing on teaching presence theory, we examine associations between two distinct BSGs' instructional configurations (competitor configuration vs. instructor configuration) and students' perceived instructional breadth, and how this perceived instructional breadth correlates with students' flow experience. We conducted an experiment to compare the flow experience of 216 business students across two distinct instructional configurations: a competitor configuration (teachers acted as competitors and delivered instruction via their own real-time firm data) and a traditional instructor configuration (teachers served as non-participating instructors and delivered instruction using student team firm data). The results suggest that (1) students perceived significantly broader instructional breadth in the competitor configuration than in the instructor configuration; (2) this perceived breadth is positively associated with students' flow experience; and (3) students' perception of instructional breadth mediates the observed association between instructional configuration and flow experience. Our study offers teachers a practical framework for shifting roles and enhancing students' perceived instructional breadth in game-based learning, while also enriching the application of teaching presence theory to BSGs.

TI Collective collapse and the paradox of resource: A latent transition
   analysis of burnout profiles among South Korean elementary school
   teachers
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher burnout; Collective collapse; Paradox of resources;
   Socio-institutional context; Latent transition analysis
ID STRESSORS; SELF; IMPACT
AB This study examined burnout dynamics among South Korean elementary school teachers using longitudinal data (2021-2024). Latent Profile Analysis identified three stable groups-Low, Moderate, and High Burnout-where burnout levels were inversely linked to engagement. Latent Transition Analysis revealed a collective collapse, marked by a precipitous shift from low to high-burnout profiles, followed by stagnation. These findings suggest burnout could be a dynamic state responsive to macro-social shifts rather than a fixed individual trait. Earlycareer status and interpersonal stress significantly hindered recovery. Notably, teacher efficacy exhibited state-dependent effects; while generally protective, it exacerbated strain for already-burned-out teachers, indicating a resource paradox. These results emphasize that teacher burnout stems from complex socio-institutional interactions, necessitating longitudinal monitoring and systemic interventions that consider the psychological state of teachers and the broader policy environment to prevent chronic stagnation.

TI Queering STEM classrooms: Exploring queer literacy and perceptions of
   relevance among pre-service teachers
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pre-service teachers; STEM education; Queer literacy; Queer theory;
   Inclusive education
ID HETERONORMATIVITY; EXPERIENCES; ORIENTATION; EQUITY; SCHOOL; YOUTH
AB With nearly 17% of Generation Z worldwide identifying as queer, creating inclusive educational spaces is highly important. While STEM is often viewed as neutral, identity-sensitive environments are especially crucial here. Grounded in Queer Theory and guided by existing frameworks for queer-inclusive teaching, this exploratory qualitative study examines queer literacy among eight pre-service STEM teachers at a German university. TI Implementation of curricular track programs at a college of pharmacy
   over a 15-year period
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE College of pharmacy; Concentration; Elective track; Curricular track;
   Curricula
ID DOCTOR
AB Purpose: To describe the history and evolution of our elective track programs and overall lessons learned and to identify the percentage of University of Oklahoma College of Pharmacy (OUCOP) graduates who completed a curricular track in ambulatory care, leadership, nuclear pharmacy, pediatrics, or research. Educational activity: The OUCOP curricular track programs were established in 2011 and require 16 h of didactic coursework and advanced pharmacy practice experiences. Most [198/377 (52.5%)] completed the leadership curricular track program. Summary: One-third of OUCOP graduates from 2011 to 2025 completed a curricular track program. Graduates pursued a variety of initial positions following graduation with a significantly higher number of OUCOP graduates completing a post-graduate education or residency position.

AB Understanding the factors underlying business success is essential for comprehending aspects that mitigate business failure, crucial for the economic development of countries. TI Silos to synergy: Developing collaborative scholarship theme teams for
   pharmacy faculty
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Faculty; Scholarship; SoTL; Theme team; Community of practice
AB Communities of Practice (CoPs) offer a powerful framework for advancing faculty collaboration, professional identity formation, and the scholarship of teaching and learning (SoTL) in higher education. This article describes the design, implementation, and evolution of the Teaching, Learning, and Student Success (TLSS) Theme Team, a context-specific CoP established within the University of Tennessee Health Science Center College of Pharmacy to promote innovation in teaching and educational scholarship. The TLSS Theme Team was created to enhance collaboration across departments and campuses, mentor junior faculty, and align SoTL initiatives with institutional priorities. Guided by the core CoP constructs of domain, community, and practice, the team functions through shared goals, structured meetings, and dissemination of scholarly work. Key features include voluntary membership, rotating leadership, and minimal resource requirements supported by modest institutional funding. Activities such as quarterly meetings, annual retreats, and internal seed grants foster engagement, accountability, and shared productivity. Outcomes include increased collaboration, development of educational research skills, and scholarly dissemination. Implementation of the theme team was associated with increased crossdisciplinary collaboration, new joint projects, and an increase in scholarly publications over five years. This model demonstrates a feasible, scalable, and cost-effective approach to fostering SoTL and faculty development within pharmacy education. The theme team framework may be adapted by other institutions seeking to strengthen scholarly collaboration, align faculty development with accreditation and institutional goals, and build enduring cultures of teaching excellence and innovation.

TI Mapping entrepreneurship education for mindset development: A decade of
   bibliometric and thematic analysis
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrepreneurship education; Entrepreneurial mindset; Pedagogical
   approaches; Technology integration; Sustainable entrepreneurial
   intentions
ID INTENTION; FUTURE; STUDENTS; IMPACT; LIES
AB This paper provides an integrative bibliometric and systematic review of Entrepreneurship Education with a specific focus on developing the Entrepreneurial Mindset at the tertiary level. This study employs Bibliometrix (R) and VOS viewer to visualise intellectual structures, thematic clusters, and collaboration networks based on Scopus-indexed articles from 2015 to 2025. The mapped primary dimensions are Entrepreneurial Mindset, Entrepreneurial Intention, Pedagogical Innovation, Technology Integration, and Sustainable Development. A complementary systematic review strengthens bibliometric results by linking theoretical foundations to empirical evidence. However, strong gaps persist: Entrepreneurship Education's Artificial Intelligence is under-theorised, and longitudinal and mixed-method research is limited. These shortcomings reflect the danger of fragmentation in the psychological, pedagogical, and technological spheres. Through conceptual synthesis and thematic analysis, the research suggests a multi-disciplinary model that synthesises psychology, pedagogy, and digital change. The model brings theoretical refinement to the Entrepreneurial Mindset while providing solutions for curriculum developers, teachers, and policymakers on how to develop innovative, inclusive, and sustainability-focused Entrepreneurship Education models. This review adds to the scholarship on Entrepreneurship Education by crossing disciplinary boundaries and relating education to international priorities.

DT Article

   profiles; Formative assessment; Primary mathematics
ID QUALITATIVE DATA; DATA LITERACY; MIXED-METHODS
AB This study analyzes how teachers utilize student data from an assessment tool called "Diagnostico Integral de Aprendizajes" to make decisions in the classroom. The study's sample comprises 17 teachers from 17 public schools and their 220 fourth-grade students. Cluster analysis was employed to identify three data-based decision profiles: (1) systematic, needs-focused adaptation; (2) reactive adjustments with concerns about report clarity and alignment; and (3) innovation-oriented responses emphasizing broader mathematical competencies. Moreover, the study provides international perspectives on how systemic reporting characteristics serve as catalysts or barriers to effective data use.

TI Cognitive and behavioral engagement in online teacher professional
   development: The role of teacher characteristics and learning
   opportunities
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Online teacher professional development; Teacher engagement; Cognitive
   engagement; Behavioral engagement; Learning opportunities; Teacher
   characteristics
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; SCHOOL; VIDEO; CURRICULUM; EDUCATION; COMMUNITIES;
   TECHNOLOGY; FRAMEWORK; IMPACT; STATE
AB Designing adaptive online teacher professional development (oTPD) requires an understanding of how both teacher characteristics and the nature of learning opportunities shape teacher engagement. While indicators of behavioral engagement (e.g., time spent) have received some attention, cognitive engagement-how deeply teachers process and reflect on learning opportunities-remains underexplored. This study investigates both behavioral and cognitive engagement across three types of learning opportunities (theoretical input, planning material, representations of practice) among N = 125 in-service teachers. Results indicate that aspects of behavioral engagement were only weakly related to cognitive engagement, and for some types of learning opportunities, not at all. In addition to prior knowledge, individual beliefs and perceived time resources emerged as relevant predictors of engagement. These findings highlight the importance of considering teachers' cognitive engagement more systematically in oTPD design and research.

SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Expectancy-value theory; Cost; Motivational profiles; Teacher
   professional development; Self-regulated learning
ID SCHOOL; MOTIVATION
AB This study explores teachers' expectancies for success, subjective values, and four dimensions of the perceived costs of integrating professional development into their teaching practice to support students' self-regulated learning (SRL). TI Teaching under scrutiny: Social studies teachers' negotiation,
   resistance and fatigue with early anti-critical race theory resolutions
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
AB Since 2021, anti-CRT legislation has proliferated across the United States, creating new pressures for teachers navigating discussions of race and inequality. This qualitative study examines how Georgia's anti-CRT resolution influenced two first-year social studies teachers during the 2021-2022 school year. Using trans-formative teacher professionalism as a theoretical framework, we analyzed data from four semi-structured interviews to understand how these policies affected teachers' willingness to discuss "divisive" topics and their professional identity. Findings reveal that both teachers modified their practice in response to the resolution-one retreating significantly due to administrative non-support and parental complaints, the other resisting more actively while strategically avoiding "conspicuous language." Regardless of approach, both experienced the resolution as a threat to their equity-oriented professional identity and their ability to prepare students for democratic citizenship. These findings suggest anti-CRT policies actively suppress transformative professionalism and may exacerbate challenges facing new teachers.

TI Digital mentor paradox: Transforming algorithmic anxiety into
   professional growth through AI-scaffolded pedagogical reasoning and
   identity
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI in teacher education; Pedagogical reasoning; Digital
   professional identity; Challenge-hindrance stressor framework; SQD
   strategies; Future teaching competence
ID PRESERVICE TEACHERS; TECHNOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE; FRAMEWORK; EDUCATION
AB The rapid integration of generative AI necessitates reconfiguring teacher preparation models. This research conceptualizes AI agents as "digital mentors" that instantiate Synthesized Qualitative Data strategies to foster professional growth. Integrating a cross-national experiment (N = 450), randomized controlled trial (N = 200), and field survey (N = 300), this study examines how AI support is associated with future teaching competence through pedagogical reasoning and digital identity. Results indicate that high-quality AI support predicts enhanced competence through deepened reasoning and consolidated identity. Crucially, the analysis reveals a "digital mentor paradox": algorithmic anxiety amplifies, rather than attenuates, the positive association between support and developmental outcomes when structured scaffolding is present. Under adequate scaffolding, anxiety functions as a challenge stressor that is associated with enhanced engagement. These findings advance the theory of human-AI teaming, illustrating how psychological tensions may drive expertise development in the digital era.

TI Effects of stem activities in virtual reality environments on preservice
   teachers' technological pedagogical content knowledge and technology
   acceptance
SO INTERNET AND HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE STEM; Virtual reality; Technological pedagogical content knowledge;
   (TPACK); Technology acceptance model (TAM); Teacher education
ID EDUCATION; TPACK; VALIDATION
AB Innovative technological tools such as virtual reality have the potential to transform educational practice. However, the complex ways in which teachers relate to innovative technologies remain under-investigated. This study examined how the technological pedagogical content knowledge (TPACK) and technology acceptance (TAM) of Finnish and Turkish preservice teachers are influenced by their participation in STEM activities in virtual reality environments. A convergent mixed-methods design was used, combining quantitative nonparametric tests conducted with TPACK and TAM scales and qualitative content analysis of participants' responses to open-ended questions. TI Teacher identity negotiation in AI-enhanced higher education and its
   implications for professional development
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Language teacher identity (LTI); Community of practice (CoP); Artificial
   intelligence (AI); Affective; Professional development
AB Although artificial intelligence (AI) has profoundly transformed educational contexts, its influence on educators' professional identity negotiation remains underexplored. This study investigates how university English teachers in China negotiate their language teacher identity (LTI) in the age of AI. Drawing on a tri-level ecosystem model informed by Communities of Practice (CoP), this narrative inquiry with 11 university language teachers reveals a dynamic identity negotiation process shaped by a distinctive affective arc. The study proposes an integrated framework linking policy, community mediation, and identity transformation, offering implications for teacher education and professional development.

TI Development, implementation, and evaluation of the elective course
   "Holistic Marketing in Pharmacy"
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Holistic marketing; Higher pharmaceutical education; Elective course;
   Soft skills; Educational process; Master's students in pharmacy
AB This article presents the development, implementation, and evaluation of the elective course "Holistic Marketing in Pharmacy" as part of the professional training for master's students in pharmacy. Developed in accordance with Ukrainian higher education standards, the course comprises 90 academic hours (3 ECTS credits) and was created in alignment with student preferences, informed by a survey of 71 participants. The results indicate a strong interest among students in topics such as continuous professional development, customer experience, stakeholder relationship management, leadership, and soft skills, including teamwork, critical thinking, and time management. The course was piloted at the Department of Organisation and Economy of Pharmacy at Bogomolets National Medical University. Following its completion, the share of students who rated the course as highly relevant to their future professional practice increased by 11.2%, and 93% of students expressed a willingness to recommend it to peers.

TI Positioning the teacher as consultant: Metaphorical understandings of
   special education consultation
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Special education teacher; Educational consultation; Metaphor analysis;
   Finland
ID INCLUSIVE EDUCATION; GENERAL-EDUCATION; STUDENTS; PERSPECTIVES;
   PARTNERSHIPS; FRAMEWORK; IDENTITY; INCREASE; BELIEFS; VOICES
AB Special education consultation aims to support class and subject teachers in meeting diverse learning needs in inclusive classrooms. It is one of the commonly used forms of teacher collaboration in schools. This qualitative study examines the meanings that special education teachers (SET) attribute to their consultative work through metaphorical expressions. The research data consisted of interviews with 16 Finnish SETs and were analysed using metaphor analysis. As a result, we identified seven metaphor categories that position consultative SETs in various roles: 1) a street-credible expert, 2) a social chameleon, 3) a peacemaker, 4) a team player, 5) an outspoken influencer, 6) a prisoner of circumstances, and 7) a miracle-worker. These metaphors portray special education consultation as interactionally demanding and context-dependent work, centred more on relationships than on the sharing of pedagogical content knowledge.

TI Investigating students' learning effectiveness and success on business
   process analysis via mobile games: A formative assessment perspective
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Mobile game-based learning; Formative assessment; ARCS motivation model;
   Perceived learning effectiveness; Learning success
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; PERFORMANCE; MOTIVATION; FEEDBACK; ONLINE; NEEDS
AB Formative assessments have been constantly utilized in e-learning environments to enhance students' learning motivation and effectiveness. However, there exist insufficient studies that have considered the impact of formative assessments on students' learning motivation, which is evaluated using the framework of four motivational dimensions of attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction (ARCS), perceived learning effectiveness, and learning success. The current investigation developed mobile game-based learning (MGBL) systems to investigate how formative assessments affect the ARCS motivational factors, students' perceived learning effectiveness, and learning success. Data were collected from 119 undergraduate students who were recruited to use the MGBL application designed for this study. A quasi-experiment was conducted to examine how different levels of formative assessments may influence students' motivation, thus affecting perceived learning effectiveness and learning success. The results show that the formative assessment of MGBL systems significantly affects students' perceived learning effectiveness and learning success (i.e., the computed normalized difference score) via the ARCS motivational factors of attention, confidence, and satisfaction rather than relevance. The results of the present work suggest that formative assessment of MGBL systems plays a critical role in improving the ARCS model of motivation among students, which could benefit instructors' teaching designs and learning procedures.

TI Digital literacy and scientific research ability among nursing
   postgraduates: The chain-mediating role of deep learning and research
   self-efficacy
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital literacy; Deep learning; Research self-efficacy; Perceived
   research competence; Nursing postgraduates
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION; ASSOCIATION; STRATEGIES; STUDENTS; OUTCOMES; MODELS;
   ONLINE
AB Background: In the era of rapid digital transformation, it is crucial to cultivate research competence among nursing postgraduates to support innovation in nursing science and strengthen the overall competitiveness of the profession. However, limited attention has been given to how digital literacy is associated with perceived (selfreported) research competence and whether this association can be statistically accounted for by deep learning and research self-efficacy. Objectives: This study examined the association between digital literacy and perceived research competence among nursing postgraduates and estimated indirect effect (statistical) pathways through deep learning and research self-efficacy in a hypothesized serial (chain) mediation model. Design: A cross-sectional study design was utilized. Settings: This multi-center study was carried out at eight universities located in three Chinese provinces: Anhui, Jiangsu, and Sichuan. Participants: Eligible nursing postgraduates from the aforementioned universities were recruited during the period of June to July 2025. Methods: Data were collected using the Digital Literacy Scale, the Deep Learning Scale, the Research Self-Efficacy Scale, and the Research Competence Scale (self-reported perceived competence). Descriptive statistics, Pearson's correlation analysis, and serial mediation analyses were conducted using SPSS version 26.0 and the PROCESS macro (version 3.5). Results: The mean score for perceived research competence among nursing postgraduates was 39.88 +/- 8.10 points. The mean scores for digital literacy, deep learning, and research self-efficacy were 85.37 +/- 11.44, 40.54 +/- 6.64, and 18.34 +/- 3.46 points, respectively. Perceived research competence was significantly and positively correlated with digital literacy (r = 0.598, p < 0.001), deep learning (r = 0.549, p < 0.001), and research selfefficacy (r = 0.523, p < 0.001). Serial mediation analysis (PROCESS Model 6) yielded statistically significant indirect effect estimates through deep learning (21.71%), through research self-efficacy (15.33%), and through the serial pathway involving both mediators (7.60%). Across pathways, the total indirect effect estimate accounted for 44.58% of the total association estimate, whereas the direct effect estimate accounted for 55.42%, suggesting that digital literacy is linked to perceived research competence largely through direct research-related digital behaviors while a substantial proportion is statistically accounted for by deep learning and research selfefficacy. Conclusions: The findings are consistent with a model in which higher digital literacy is associated with higher levels of deep learning and research self-efficacy, which in turn are associated with higher perceived research competence. Given the cross-sectional, self-report design, the serial mediation model should be interpreted as a statistical decomposition of contemporaneous associations rather than evidence of temporal ordering or causal relationships. Importantly, the outcome reflects perceived (self-reported) competence and was not corroborated by objective performance indicators (e.g., publications, project outputs, or externally assessed research skills). Nursing education institutions may consider integrating digital literacy training, deep learning-oriented pedagogy, and supports for research self-efficacy into postgraduate curricula, while evaluating their causal impacts and objective outcomes in longitudinal or intervention studies.
   The generalisability of these findings may be limited because participants were recruited from eight universities in three provinces; replication in more diverse regions and institution types (including less-resourced settings) is warranted.

TI Undergraduate nursing students' perceptions of using holopatient in
   learning and clinical training: An exploratory-descriptive qualitative
   study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Simulation training; Mixed reality; Qualitative research; Saudi Arabia;
   Students, nursing; Education, nursing
AB Background: Simulation-based education is central to nursing curricula, supporting clinical reasoning, confidence, and safe practice. Mixed reality (MR) applications such as HoloPatient provide immersive, life-sized patient encounters that may enhance student learning. Although international evidence highlights benefits in knowledge acquisition, critical thinking, and confidence, research in Saudi Arabia remains limited. Objective: This study aimed to explore undergraduate nursing students' perceptions of HoloPatient, focusing on its educational value, challenges, and ethical considerations within the Saudi context. Methods: An exploratory-descriptive qualitative design was employed. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 32 nursing students (second to internship years) at the University of Tabuk, Saudi Arabia (mean age 21.8 years; 56.3% female). Participants were purposively sampled to capture diversity in year, gender, language, and HoloPatient use. Data collection occurred through 45-60 min interviews in Arabic or English, audiorecorded, transcribed, and translated. Reflexive thematic analysis was applied, guided by the Technology Acceptance Model, using NVivo software. Results: Students identified key benefits: enhanced clinical reasoning (81.3%), increased confidence and readiness (65.6%), and realism and engagement (59.4%). Challenges included technical constraints (56.3%), ergonomic discomfort (37.5%), and limited device availability (28.1%). Ethical concerns centered on over-reliance on technology (46.9%), academic integrity (40.6%), and privacy/professionalism (34.4%). Training needs included structured debriefing (75.0%) and device orientation (62.5%). Conclusion: Findings highlight both opportunities and barriers to integrating MR in nursing education. While HoloPatient strengthened reasoning, confidence, and engagement, implementation challenges and ethical concerns require careful attention. Structured debriefing, comprehensive orientation, faculty development, and robust technical support are critical to maximise educational value. In Saudi Arabia, these insights provide timely guidance for aligning MR adoption with national strategies for digital transformation in education.

AB This article explores pre-service teachers' (PST) life stories in the context of identities and professional development. TI Exploring pharmacy professionals insights for advancing the pharmacy
   curriculum: A qualitative study
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING

AB Objective: To explore the gaps, needs, and priorities in the pharmacy curriculum of Pakistan and synthesize pharmacy professionals' perspectives to develop evidence-based recommendations for curriculum updating. Methods: A qualitative study conducting semi-structured face-to-face interviews with 23 registered pharmacy professionals in Pakistan, consisting of academicians, hospital and clinical pharmacists, regulatory authorities, and industrial pharmacists, was carried out from November 2024 to March 2025. The interviews were inductively coded and analyzed to generate themes and report on persistent trends with emerging patterns. Conclusion: Urgent and continuous pharmacy curriculum reform is needed in Pakistan. Realigning the curriculum toward a competency-based, practically focused, and globally standardized approach is crucial for preparing pharmacists for advanced clinical, analytical, and leadership roles in modern healthcare settings.

TI Analysing the professional identity and discursive positioning of
   English language teacher educators
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Positioning theory; Teacher educators; Grammar of agency; Teacher
   educator identity; TEFL/TESOL teacher education
ID AGENCY
AB Despite growing recognition of the critical role teacher educators (TEs) play in shaping preservice teachers' (PSTs) professional learning, limited research has examined how TEs position themselves and PSTs through discourse. This study investigates how TEs in Chile construct professional identity through their self-positioning and positioning of PSTs. Drawing on positioning theory, we analyzed interviews and narrative frames from eight TEs. TI When "past" meets "present": Effects of preservice teachers' initial
   career choices and current plans on teaching values, self-efficacy, and
   person-vocation fit
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Career choice; Teaching motivation; Teaching self-efficacy;
   Person-vocation fit; Mixed methods; Interaction analysis; Thematic
   analysis
AB This mixed-methods study examined how preservice teachers' career choices may change during training and their associations with teaching motivation, including utility values, self-efficacy, and person-vocation fit. Results from structural equation modeling analysis with 1,143 survey responses, followed by 14 interviews, identified four teacher profiles with distinct motivational patterns: committed teachers, reconsidering teachers, emerging teachers, and consistently non-teachers. The results indicate a significant interaction between initial career choice and current career plans, showing that preservice teachers with committed career plans reported high utility values and a strong perceived fit in teaching. Conversely, those who had initially aspired to teach but later reconsidered their teaching path exhibited the lowest levels of utility values and perceived fit. The findings imply that the teacher education program plays a crucial role in developing strategies to enhance preservice teachers' motivation and strengthen their commitment to teaching careers.

TI Why pre-service teachers do not use social media for professional
   purposes: A mixed-methods study using the will-skill-tool framework
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Social media; Teacher education; Teacher professional development;
   Informal learning; Reasons for non-use; Will-skill-tool; Mixed methods
ID PEER SUPPORT; TWITTER; MODEL; NETWORK
AB Social media can support teachers' informal professional learning, yet professional non-use remains under-examined. This mixed-methods study investigates pre-service teachers' non-use of social media for professional purposes using the Will-Skill-Tool (WST) framework. In a cross-sectional survey of 147 pre-service teachers, users and non-users are compared on motivation, perceived relevance, and self-assessed skill. A MANOVA indicates significant group differences, with users scoring higher across all WST dimensions; differences are strongest for Will (motivation and relevance). Open-ended responses from non-users are coded into eight reason categories. The most frequent reasons are maintaining boundaries between private and professional life and perceiving no added professional value. Additional reasons include exclusive private use, lack of prior professional use without a specific reason, limited knowledge of professional use, self-protection, time/technical constraints, and privacy/legal concerns. Findings suggest teacher education should offer low-threshold, critically guided opportunities to explore professional social media use while respecting deliberate non-use.

TI Career development barriers encountered by Taiwanese pharmacy students:
   A qualitative study across levels of career adaptability
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; Career barriers; Career adaptability; Qualitative
   study; Taiwan
ID ADAPT-ABILITIES SCALE; ASIAN-AMERICAN; SELF-EFFICACY; CONSTRUCTION
AB Background: Career development is critical in pharmacy education; however, many students encounter personal, academic, and structural obstacles that complicate their career decision-making and professional identity formation. Although researchers have investigated students' career adaptability, limited attention has been given to specific barriers faced by pharmacy students in Asian contexts, particularly the barriers embedded within cultural expectations and curricular structures. Methods: This qualitative study examined career development barriers perceived by Taiwanese third-year pharmacy students. A total of 12 students were recruited through purposive sampling, with equal numbers of students with high and low career adaptability, as identified in a previous quantitative phase. Semi-structured interviews were conducted, audio-recorded, and transcribed verbatim in Chinese. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis. To ensure trustworthiness, we performed independent coding, peer debriefing, member checking, and an audit trail. Results: Twelve career barrier dimensions were identified: lack of clear direction, low confidence, learning interference, lack of persistence, developmental barriers, low willpower, hesitation, distress regarding academic major, decision-making interference, interpersonal relationships, financial issues, and curriculum design. The students with low adaptability tended to internalize difficulties as personal inadequacies and exhibited greater indecision, whereas those with high adaptability reframed obstacles as manageable challenges and employed proactive coping strategies. Conclusions: Pharmacy students' career barriers stem from intertwined personal, interpersonal, and structural factors shaped by cultural norms and curricular design. Addressing these obstacles, through earlier career exposure, improved curriculum pacing, financial and psychosocial support, and targeted adaptability-building interventions, may enhance students' readiness for career decision-making and improve their professional identity development.

TI Designing educational architectures for global competence: Evidence from
   four Internationalisation-at-home contexts in business schools
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Global competence; Educational architecture; Internationalization at
   home; Business education; Management curricula; Experiential learning;
   Equity
ID MANAGEMENT
AB This study investigates how four distinct educational architectures in business and management education produce different outcomes in students' global competence within Internationalizationat-Home settings. Employing a cross-sectional quasi-experimental design, data were collected from 421 business students across five institutions in Northern Europe and East Asia. Participants experienced one of four architectural designs, systematically varied in diversity exposure and experiential intensity: multicultural experiential learning, monocultural experiential learning, lecture-based instruction, and a minimal-exposure orientation. Six global competence dimensions-including four competencies, each with two sub-dimensions for global mindset and communication competence-were measured using validated scales and analyzed using multivariate statistical methods to identify architecture-specific developmental patterns. Findings demonstrate that global competence is not a uniform outcome of international experience but depends on the learning environment's structural design. Monocultural experiential programs produced the strongest gains in self-efficacy, highlighting the role of psychological safety in early competence development. Brief multicultural orientations produced gains in global mindset comparable to those from sustained intercultural programs, challenging the assumption that prolonged physical mobility is necessary. Experiential pedagogies yielded consistent improvements in communication competence, while empathy remained largely stable without structured reflection. This study presents a comparative competence signature model that links specific competencies to particular architectural configurations, providing business schools with actionable guidance for designing equitable and scalable Internationalization-at-Home architectures. These findings enable curriculum designers to make evidence-based decisions that expand access to global competence development without requiring expensive mobility programs, thereby advancing both educational quality and equity in management education while meeting accreditation standards.

TI Embodied learning-driven hospital simulation management training digital
   textbook
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Embodied learning; Digital textbook; Management practical training
AB The digital transformation of education requires new approaches in practice-oriented disciplines like management. To solve the lack of personalized and self-directed learning in existing courses, this conceptual and design-oriented study developed a digital textbook for virtual operations simulation. Guided by embodied learning theory and Kolb's experiential learning model (Kolb, 1984), the textbook adopts a four-stage approach: "Theoretical Preloading - Sandbox Simulation - Reflective Review - Competency Transfer." It integrates a custom virtual simulation and an AIpowered guidance system, such as knowledge bubbles and a virtual teaching assistant, to support "learning by doing, reflecting, and applying." This study explains the textbook's design, architecture, and implementation. It also conceptually discusses its potential role in moving management training from standardized knowledge-sharing to personalized competency development, and proposes future research directions to provide a reference for developing similar digital textbooks. It should be noted that the textbook has not yet been formally implemented in teaching, with empirical verification of its educational effectiveness reserved for future research.

TI Surviving the tsunami of an ageing academic workforce: Mentorship for
   the next generation
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Mentorship; Nursing academia; Workforce sustainability; Succession
   planning; Institutional knowledge loss; Academic retention
ID INTENT; STAY
AB Background: The Australian nursing academic workforce is undergoing a significant demographic shift, characterised by accelerated retirement and departure of senior academics. This trend threatens continuity of mentorship, academic leadership, and institutional knowledge, with potential implications for early- and midcareer nurse academics. Objectives: To explore nurse academics' lived experiences of senior mentorship loss and to examine perceived impacts on induction, workload, role clarity, succession planning, and resilience within a regional university context. Design: A qualitative study informed by a hermeneutic phenomenological orientation, an interpretive approach concerned with understanding meaning derived from lived experience. Methods: Three face-to-face focus groups were conducted with early- and mid-career nurse academics (3 groups; N = 15; n = 5 per group) at a regional Australian university. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke's six-phase analytic process to identify shared patterns of meaning across participants' accounts. Results: Five themes were identified: (1) Loss of Institutional Knowledge and Mentorship; (2) Inadequate Induction and Orientation Processes; (3) Workload Intensification and Role Ambiguity Following Senior Academic Loss; (4) Organisational Gaps in Succession Planning and Communication; and (5) Strategies for Recovery, Retention, and Resilience. Participants described emotional and professional strain associated with mentorship voids, unclear expectations, increased invisible workload, and inconsistent organisational responses during workforce transition. Conclusions: The findings underscore mentorship as a critical element of academic sustainability and highlight limitations in existing induction, workload, and knowledge-transfer systems during periods of senior workforce attrition. Strengthening formalised and integrated mentorship and succession-support mechanisms may assist nursing education leaders to enhance retention, professional identity, and workforce resilience.

TI Learner autonomy driven by (generative) artificial intelligence as a

   tertiary-level language teachers

LA English
DT Article

ID EDUCATION
AB Motivated by debates about teachers' roles in (generative) artificial intelligence (Gen) AI-mediated language education and the relative lack of empirical evidence regarding the associated challenges faced by language teachers, this study investigated how learners' (Gen)AI-driven autonomy interacts with mid-career tertiary-level EFL teachers' emotional vulnerabilities and identity tensions. TI AI literacy alone is not enough: Student AI readiness and career
   adaptability in business and management education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence literacy; AI readiness; Career adaptability;
   Management education; Graduate employability
ID USER ACCEPTANCE; EFFICACY
AB Purpose: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in organizational and educational systems, higher education faces increasing pressure to support graduates' adaptability in AI-mediated labor markets. This study examines how AI-related competencies contribute to career adaptability, focusing on AI readiness as a key developmental mechanism linking learning to careerrelevant outcomes. Design/methodology/approach: Survey data were collected from 339 university students enrolled in economics-, management-, and business-related degree programs in Italy and exposed to AIrelated learning activities. A moderated mediation model was employed to analyze the relationships among AI literacy, AI readiness, AI self-efficacy, and career adapt-abilities. Findings: AI readiness mediates the relationship between AI literacy and career adapt-abilities, with the indirect effect varying across levels of AI self-efficacy. AI self-efficacy positively moderates the relationship between AI literacy and AI readiness and shows a direct association with career adapt-abilities, indicating that motivational resources shape how AI-related knowledge becomes career-relevant. Research limitations and implications: The cross-sectional design limits causal inference. Future research could examine the developmental role of AI readiness across professional contexts and over time. Originality/value: The study contributes to management education research by clarifying the distinct roles of AI literacy, AI self-efficacy, and AI readiness in the education-to-work transition, positioning AI readiness as a central mechanism through which AI-related learning supports career adaptability.

TI The occupational well-being of nurse educators, its related challenges,
   stressors and their reduction in work life balance-A systematic
   mixed-methods study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Occupational well-being; Nurse educators; Burnout; Work-Life Balance;
   Mixed-methods systematic review
ID RESILIENCE; BURNOUT
AB Background: Nurse educators play an essential role in shaping future nursing competencies and healthcare quality. However, the occupational demands of their roles often result in high levels of stress and burnout, affecting their well-being, job satisfaction, and retention. Objectives: This systematic mixed-methods review aimed to explore nurse educators' occupational well-being, identify associated challenges and stressors, and evaluate strategies to enhance their professional quality of life and retention. Design: A systematic mixed-methods review was conducted, integrating quantitative and qualitative evidence in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Methods: Data were collected from six databases: CINAHL, PubMed, ERIC, PsycINFO, SCOPUS, and Web of Science. Studies from 2014 onwards examining nurse educators' occupational well-being were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT), with a convergent integrated approach for data analysis. Results: Of the 850 records retrieved, 14 studies met the inclusion and quality criteria. Key findings highlighted factors contributing to occupational stress and burnout, including workload pressures, dual responsibilities (teaching and clinical practice), emotional labour, and insufficient institutional support. Effective strategies identified for enhancing occupational well-being encompassed mindfulness and resilience training, improved workplace engagement, supportive leadership, and a positive work culture. Conclusions: Addressing nurse educators' occupational well-being is critical for sustaining a competent and stable nursing education workforce. Implementing targeted interventions to manage workloads, foster resilience, and enhance institutional support can significantly reduce burnout, increase job satisfaction, and improve retention rates among nurse educators.

TI Emotional experiences of English language teachers in the age of
   generative AI
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Emotional experiences; GenAI; EFL teachers; Control-value theory;
   Language education
AB This study explored the emotional experiences of English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers using generative AI (GenAI) tools in classroom instruction. Twenty-five teachers (11 frequent, 14 infrequent users) participated. Data analysis, guided by Pekrun's (2024) Control-Value Theory (CVT), examined how emotions were shaped by perceived competence and the pedagogical value of GenAI tools. Frequent users reported mainly positive emotions (excitement, happiness, confidence), but also anxiety and confusion over implementation. Infrequent users expressed a narrower, more negative range (mistrust, worry, guilt) which reflects lower perceived control and value. Both groups showed curiosity and interest in AI which highlights the need to address emotional hesitancy alongside technical barriers. The study concludes that teachers' emotional experiences and adaptation are central to effective AI integration and recommends tailored emotional and pedagogical support to foster confidence, awareness, ethical, and sustainable AI use in teaching.
