TI Kakemongen MapuMew (The Other Forms of Life): Translationof the Periodic
   Table of Elements into Mapudungun
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Periodic Table; Mapudungun; IndigenousLanguages; Intercultural
   Education; Chemistry Education; Translation
AB This paper presents a systematic translation of the periodic table of chemical elements into Mapudungun, the language of the Mapuche people of Chile. The periodic table is a foundational tool in chemical education, yet for Indigenous students, the exclusively Western framing of its content can create epistemological barriers. This work develops Mapudungun names for the elements of the periodic table, including individual translations for elements 1-89 and the lanthanide series, and a family level translation for the actinide series, using a set of translation criteria that combine etymology, observable qualities, practical uses, historical context, and connection to Mapuche culture. The translation was culturally validated by Mapuche researchers and educators, cross-referencing proposed terms with oral traditions and established Mapudungun dictionaries. Through examples such as hydrogen (Choyukey Ko, "where water is permanently born") and bismuth (Relmu Panilwe, "metal of the rainbow"), we illustrate how the translated names ground chemical concepts in Mapuche epistemology. This work represents a linguistic and theoretical proposal that could serve as a foundation for future intercultural chemistry curricula. Potential pedagogical benefits, including improved comprehension, strengthened cultural identity, and more equitable dialogue between knowledge systems, remain hypotheses for future classroom research.

TI Preparing theNext-generation Chemistry Students forSystems Thinking:
   Bridging Secondary and Higher Education
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Systems thinking; conceptual modeling; secondaryeducation; chemistry
   education
ID SYSTEMS THINKING; SCIENCE; INQUIRY; COMPLEXITY
AB Systems thinking emphasizes the analysis of the interconnectedness of system components and processes, making it particularly useful for addressing 21st-century challenges. However, the question is When should we prepare the next-generation students for systems thinking skills? This work started with the anticipation that engaging students with societal challenges in secondary education will make their learning experience meaningful and may enhance their motivation toward contributing to solving them. We developed a set of learning materials and investigated if conceptual modeling can be used as a tool to support students in developing systems thinking skills. The research was carried out with 156 students (eighth and ninth grade at the Dutch VWO-4 and VWO-5 levels) of four secondary schools. We used questionnaires and semistructured interviews to demonstrate that the learning materials could indeed support students' individual development of conceptual models. In addition, both students and teachers praised that the learning materials stimulated a collaborative learning environment for structuring ideas. Our results suggest that systems thinking skills can already be applied in practice, even without specific prior training, as the development of conceptual models implicitly requires systems thinking. Overall, the learning materials developed in this work could be broadly applicable to many educational settings and we envision that they enable the increase in teachers' involvement in innovating education and students' engagement in science, preparing the next-generation researchers for systems thinking.

TI Bridging Observation and Explanation: Scientific Writingas Epistemic
   Practice in Biochemistry Laboratory Education
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Biochemistry; Laboratory Instruction; ScienceCommunication; Chemical
   Education; Pedagogy
ID INQUIRY
AB Laboratory reports serve as critical tools for assessing students' ability to engage in scientific discourse. This study examines how allied health students construct written descriptions of biochemical phenomena in laboratory settings, with a particular focus on their ability to observe, describe, and conceptually explain experimental outcomes. We analyzed 320 lab reports using a rubric evaluating clarity, accuracy, and depth. We found that while students performed moderately well in presenting observable features, their ability to connect observations to theoretical concepts remained underdeveloped. Drawing on insights from science education, language theory, and cognitive psychology, we argue that challenges in descriptive writing reflect deeper issues in conceptual understanding and disciplinary discourse. Instructional interventions are proposed to bridge these gaps, including scaffolding, conceptual framing, and formative feedback. Findings inform the design of laboratory courses that prepare future health professionals for the precision and reasoning demanded in clinical communication. This study contributes to understanding the language demands of scientific communication and emphasizes the need to align writing instruction with epistemological goals of science learning.

TI The COVID-19Pandemic and Ph.D. Students in the ChemicalSciences:
   Influences on Degree Completion and Commitment to the Field
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Graduate Education; Graduate Students; COVID-19; Career Commitment
AB Using survey data collected by the American Chemical Society (ACS), this paper examines the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on doctoral students' plans to complete their degree, stay in the field, and pursue postdoctoral study. Two research designs are used: a cross-sectional design, using data from 2022 and a trend analysis examining changes from 2013 to 2022. Almost all students were negatively impacted by the pandemic, especially regarding mental health; and issues persisted two years after the pandemic started. Students who experienced more severe personal impacts of the pandemic were significantly less likely to believe that they would finish the Ph.D. or stay in the chemical sciences. Starting in 2013 the likelihood that students would finish their degree declined significantly, but the decline was significantly greater during the pandemic. There were also significant declines in the percentage of students planning to pursue postdoctoral studies.

TI Learning Synthesisand Property Measurements of NanoporousMetal-Organic
   Framework ZIF-8
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Third-Year Undergraduate/General; Analytical Chemistry; Distance
   Learning/Self Instruction; Solid State Chemistry; Crystals;
   Organometallics; X-ray Crystallography; Raman Spectroscopy
ID ZEOLITIC IMIDAZOLATE FRAMEWORK; WATER-BASED SYNTHESIS; ASSISTED
   SYNTHESIS; ADSORPTION; CHEMISTRY
AB This laboratory module is designed for upper-division undergraduate students enrolled in an applied physical chemistry course and integrates the synthesis, multitechnique structural characterization, and adsorption-based evaluation of zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) within a three-week module. Students prepare ZIF-8 using a water-based synthesis protocol at ambient temperature and pressure, replacing dimethylformamide, and other hazardous organic solvents commonly employed in metal-organic framework (MOF) synthesis. They then characterize the synthesized ZIF-8 using scanning electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and Raman spectroscopy and analyze thermogravimetric analysis, N2 sorption, and CO2 sorption datasets to evaluate thermal stability, microporosity, and adsorption-based structure-property relationships. Student learning outcomes are assessed through performance-based assignments, supervised laboratory activities, interviews, and a self-diagnostic questionnaire. Through this connected workflow, students gain hands-on experience in MOF synthesis and characterization, develop quantitative data analysis skills, and strengthen their understanding of reticular chemistry, porous materials, and CO2 adsorption behavior.

TI Blinded by Envy, Protected by Identification: How Envy Affects Creative
   Evaluation
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE creativity evaluation; decision making; envy; identification
ID SOCIAL-CONTEXT MODEL; ORGANIZATIONAL IDENTIFICATION; TRANSFORMATIONAL
   LEADERSHIP; INNOVATION; BEHAVIORS; EMPLOYEES; ATTITUDES; JUDGMENT; WORK;
   SIDE
AB Though envy is a commonly experienced emotion in today's fast-paced, competitive workplaces, its influence on how we judge others' outputs in terms of creativity remains largely unexplored. This paper investigates how different types of envy-malicious and benign-impact creative evaluations of ideas. Through three studies (N = 1374) (two pre-registered), we find that benign and malicious envy have divergent effects on creativity evaluation and investment decisions. Specifically, we find that individuals experiencing benign (vs. malicious) envy evaluate ideas generated by an envied target as more creative and subsequently exhibit greater willingness to invest in those ideas (Studies 1 and 2). We find that this effect is driven by personal identification with the envied target: benign (vs. malicious) enviers are more likely to personally identify with the envied target, resulting in higher creative evaluations and increased willingness to invest in the idea (Study 2). Study 3 revealed that higher (vs. lower) organizational identification weakens the negative impact of malicious envy on creative evaluation, which in turn reduces its detrimental effect on investment decisions. These findings shed light on the nuanced dynamics of envy and its impact on creativity evaluation.

TI Revisiting the Four Stages of Creativity: The Role of Metacognition
SO JOURNAL OF CREATIVE BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE creative process; metacognition; self-regulation; standards; Wallas
   model
ID SELF-REGULATION; PERFORMANCE; KNOWLEDGE; FEEDBACK; EDUCATION; INSIGHT;
   EXPERT
AB Wallas' four-stage model has long served as a heuristic for understanding creativity, but contemporary metacognitive theory clarifies the mechanisms within each stage. This article reconceptualizes the model through the lens of metacognition, focusing on the role of knowledge, regulation, and experiences. In the Preparation stage, declarative, procedural, and conditional knowledge guide planning and problem representation. In the Incubation stage, stepping back from effortful processing while remaining open to associations represents a regulatory decision. In the Illumination stage, the sudden "Aha!" moment is best understood as a metacognitive experience that flags a candidate solution and signals further regulation. In the Verification stage, ideas are judged against internalized standards through monitoring, with subsequent regulatory decisions determining whether ideas are pursued, adapted, or discarded. Across stages, transitions are emphasized, and creativity is framed as a dynamic, self-regulatory system. Revisiting Wallas' model in this way highlights that each stage involves distinct forms of knowledge, monitoring, and regulation, offering a more precise account of processes underlying his framework. This perspective yields testable hypotheses about stage-specific regulation and points to interventions, such as explicit instruction and metacognitive feedback, that can strengthen creativity.

TI Identifying Key Gaps: A Qualitative Exploration of
   Physicians-in-Training Caring for Adults With Intellectual and
   Developmental Disabilities
SO JOURNAL OF INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE developmental disability; graduate medical education; intellectual
   disability; qualitative; residency; training
ID MEDICAL-STUDENTS; PEOPLE; ATTITUDES; CARE; INTERVIEWS
AB Background As increasing numbers of individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities (IDD) live into adulthood, they struggle to access high-quality, age-appropriate healthcare. Physicians who feel ill-prepared to care for adults with IDD contribute to worsened access to and quality of care, which can ultimately lead to poorer health outcomes for this population.Objective Investigate physician-in-training perceptions of, experiences with and needs for treating patients with IDD.Methods We conducted qualitative, semistructured interviews with 20 senior resident physicians from five residency programs affiliated with the University of Colorado. We analysed data using thematic content analysis to identify and develop overarching themes.Results Four major themes emerged using thematic content analysis. First, communication challenges decreased resident confidence in the quality of care they provide. Second, residents felt that they did not have adequate skills to treat patients with IDD. Third, residents felt that this population of adults is not within the purview of most of their practice specialties. Lastly, physicians-in-training felt that more exposure to and support in caring for patients with IDD would increase their comfort treating patients with IDD.Conclusion Residents in adult specialties felt ill-equipped to care for adults with IDD and limited experiences heightened their fear of making mistakes. Greater experiential learning and better support resources could improve their confidence and future care quality for this important population.

AB Mathematics writing is increasingly recognized as an important component of mathematical competence. TI Tracing the learning experience in a digital learning environment:
   Insights from pen pressure and facial expressions in primary school
   children
SO METACOGNITION AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-regulated learning; Trace data; Pen pressure; Facial expression;
   Children; Mathematics
ID EMOTION
AB Learning independently involves not only cognitive but also emotional, motivational, and metacognitive challenges, particularly for children still developing their self-regulated learning skills. Consequently, children's learning experiences can fluctuate rapidly within one learning activity, and assessing these experiences without disrupting learning remains an important research aim. In the present study, the feasibility of unobtrusively collecting two forms of trace data-pen pressure and facial expressions-from young learners in authentic classroom contexts was investigated, and the validity of the resulting indicators was tested. Data was analysed from two classroom studies with over 580 third- and fourth-grade children in Germany, who learned mathematics content in a tablet-based digital learning environment using digital pens and integrated webcams. Pen pressure was recorded in three phases of the learning task, facial expressions following feedback were coded for valence, and linear mixed-effects models tested how these indicators varied with item accuracy and difficulty. Mean and variance in pen pressure increased with item difficulty and after positive feedback, suggesting pen pressure indicators reflect both cognitive load and arousal. More varied pen pressure on difficult items that were answered incorrectly may reflect the metacognitive experience of uncertainty. Children's facial expressions were rated more positively after positive feedback than error feedback and when they self-reported higher valence, while nuanced effects of item difficulty pointed to attributional processes shaping children's emotional reactions. Overall, the findings demonstrate that pen pressure and facial expressions can be collected unobtrusively in real classroom contexts and provide valuable insights into young learners' experiences.

TI Does Information About the Origins of Figurative Idioms Help Learners to
   Remember Them? A Multi-Site Study
SO MODERN LANGUAGE JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE etymology; idioms; inferencing; metaphor; mnemonics; replication
   research
ID LANGUAGE; WORDS
AB It has been suggested that informing language learners about the original, literal meaning of idioms helps them to remember these expressions, but the empirical evidence is limited. A new study was conducted with three groups of learners of English (53 Chinese students at a university in Canada, 56 students at a university in China, and 77 high school students in Belgium). Each time, the students were randomly assigned to one of two conditions. In both conditions, they were asked to infer the meanings of 18 idioms, followed by feedback. In one condition, the inference task was supported by two illustrative sentences. In the other condition, it was supported by one such sentence and a note about the original, literal meaning of the expression (e.g., that jump the gun alludes to a false start in track athletics). The students' ability to recall the figurative meanings was assessed 1 week later, after which they were also quizzed about the origins. Multilevel regression modeling revealed better meaning recall after the learning condition that included notes about the idioms' origins, especially for the students who remembered these notes. Inference accuracy at the learning stage also emerged as a strong predictor of meaning recall.

TI Why and how do people become teachers in the Australian VET sector?
SO RESEARCH IN POST-COMPULSORY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Attractiveness of VET (FE) teaching; VET teacher salaries; career
   change; status of VET; motivation to teach
AB The paper reports on research undertaken to inform public debate on shortages of teachers in and for the vocational education and training (VET) sector, in Australia and elsewhere. The project surveyed currently employed VET teachers about their motivations for becoming VET teachers, and reasons for staying in the job. This paper analyses the findings relating to motivations for entering the occupation. An on-line survey was administered to all students enrolled in 'in-service' VET teacher-training qualifications at two universities in mid-2023, and those who had recently finished their studies. The respondents exhibited similar characteristics to the VET teaching workforce overall. The data from the survey, which included both quantitative and qualitative questions, were analysed by several variables, including industry/discipline area of teaching, age, gender, prior jobs, employment status, and length of service. Responses to qualitative questions were also analysed thematically. We also sought respondents' general ideas about barriers to entering the occupation and how to attract more people into VET teaching. The findings challenge some current Australian assumptions and debates. They indicate that the primary motivations for people to become a VET teacher are largely intrinsic rather than extrinsic. Suggestions for attracting more people to the occupation are provided.

TI Socio-economic factors shaping students' enrolment decisions in JCT
   training programs: a quantitative study
SO RESEARCH IN POST-COMPULSORY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE TVET; students' perception; socio-economic factors; Chi-square test;
   Holm-Bonferroni correction; ranking method
ID TVET
AB The paper investigates seven socio-economic factors influencing Saudi students' perception of enrolling in Jeddah College of Technology (JCT). The student survey is composed of 340 students pooled in three strata, i.e., sampling by department, by living place, and by students' seniority at the JCT. The study has used a five-point Likert scale questionnaire, which was analysed using the Chi-square test. The prevalence of the socio-economic factors is appraised using an original ranking method, which combines the Chi-square significance level and the pooling method. The study findings disclosed that the primary motivating factors to enrol at the JCT are, in order, the "location proximity", the "family professional success", and the "job availability at graduation", and equally the "parents' aspiration" with the "society esteem". The "Peers' influence" and the "Aversion to theoretical classes" factors are not influential with regard to the students' perception. To account for the inflation of Type I error rates resulting from multiple comparisons, a Holm-Bonferroni correction was applied. Only one factor, "location proximity", was interpreted as statistically significant despite that the Cramer's V of the other factors shows a medium association with students' perception.

TI Navigating the unknown: How principals discover and evaluate innovative
   opportunities
SO REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE discovery theory; Hong Kong; opportunity recognition; principals;
   psychological capital; school innovation
ID SCHOOL; ENTREPRENEURSHIP; SERENDIPITY; LEADERSHIP; COGNITION; TEACHERS
AB Guided by Discovery Theory and the framework of human, social and psychological capital, this study investigated how school principals recognize and evaluate innovative opportunities. Using a case study approach, data were collected through multi-phase interviews with eight principals who had implemented notable innovations in Hong Kong. The findings reveal two distinct recognition patterns, socially and psychologically driven, showing that psychological capital plays a dominant role in recognizing and evaluating opportunities. Our findings reveal that human capital (e.g., prior experience) was not central to opportunity recognition but instead was used to assess technical feasibility. Social capital supported serendipitous discovery, while psychological capital guided intentional searching and final decision-making. The study offers a novel, capital-integrated perspective on the discovery process by school principals and highlights the deeply personal and belief-driven nature of decisions regarding innovation in schools.Context and implications Rationale for this study: Little is known about how school principals actually recognize and evaluate innovative opportunities within complex educational contexts. Guided by the Discovery Theory, this study examines how human, social and psychological capital shape that process. Why the new findings matter: The study reveals that innovation decisions are driven less by experience and more by principals' moral conviction and school vision, reframing psychological capital as a value-anchored resource for educational leadership. Implications for practitioners, policy-makers and researchers: For practitioners, the findings highlight how personal beliefs and vision guide principals' judgements, suggesting reflective training to balance conviction with evidence-based decision-making. For policy-makers, the results emphasize the importance of leadership development that integrates psychological and relational capacities alongside technical expertise. For researchers, the work extends Discovery Theory by evidencing the hierarchical and belief-driven interplay of capitals, opening new directions for examining value-based educational entrepreneurship.

TI The problem of virtue translation from sports
SO THEORY AND RESEARCH IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE virtue; character education; sports; situations; mixed traits
ID PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; PERSONALITY; CHARACTER; SITUATIONS; ETHICS
AB There is a rising tide of incorporating virtue education into athletic programs in schools. The animating thought is that learners can cultivate virtues, like courage and resilience, which may carry over into the rest of their lives. However, from the virtue theory literature, we know that virtues are often situation-restricted traits. People act in terms of virtues in some areas of life, yet not in others.    for Intelligence and Learning Disabilities (SCIL) Among Adolescents in
   Nigeria

DT Article

ID INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY; IQ; GUIDELINES; CHILDREN; BEHAVIOR; OUTCOMES;
   PEOPLE; LIVES; STAKE
AB Background There are few screening tools for intellectual disabilities that have been developed and used within Africa. This study aimed to examine the psychometric properties of the English version of the adolescent Screener for Intelligence and Learning Disabilities (SCIL) when used with Nigerian adolescents and young people.Method Two hundred nine adolescents and young people (aged 11-26 years) completed the SCIL and took part in an assessment of their level of general intellectual functioning and adaptive behaviour. AB This study addresses the important yet underexplored question of whether the Common Core State Standards in Mathematics, first introduced in the United States in 2009 and which emphasize critical thinking and problem-solving, as well as the computer-based assessments aligned with the Common Core, have facilitated or hindered learning for students with disabilities. TI Fluid Multilingualism: Classroom Talk in English and French Classes in
   England, France and Norway
SO MODERN LANGUAGE JOURNAL
LA English
DT Article
DE comparative analysis; English; French; multilingualism; multiple
   contexts; student and teacher talk; anglais; fran & ccedil;ais;
   participation orale des & eacute;l & egrave;ves et des enseignants;
   multilinguisme; contextes multiples; analyse comparative
ID FOREIGN-LANGUAGE
AB Despite indications that creating opportunities for student talk in language classrooms is crucial for language development and educational outcomes, few studies have compared the amount of student talk in first (L1) and second or foreign (L2/L3) language classrooms. To address this gap, this article presents findings from the large-scale European project LANGUAGES. By using a sociocultural lens on classroom talk in 48 secondary classrooms of English and French, we examined 192 video-recorded lessons in England, France and Norway among students aged 13-15 years. We conducted descriptive and inferential statistics and identified a striking contrast. On average, student talk accounted for 20% of the total lesson time (regardless of L1 versus L2/L3 contexts), while teachers talked more than twice as much (58% in L1 contexts; 42% in L2/L3 contexts). We found significant differences between countries and languages for teacher and student talk. Students mainly talked in the L1, even in L2/L3 contexts, while using the target language (TL) sporadically. Teachers also predominantly used the L1, except in L2 English contexts. However, while we observed infrequent use of other languages, students and teachers regularly engaged in fluid language mixing of L1/TL, which we propose can increase student talk in L2/L3 classrooms.

TI The DecliningLikelihood of Completing the Ph.D. inChemical Sciences: The
   Role of Graduate School Experiences
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Graduate Education; Graduate Students; GraduateStudent Experience;
   Mentoring; Graduate Funding; Degree Completion; Advisor-Student
   Relationship
AB Maintaining a strong and diverse group of Ph.D.s is vital to the growth and productivity of the chemical sciences. Yet there are concerns this group has become relatively smaller over time as fewer Ph.D. students definitely plan to complete their degree. Using survey data gathered by the American Chemical Society (ACS), we analyze factors that may have contributed to this decline. Specifically, we address the following questions: (1) To what extent is the likelihood of chemical science Ph.D. students' completing their degree related to socio-demographic characteristics, preferences regarding their future careers, and graduate school experiences? (2) To what extent can these variables account for declines in expressed likelihood of degree completion? Using data gathered in 2013 and 2019, we find students' experiences in graduate school had a substantially greater influence on the likelihood of degree completion than individual characteristics or career preferences. While students who had adequate funding and more support from faculty and other staff were more likely to expect they would complete the degree, these associations declined markedly when encountering problems and interactions with advisors were controlled. Students reported encountering significantly more problems in their graduate program in 2019 than in 2013, and this difference could account for part of the decreased likelihood of degree completion in 2019. Data gathered in 2022 indicate that the decreased likelihood of degree completion became increasingly more serious over time, especially among students who were more advanced in their program.

TI "Bendto Send": A Wearable Alginate-BasedHydrogel Sensor for Morse Code
   Communication
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Polymer Chemistry; Hands-On
   Learning/Manipulatives; Materials Science; Hydrogel; Strain Sensor;
   Morse Code
AB This laboratory experiment introduces undergraduate students to the preparation and utilization of flexible and wearable hydrogel sensors consisted of sodium alginate, poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) polystyrenesulfonate, and an ionic liquid. The hydrogel is synthesized through ionic cross-linking and its resistance variation with stretching strain is evaluated, from which the gauge factors are calculated. The bending-sensing performance is then studied via current-time measurements on an electrochemical workstation, allowing students to directly correlate mechanical strain with electrical response. As a practical application, Morse code messages such as "GO", "SOS", and "HELP" are transmitted through controlled finger bending, demonstrating the translation of mechanical signals into communication codes. Beyond these guided tasks, students are encouraged to extend the experiment by designing their own messages or modifying sensing conditions. This activity provides hands-on experience in polymer cross-linking, flexible sensor fabrication, electromechanical signal conversion, and basic data acquisition, while fostering creativity in applying chemical principles to real-world communication systems.

TI Recontextualizing Literature Circles for Arabic Literacy Classrooms: A
   Human-Centred Approach to Fostering Belonging
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN READING
LA English
DT Article
DE Arabic literacy; bilingual education; dialogic pedagogy; literature
   circles; reading comprehension; school belonging
ID MOTIVATION
AB Background Literature circles are widely associated with gains in reading comprehension and engagement, yet their application in Arabic literacy classrooms, particularly those shaped by diglossia and bilingualism, remains underexplored. In the United Arab Emirates, many adolescents experience academic Arabic as linguistically distant and emotionally disengaging, with implications for comprehension, motivation and classroom belonging. Methods This mixed-methods quasiexperimental study examined the effects of peer-led literature circles on reading comprehension and social-emotional engagement among bilingual middle school students in two public schools in the UAE. Over an 8-week intervention, students in the experimental group participated in structured literature circles using curriculum-aligned and culturally relevant Arabic texts. Quantitative outcomes were analysed using paired and independent-sample t-tests, whereas qualitative data from student journals, classroom observations and teacher interviews were examined through thematic analysis. Results Students participating in literature circles demonstrated statistically significant gains in vocabulary knowledge, inferential comprehension and cause-effect reasoning compared with peers receiving traditional instruction (p < 0.001), with large effect sizes. Qualitative findings indicated increased reader agency, greater dialogic participation, enhanced linguistic confidence and stronger perceptions of classroom belonging. Students reported feeling more willing to speak, interpret and engage with Arabic texts. Conclusions The findings suggest that literature circles may offer a promising human-centred approach to literacy instruction in diglossic and bilingual contexts. By integrating dialogic interaction with culturally responsive texts, literature circles may support both comprehension processes and students' sense of belonging, positioning reading as a socially meaningful and emotionally grounded practice.

TI The Butterfly Effect of Integrating Technological Tools in Teacher
   Education: Small Innovations, Collaborative Reflective Practice, and
   Large-Scale Pedagogical Transformations
SO TECHTRENDS
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Augmented reality; Butterfly effect;
   Collaborative reflective practice; Virtual reality
AB This study probes the transformative potential of integrating developing technological tools-including artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and learning management systems (LMS)-with collaborative reflective practice (CRP) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teacher education. Building on butterfly effect, this study explores the process through which small-scale technological innovations, when processed through CRP, catalyze large-scale instructional transformations. Using an explanatory case study design, the study probes the experiences of 15 EFL student teachers and two teacher educators at Iran's Teacher Education University. Data were collected through reflective journals, semi-structured interviews, classroom observations, and artifacts, and analyzed thematically to expose the mechanisms directing these transformations. Findings indicate that immersive technologies including AR and VR make safe, simulated environments for practicing pedagogical strategies, whereas AI-driven tools support personalized learning and feedback. CRP and technological tools can develop critical reflection, collaboration, and continuous professional development, producing innovative teaching practices. However, challenges like resistance to change, technical issues, ethical concerns, and inequities in access to technology were acknowledged as barriers to active application. The study highlights the ripple effect of these novelties, representing how small-scale modifications in classroom management and lesson planning can produce inclusive shifts in organizational policies and learner-centered learning atmospheres. This research underscores the importance of leveraging technological integration with CRPs, emphasizing culturally sensitive approaches and systemic support to guarantee equitable and continuous development.

TI Integrating Ethical GenAI Use in Assessment: A Pilot Study in
   Postgraduate Health Leadership Education
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; ethical AI use; postgraduate
   education; assessment design; leadership
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly reshaping higher education, prompting institutions to reconsider how students demonstrate capability in an environment where text can be generated, refined, and summarised with ease. Previous research shows that students use GenAI to improve efficiency, reduce workload, and support comprehension, yet continue to seek clearer guidance on acceptable use. This gap between widespread adoption and limited pedagogical direction underscores the need for structured approaches that help students understand how, when and why GenAI can be used. Within postgraduate health leadership education, cultivating digital literacy, critical reasoning, and ethical judgement are important, as future leaders must model responsible technology use within their organisations. Thirty-nine responses from previous students provide early insight into how structured, ethical integration of GenAI within assessment design may influence student behaviour and support the development of responsible, critically informed GenAI use in postgraduate health leadership programs.

TI Framing analysis as a pedagogical tool for broadening medical students'
   understanding of cancer: a course evaluation
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; Cancer communication; Framing analysis;
   Interdisciplinary learning; Critical thinking; Reflective practice;
   Media literacy
ID EDUCATION
AB Background Cancer is a complex phenomenon encompassing a range of cultural and biomedical dimensions. Traditional medical curricula often fail to reflect this complexity, highlighting the need for interdisciplinary approaches that help medical students develop a more integrated understanding of disease by connecting diverse knowledge, patient perspectives, and societal contexts. This study evaluates how framing analysis-a method from communication studies-can be used as a pedagogical tool to broaden medical students' understanding and critical thinking about complex health issues, using cancer as a key example.Methods We conducted a course evaluation of a two-week elective titled "Cancer Communication" within the University of Oslo's medical program, offered annually to approximately 20 third-year students. Working in teams, students explored research questions related to cancer communication through lectures, workshops, guided research, and excursions. They learned framing analysis by applying a published tool for examining public cancer discourse. Anonymous pre-course free associations and post-course reflections were analyzed thematically to identify changes in students' understanding of cancer during the course. Students' team presentations, orally evaluated as part of the final course examination, supported our assessment of how students applied framing analysis to cancer-related communication topics.Results Students' initial responses reflected relatively simple and emotionally charged associations with cancer, often centered on fear, death, treatment burden, and familiar cancer stereotypes. Their post-course reflections suggested increased media literacy, critical thinking, and the ability to integrate multiple narratives about cancer. In their final presentations, students applied framing analysis to critically evaluate media portrayals and reflect on how different framings shape public and professional perceptions of disease. The post-course reflections further suggested greater empathy for cancer patients and an increased awareness of social and cultural influences on medical practice.Conclusions Integrating framing analysis into medical education appeared to broaden students' understanding of cancer as a multidimensional phenomenon, supporting reflective and interdisciplinary thinking and encouraging them to move beyond traditional biomedical perspectives. These findings suggest that framing analysis and similar communication-based approaches may serve as useful pedagogical tools in health professions education to enhance critical reflection.

AB Background The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of electrocardiography lead placement training on the performance and satisfaction of medical students using VR and compare it with training on a real patient and training on a mannequin. Methods This was a true experimental study. Ninety undergraduate medical students in the internal medicine rotation course were included in the study. The simulation software for the insertion of electrocardiography lead placement training was designed. The students were then divided into three groups. Practical training for lead placement was conducted via three methods: training on a real patient, a mannequin, and training through VR simulation. The course was evaluated through the DOPS (Direct Observation of Procedural Skills) test and the satisfaction survey form. Results The analysis of the DOPS test scores revealed a significant difference between the VR group and the other two groups (patient: 15.2 (1.89), mannequin: 15.3 (1.71) and VR: 17.5 (1.35)) (P value < 0.001). The results of the survey also indicated that the satisfaction of the students in the VR group was significantly greater than that of the other two groups of patients: (0.24) 1.74, (0.18) 1.76 and (0.18) 2.35 (P value < 0.001). Conclusion Considering the attractiveness of VR, the use of this software along with other teaching models in anatomy education can increase the motivation and satisfaction of learners.

TI Views and reported practices of South African speech-language therapy
   and audiology undergraduate students on linguistic and cultural
   integration in training
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Speech-language therapy; Audiology; Cultural competence; Linguistic
   integration; Curriculum reform; South Africa; Healthcare education;
   Cross-cultural practice
ID HEALTH; EDUCATION
AB Background South Africa's speech-language therapy (SLT) and audiology professions face challenges in achieving linguistic and cultural integration (i.e., the meaningful incorporation of diverse linguistic and cultural perspectives into training and practice), a critical aspect for effectively serving the country's diverse population. Limited curriculum content on indigenous languages and cultural competence, along with low diversity of academic and clinical training staff (staff), may hinder students' preparedness for multilingual and multicultural clinical practice. This study explored undergraduate students' views and self-reported practices regarding linguistic and cultural integration during their professional training. Aim To explore the views and practices of South African SLT and audiology undergraduate students concerning linguistic and cultural integration in their training. Methods A cross-sectional convergent mixed-methods survey design was used to gather quantitative and qualitative data from a purposive sample of 48 third- and fourth-year SLT and audiology students across four South African universities. Data were collected using a structured online questionnaire, including Likert-scale items and open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while thematic analysis was applied to qualitative responses. Results Within this sample, participants recognised the importance of linguistic and cultural competence but report feeling inadequately prepared to implement these skills in clinical settings. Key barriers included insufficient curriculum coverage of cultural topics, reliance on untrained interpreters, and a lack of bilingual resources. Students from indigenous language backgrounds reported higher ratings of the importance of linguistic integration than their English-speaking peers (p < .05). Qualitative themes suggested a perceived need for greater curriculum responsiveness, increased staff diversity, and enhanced institutional support to facilitate culturally competent practice. Conclusion These exploratory findings suggest that curriculum responsiveness, institutional support, and staff diversity may warrant further consideration within ongoing efforts aimed at improving student preparedness for practice in South Africa's multilingual and multicultural healthcare environment. These findings point to the need for ongoing educational transformation efforts to better serve the diverse needs of the South African population.

TI Skill-based competencies, not traits, are associated with design
   thinking-aligned teaching behaviours in nursing education: a
   cross-sectional survey
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Design thinking; Faculty development; Nursing education; Teaching
   behaviours; Creative synthesis
ID REGRESSION; CORE
AB Background Healthcare systems' growing complexity has driven the adoption of design thinking (DT) pedagogies to cultivate creativity, collaboration, and adaptive expertise among nursing graduates. Faculty teaching behaviours play a critical role in how DT curricula are enacted, yet it remains unclear whether skill-based DT competencies or trait-based dispositions are more strongly associated with DT-aligned teaching behaviours. This study examined their relative and indirect associations among interdisciplinary faculty involved in DT-integrated nursing education in Taiwan. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 95 faculty members from 12 Taiwanese institutions offering DT-integrated nursing courses. Measures included the 14-item Creative Teaching Behaviours Scale (CTBS) as a proxy for DT-aligned teaching behaviours, the 18-item Creative Synthesis Inventory-Taiwan version (CSI-TW) for skill-based DT competencies, and the 9-item Design Thinking Traits Questionnaire-Taiwan version (DTTQ-TW) for trait-based DT dispositions. Analyses included exploratory group comparisons, hierarchical multiple regression, and mediation analysis, controlling for demographic characteristics and DT-related teaching experience. Results Faculty with higher CTBS scores demonstrated significantly higher levels of both skill-based and trait-based DT competencies at the descriptive level. Hierarchical regression analysis showed that skill-based DT competencies (beta = 0.429, p < 0.05) and DT teaching experience (beta = 0.379, p < 0.05) were independently associated with DT-aligned teaching behaviours, explaining 27.2% of the variance. Trait-based DT dispositions did not contribute additional explanatory value once skills were taken into account (Delta R & sup2; = 0.001, p = 0.784). Mediation analysis further suggested an indirect association, whereby trait-based DT competencies were related to teaching behaviours through skill-based competencies, with no detectable direct association. Conclusions Within this cross-sectional sample, DT-aligned teaching behaviours were more closely associated with skill-based DT competencies and accumulated teaching experience than with trait-based dispositions. The findings are consistent with a distal-proximal interpretation derived from social cognitive theory and suggest that faculty development initiatives should prioritise sustained, hands-on training in DT process skills and authentic teaching practice opportunities rather than trait-based selection.

TI MEET & MAKE CleaR PROCESS: a new framework for sharing serious
   information
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sharing serious information; Breaking bad news; Communication; Medical
   education; Cognitive aid; Simulation in healthcare
ID BREAKING BAD-NEWS; MEDICAL-STUDENTS; CANCER-DIAGNOSIS; HEALTH-CARE;
   COMMUNICATION; PHYSICIANS; SIMULATION; PROTOCOL; REFLECTION; GUIDELINES
AB Introduction Sharing serious information (SSI) is a critical communication skill for physicians. Existing frameworks vary in their teaching and application, and many physicians desire better training. This study aimed to develop a theory-informed framework and cognitive aid for sharing serious information (SSI) through a multiphased development process involving a systematic review and expert focus groups.Method A multiphased approach was used: (1) a systematic review of four databases (1983-2024) to identify core components of SSI; and (2) twelve multidisciplinary focus groups (2022-2024) using the nominal group technique to integrate these components into a structured framework. A modified PICO/PEO approach (Population, Exposure/Intervention, Outcomes) guided study selection, and the AMSTAR2 tool was only used for quality appraisal of systematic reviews. From 4,892 titles/abstracts, 52 were selected for inclusion.Results Thematic synthesis identified eight themes for optimal SSI: (1) limiting delay between diagnosis and SSI, (2) preparation time for meetings, (3) patient-centered communication, (4) discussion of emotions, (5) verifying understanding, (6) affirmation of treatment options, (7) offering a confidant, and (8) providing information resources. These themes, interpreted cautiously across heterogeneous evidence sources, informed the development of the MEET & MAKE CleaR PROCESS framework, encompassing preparation (MEET), sharing (MAKE), clarification (CleaR), and ongoing plan (PROCESS).Discussion The MEET & MAKE CleaR PROCESS framework and its cognitive aid aim to equip educators and clinicians with a structured approach to instructing and managing SSI encounters especially with simulation-based education. We believe this up-to-date framework could minimize the negative impact of SSI on patients, relatives, and physicians.

TI Integrative character education: Valuing both epiphanic and incremental
   routes to moral growth
SO JOURNAL OF MORAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Epiphany; mundanity; Structured Wholeness Theory; flourishing; character
   education; Integrative Character Education
AB In the first of two Target Articles for the current Special Issue on Epiphanies and Moral Education, Kristj & aacute;n Kristj & aacute;nsson contrasts fast and epiphanic with slow and incremental approaches to moral growth, argues for the value of the former, and points out various obstacles to its realization. In this second Target Article, I argue that these obstacles can be overcome through a capacious understanding of epiphany and by means of the Structured Wholeness Theory of Human Flourishing, which focuses on a healthy integration of epiphanic and non-epiphanic (mundane) experience. I then introduce Integrative Character Education, a new field of inquiry and practice that is based on the Structured Wholeness Theory and thus emphasizes the moral growth that can come from valuing epiphany, mundanity, and their integration. Finally, I point out the importance of scaffolding for autonomy in character education and recommend next steps for the future development of Integrative Character Education.

TI Associations between nutrition knowledge and anthropometric indicators
   in a pre-professional health population: a cross-sectional study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Nutrition knowledge; Anthropometric measurements; Body composition;
   Bioelectrical impedance analysis; Midwifery students
AB Background Anthropometric indicators are widely used to assess nutritional status and obesity-related health risks; however, body mass index (BMI) alone may inadequately reflect central adiposity. Nutrition knowledge has been associated with healthier dietary behaviors, yet evidence linking detailed anthropometric and body composition measures with nutrition knowledge remains limited, particularly among pre-professional health students. This study aimed to examine the associations between general nutrition knowledge and anthropometric and body composition indicators among midwifery students. Methods This cross-sectional study included 126 first-year female midwifery students (mean age: 19.83 +/- 1.08 years). Anthropometric measurements (BMI, waist circumference [WC], waist-to-hip ratio [WHR], waist-to-height ratio [WHtR], and neck circumference [NC]) and body composition parameters were assessed using standardized procedures and bioelectrical impedance analysis. Nutrition knowledge was evaluated using the General Nutrition Knowledge Questionnaire-Revised (GNKQ-R). Pearson correlation, group comparisons (t-test/ANOVA), and multivariable linear regression analyses were performed. Subscale analyses were adjusted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate method. Results Higher GNKQ-R total scores were significantly associated with lower BMI (r = - 0.27), WC (r = - 0.36), WHR (r = - 0.23), WHtR (r = - 0.36), and body fat percentage (BF%) (r = - 0.25), and with higher fat-free mass percentage (all p < 0.05). Among GNKQ-R subscales, Healthy food choices and Diet-disease relationships demonstrated the most consistent inverse associations with adiposity-related measures. Group-based analyses showed progressively lower nutrition knowledge scores across increasing WC, WHtR, and body fat risk categories. In multivariable models adjusted for age and income-expense status, WHtR demonstrated the largest independent inverse association with GNKQ-R total score (beta = -0.339, p < 0.001). BMI and BF% were also independently associated, although with lower explanatory power. Conclusion Among midwifery students, higher nutrition knowledge was associated with more favorable anthropometric and body composition profiles, particularly indicators of central adiposity. Within this relatively homogeneous cohort of young, predominantly normal-weight female students, WHtR showed the strongest association with nutrition knowledge among the anthropometric indicators assessed. These findings should be interpreted in light of the cross-sectional design and the limited range of behavioral and sociodemographic variables assessed. Further research is needed to clarify the underlying mechanisms and to determine whether similar associations are observed in more diverse student populations.

TI A Serious Board Game for a Serious Problem: Improving (Preservice)

AB Following an Educational Design Research approach, this study described the design process and evaluation of a serious board game concerning giftedness for preservice teachers called enIQma. TI Exploring The Use Of Custom Chatbots In Marketing Education
SO MARKETING EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
AB This study investigates the effectiveness of custom chatbots in marketing education, examining their impact on student engagement and learning. The researcher compared students in two course sections using either traditional study methods or a custom chatbot. Using a standardized exam (n = 96) and a voluntary engagement survey (n = 75), the study employed Social Cognitive Theory and the Stimuli-Organism-Response framework to interpret how custom chatbots impact student learning and engagement. Results demonstrated that marketing students using the custom chatbot achieved statistically significantly better learning outcomes compared to the control group. While the custom chatbot section showed higher engagement levels, this difference was not statistically significant, suggesting custom chatbot use can enhance learning outcomes even when engagement levels remain stable. The research also provides a step-by-step guide for educators to create custom chatbots, offering recommendations. The study also acknowledges several ethical considerations pertaining to costs of and access to AI tools. While limited by sample size and duration, findings suggest custom chatbots can serve as pedagogical tools. This research contributes to AI integration literature in business education and offers practical implications for marketing educators seeking to enhance student learning through technology-enabled instruction.

TI INTEGRATING GENERATIVE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (GEnAI) IN A PROFESSIONAL
   SELLING COURSE: APPLICATION OF PROMPT ENGINEERING
SO MARKETING EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
ID SALES EDUCATION; PERSPECTIVE
AB As the adoption of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) gains momentum in both academic institutions and the business sector, the imperative for future sales professionals to harness technologies like ChatGPT is becoming increasingly pronounced within marketing curricula. This paper introduces an experiential learning innovation that empowers sales students to utilize GenAI effectively within the sales process, focusing on the nuanced art of "prompt engineering." This technique involves crafting specific inputs to elicit desired outputs from an AI model, a skill vital for navigating the complexities of modern sales environments. The authors detail a structured experiential learning exercise, highlighting how students were tasked with refining their prompts to achieve more precise outcomes in several stages of the sales process. This hands-on approach not only bridges the Theory-Practice Gap by grounding students in both the theoretical underpinnings and practical applications of Generative AI but also underscores the relevance of generative AI in the marketing curriculum. We also employ Algorithmic and Data Dependency Theories in evaluating the role of GenAI in sales education. Participant feedback underscores significant gains in understanding and applying GenAI in sales, affirming the curriculum's role in equipping a future-ready salesforce. The paper concludes with insights into the ongoing integration of GenAI into sales education, advocating for a curriculum that is both technologically advanced and practically oriented.

TI Curricular advances to develop medical students' knowledge, skills, and
   attitudes in health advocacy
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Health advocacy; Advocacy education; Undergraduate medical education;
   Competency-based education; Assessment; Evaluation
ID PERSPECTIVE; EDUCATION
AB Background The American Medical Association's Declaration of Professional Responsibility is an important covenant obligating present-day physicians to transcend personal beliefs and affiliations to advocate for changes that alleviate suffering and promote human health. Despite this recognition of advocacy as a pillar of physician duty, advocacy training in undergraduate medical education remains variable across institutions, elective in nature, and often insufficient in developing trainees' professional identities and competence as health advocates. Methods Educators at the UCLA David Geffen School of Medicine designed and delivered a novel half-day session required for all first-year medical students to nurture their professional identities as health advocates and empower them with knowledge, skills, and attitudes (KSA) needed to give voice to issues impacting the patients and communities they serve. Students attended a shared didactic followed by two focused workshops. The session was conducted annually from 2023-2025. Pre-and post-session data was collected after each iteration to evaluate changes in KSA. Results A total of 509 first-year medical students participated in the session from 2023-2025 with 477 (94%) partaking in the session synchronously. All 509 participants (100%) completed at least one survey, and 361 (71%) completed both pre-and post-surveys. Pooled data showed that participation led to statistically significant improvement on a 7-point Likert scale at similar rates in all three cohorts in each of the measured domains: knowledge (Delta 1.45, p < 0.001), skills (Delta 1.37, p < 0.001), and attitudes (Delta 0.44, p < 0.001). Conclusions A required half-day advocacy session supported trainees in developing their professional identities and acquiring foundational KSA needed to fulfill their roles as health advocates. Implementing this session across institutions can broaden its impact. Longitudinal data collection can clarify its long-term influence on physician engagement in advocacy and on health outcomes of patients and communities.

TI Multiple texts, culture, marginalization, and generative AI: An
   introduction to the special issue
SO EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGIST
LA English
DT Article
ID EXTERNAL VALIDITY; INFORMATION; RACE; INTEGRATION; FRAMEWORK; POLICY;
   TRUTH
AB In this Introduction to the Special Issue, our aims are three-fold. First, we provide the motivation for and explain the timing of this Special Issue. We also introduce three dimensions of analysis to justify why we asked authors to consider issues of culture, marginalization, and generative AI in relation to the literature on learning from multiple texts. These dimensions include that the analysis of culture, marginalization, generative AI, and multiple texts all require the critical consideration of language and source, reflect processes of homogenization and perpetuation, and demand individuals' sense-making of and within broader social experience. Second, we analyze the Special Issue contributions to identify three unifying themes in the critiques introduced about the literature on learning from multiple texts. These critiques include the multiple texts literature's (a) neglect of affect, (b) over-reliance on researcher-determined and constrained document sets, and (c) insufficient consideration of the sociotechnical context shaping students' multiple text use and students' own emerging conceptions of this context. Third, we introduce the idea of texts models as an epistemic tool that can be used to address some of these concerns by structuring students' reflections on the affective, epistemic, technical, and social justice dimensions of their interactions with information.

TI Proficiency-Calibrated AI-Generated Reading Input in EFL: A CEFR-Aligned
   Comparison of Extensive- and Intensive-Oriented Pathways
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI-assisted extensive reading; AI-assisted intensive reading; reading
   comprehension; EFL learners; proficiency levels; input comprehension
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; VOCABULARY; EDUCATION; TRENDS
AB Artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities to generate instructional materials calibrated to learners' proficiency levels; however, evidence on its use in extensive and intensive reading instruction remains limited. This mixed-methods quasi-experimental study examined the association between CEFR-calibrated AI-generated reading texts and EFL learners' reading comprehension and attitudes. A total of 171 Saudi undergraduate EFL learners participated in a 13-week intervention and were assigned to one of three instructional conditions: Intensive Reading using C1-level texts (G1, n = 55), Extensive Reading using B2-level texts (G2, n = 58), or Extensive Reading using A2-level texts (G3, n = 58). AI-generated reading materials were independently validated using Text Inspector and the Pearson GSE Toolkit before implementation. Reading comprehension was assessed using common pre- and post-tests, and learner perceptions were measured using a post-intervention questionnaire. All three instructional conditions were associated with statistically significant improvements in reading comprehension over the intervention period. Among the three groups, the B2 Extensive Reading condition achieved the highest post-test reading comprehension scores, whereas the A2 Extensive Reading condition received the most favorable evaluations across the questionnaire dimensions. These findings suggest that, within the instructional configuration examined in this study, moderately challenging AI-generated texts were associated with stronger reading-comprehension outcomes, whereas less demanding texts were associated with more positive learner perceptions. The study extends current research by providing empirical evidence on the use of CEFR-calibrated AI-generated reading materials within extensive and intensive reading contexts and offers practical implications for integrating AI-supported reading instruction in EFL classrooms.

TI Stepping into Higher Education: Exploring Students' Pre-Arrival
   Nervousness Across an English University
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; nervousness; pre-arrival; transition; undergraduate
AB The transition to university is a major life shift shaped by academic, social and personal change. Guided by Schlossberg's Transition Theory, this study provides rare insight into pre-arrival nervousness among first-year undergraduates (UG) entering an English university. This paper reports findings from the qualitative component of a wider study exploring students' pre-arrival experiences and expectations. A total of 1578 incoming UG students across twelve academic schools at a UK university provided qualitative responses to an open-ended survey question designed to capture self-reflective accounts of nervousness prior to enrolment. Using an inductive content analysis approach, four key themes were identified: social integration and belonging, academic adjustment and workload, health and wellbeing, and financial and practical concerns. Findings highlight the multi-faceted and anticipatory nature of transition, demonstrating that students' perceptions of readiness are formed before direct engagement with the university environment. The study extends existing literature by positioning nervousness as an integral component of the transition process rather than a reaction to it. These insights offer evidence-based guidance for institutions to implement proactive, inclusive pre-arrival strategies that support early engagement, enhance student confidence and promote successful adjustment to higher education settings.

TI Students' Mathematical Argumentation with Guiding Interactive Diagrams:
   A Case Study of Semiotic Conflict and Rebuttal Formation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE argumentation; interactive materials; pedagogical functionality of
   interactive diagrams; semiotic conflict; Toulmin model
ID COLLECTIVE ARGUMENTATION; FRAMEWORK; DISCOURSE; SUPPORT; DESIGN
AB This study aims to identify math students' argumentation processes and how the design of interactive materials may serve such processes. Despite the increasing use of such materials in mathematics education, their role in shaping students' argumentation processes remains underexplored. The case study to be reported here is part of a project aimed at examining the potential of interactive materials to support students' argumentation processes. TI Children's Multilingualism in Inclusive Preschools in Iceland
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE multilingual children; language agency; inclusive preschools; language
   policies; multilingual practices
AB This research project aims to explore children's multilingualism and how children's preschools build on the language resources which families and children bring to their preschools. Research has shown that children actively create their own knowledge and can express themselves regarding their views on language learning and that each child has a unique bilingual or multilingual experience. This qualitative research study contributes to in-depth research with children on their multilingual experiences as described by their parents, preschool teachers and principals. Data was collected from 2022 to 2025 in semi-structured interviews with six parents, their children's preschool teachers and principals in three preschools in Iceland. The findings indicate that the parents value their children's language repertoire and use diverse tools to support their children's multilingualism. The teachers in the study are all interested in supporting the children's multilingualism, although some of them claim that they lack knowledge, training, and support in implementing multilingual practices. The children are active agents in developing language policies and practices in their families. They contribute to their families' language practices with their input, ideas, choices, and language preferences. Although Icelandic is the main language used in the preschools, the children, supported by their teachers and principals, have the opportunity and agency to develop their multilingualism. The research findings provide practitioners, policy makers and parents with suggestions as to how children can and will benefit from support in maintaining their heritage languages. More structured collaboration and policy guidance are likely to strengthen children's multilingualism.

TI Blended Intensive Programs as a Pedagogical Approach: Fostering Digital,
   Collaborative, and Intercultural Skills in Advanced Civil Engineering
   Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES

DT Article
DE civil engineering education; Blended Intensive Program (BIP); pedestrian
   safety; active learning; multicultural education; digital pedagogy
AB This paper presents the design, implementation, and assessment approach of the Blended Intensive Program (BIP) "Towards Enhanced Pedestrian Safety", developed under the Erasmus+ framework at the University of Beira Interior in collaboration with four partner universities from Slovenia, Poland, and Croatia. The study applies the EPIC framework (Embedded, Pluralistic, Internationalized, and Connected) to the design and evaluation of a short-term, hybrid, and international learning format in Civil Engineering, addressing a gap in the literature regarding the limited availability of structured and empirically grounded approaches for the design and assessment of Blended Intensive Programs in engineering education. The study highlights the pedagogical value of integrating international collaboration, digital tools, and active learning strategies, while aligning with SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities).

TI Understanding Professional Identity Through Policy and Support
   Perceptions: A Latent Profile Study of Pre-Service Preschool Teachers in
   China
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE pre-service preschool teachers; professional identity; policy
   satisfaction; teacher support; latent profile analysis
ID STUDENTS
AB Government-funded teacher education in China links financial support, teacher preparation, employment expectations, and post-graduation service obligations. Understanding how pre-service preschool teachers perceive this policy-based pathway is important for explaining their professional identity development; therefore, this study examined how policy satisfaction and perceived teacher support were associated with the professional identity of government-funded pre-service preschool teachers in Chongqing, Southwest China. Based on paper-based questionnaire data from 620 participants, Latent Profile Analysis identified four profiles: Dissatisfied-Low Support, Moderately Satisfied-Moderate Support, Highly Dissatisfied-Low Support, and Highly Satisfied-High Support. AB Amid the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) and the digital transformation of schooling, computational thinking has become a foundational competency for K-12 learners and an organizing principle for AI education. Existing research suggests that students need not only programming knowledge, but also the ability to analyze problems, reason with data and models, and evaluate intelligent systems responsibly. We argue that AI education should move beyond tool demonstration and code production toward authentic problem solving, model understanding, responsible human-AI collaboration, and reflective innovation. The framework offers guidance for cultivating students' computational thinking, AI literacy, and creative problem-solving capacity, while identifying directions for empirical validation.

TI AI literacy as contextual judgement: postgraduate researchers'
   appropriateness judgements of generative AI use in a multilingual
   Chinese setting
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI literacy; appropriateness judgements; research lifecycle; academic
   integrity; multilingual research writing; generative AI; postgraduate
   researchers
ID HIGHER-EDUCATION
AB Introduction The integration of generative AI (GenAI) into academic research has reshaped scholarly practices, yet how researchers-in-training develop AI literacy and make contextualised appropriateness judgements across the research lifecycle remains underexamined, particularly in multilingual contexts.Methods This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study investigated 126 postgraduate and doctoral students at a Chinese university. Questionnaire data measured AI literacy across four dimensions-understanding, applying, evaluating, and ethical awareness-and appropriateness judgements across five research stages. Semi-structured interviews with 19 participants were then analysed thematically to explain and extend the quantitative findings.Results Descriptive results revealed an uneven AI literacy profile, with ethical awareness scoring highest and understanding scoring lowest. Multiple regression analyses showed stage-specific associations between AI literacy and appropriateness judgements. Ethical awareness was positively associated with judgements in conceptualising, drafting, and transparency and honesty. Applying ability was positively associated with conceptualising, drafting, and revising/editing. Understanding was negatively associated with revising/editing, suggesting a "knowledge-trust paradox," while evaluating showed no significant association across the five stages. Qualitative findings explained these patterns through an "assistance-then-verification" principle in data-related work, research experience as a critical moderator, task-dependent differences between coursework and publication-oriented writing, and a tiered disclosure strategy shaped by perceived desk-rejection concerns and normative ambiguity.Discussion The findings advance AI literacy theory from generic competence toward stage-sensitive, contextualised judgement. They also provide empirically grounded implications for postgraduate research training, academic integrity education, and institutional governance of responsible GenAI use in multilingual research writing contexts.

TI The grammar, punctuation and spelling test: an evaluation of the
   disconnect between declarative knowledge and applied knowledge
SO ENGLISH IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Metalanguage; metalinguistic knowledge; education policy; grammar
   testing; knowledge about language
ID TEACHERS
AB This research contributes to the limited literature on the Grammar, Punctuation and Spelling (GPS) Test by examining its value for retention and application of knowledge to pupils' writing, over a period of 10 years. It explores the disconnect between declarative knowledge and applied knowledge to writing, highlighting broader tensions between policy and classroom practice. Through an analysis of pupil GPS Tests and writing samples at Key Stages 2 and 4, it shows that while the test improves metalanguage, it does not necessarily translate to improvements in written composition, a finding with implications for pedagogy, curriculum design and testing. If the purpose of the GPS Test is to improve decontextualised grammatical knowledge, then it could be considered a success. However, if its implementation is intended to raise writing standards, then much more needs to be done to address the disconnect between knowing grammar and applying it in meaningful ways to improve pupils' writing. This paper calls for a reduction in metalinguistic knowledge taught at primary and breadth across Key Stages 3 to 4.

TI Grammar as ideology, writing as evidence: diachronic insights from Noun
   Phrase use in the primary school context (1979-2021)
SO ENGLISH IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE English language; National Curriculum; Noun Phrase; grammar; education
   discourses
ID TEACHERS; COHESION
AB This paper explores the long-term ideological association between grammar teaching and children's writing development through a small case-study of Noun Phrase (NP) use across time and curricular contexts. Drawing on the Writing over Time corpus (1979-2021), a collection of narrative and argumentative writing from primary schoolchildren in Merseyside, it compares texts produced before and after the institutionalisation of explicit grammar instruction in the English National Curriculum. At the linguistic level, quantitative and qualitative analyses of NP complexity reveal both stability and change in NP use across time and genres. At the wider, socio-educational level, the linguistic findings are used to (a) question the historical standing of ideological associations between explicit grammar teaching and "rising standards" of language proficiency and (b) highlight, in line with previous synchronic-oriented scholarship, the need for more coherent, meaning-oriented models of grammar pedagogy as part of curricular language models and teacher training.

TI How do we compare with other countries?
SO ENGLISH IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Russia; France; The Netherlands; Estonia; Finland
ID GRAMMAR; PEDAGOGY
AB How does language education (L1 and L2) in England compare with that of other countries? I survey policy and practice in teaching about language in England with Russia, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Estonia, and Finland, and show that these other systems place language at the core of the curriculum, integrate first and second language instruction, and value explicit, linguistically informed teaching. In contrast, England, despite its pioneering contributions to language education theory, has largely abandoned many of its own innovations and gives language very little attention. The review concludes with policy recommendations for embedding linguistic knowledge and teacher expertise in the curriculum for English.

TI 'That's you being a good reader': the impact of training in cognitive
   stylistics for teachers of English in UK secondary education
SO ENGLISH IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Cognitive stylistics; subject knowledge; teacher/student confidence;
   continuous professional development; grammar
ID GRAMMAR; PEDAGOGY
AB This article argues that opportunities for teachers to develop subject-knowledge in cognitive stylistics can support the teaching of English in secondary schools. In 2022, the Aston Stylistics Research Centre ran three workshops on cognitive stylistics for English teachers from across England. This article analyses interviews with 6 of these teachers 3 years later, exploring their experiences of applying cognitive stylistic frameworks at Key Stages 3-5. We examine any long-term impacts in the schools at which the teachers taught, and beyond, including any changes to teachers' subject knowledge and attitudes, and to those of their students. Finally, the teachers provide an insight into experiences of disseminating the training with colleagues, and some of the challenges faced in doing so.

TI Sacred spaces in English classrooms: utilizing religious registers as a
   pedagogical bridge in multilingual Indonesia
SO ENGLISH IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom discourse; English education; interpersonal meaning;
   multilingual pedagogy; religious registers; recognizes
ID SYSTEMIC FUNCTIONAL LINGUISTICS; INTERSECTIONS; EDUCATION
AB Religious language is often overlooked in English education, where effective teaching is commonly associated with linguistic proficiency and secular, English-dominant norms. While multilingual pedagogy recognises learners' cultural and linguistic resources, the interpersonal role of religious expressions in English classrooms remains underexplored. This study examined how religious registers function as pedagogical resources in multilingual English instruction through the lens of Systemic Functional Linguistics, focusing on tenor as the dimension of social relations, authority, and alignment.
