TI The road almost taken: nearly having 'Knowledge About Language', the
   enduring significance of the Kingman Report
SO ENGLISH IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Kingman Report; linguistics; grammar; Standard English; censorship
ID PERSONAL GROWTH; ENGLISH; MODEL
AB The 1988 Kingman Report was the result of an enquiry into how the English language should be taught in School Subject English, and its story has a permanent significance. The report represents a key moment in the history of the subject when there might have been the key "linguistic turn". Certain historical forces combined in the report to make it unintentionally a manifesto for sociolinguistics and progressive English, and it firmly rejected a return to formal grammar teaching. However, it was overtaken by the National Curriculum of 1989. Its potential legacy, through the "Language in the National Curriculum" (LINC) Project of professional development for all English and primary teachers and provision of comprehensive teaching materials, was banned by the government of the day; an outrageous act of censorship. As a result, the Kingman Report was quickly ignored or forgotten. However, its significance was as a middle way, enabling teachers to address students' need to develop "Knowledge About Language" but without imposing rigid notions of Standard English. There is a profound need to revitalise the teaching of English, and the spirit of Kingman and LINC can be an inspiration towards a new mode of critical language awareness. The lesson from the banning of LINC is that rightwing traditionalists are determined to resist democratic conceptualisations of language by whatever means. The residual and valuable legacy of Kingman is that it shows a way can be found to address the need for much improved linguistic knowledge for teachers, coupled with much more progressive content in the curriculum.

TI Cultural heritage and transdisciplinary approaches in modern art
   education: influence on artistic perception, interpretation and
   development of creative thinking of students
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE art education; artistic perception; creative thinking; cultural
   heritage; interpretation; transdisciplinary approach
AB Cultural heritage and transdisciplinary learning are increasingly recognized as important components of modern art education. However, limited empirical evidence exists regarding their influence on students' artistic perception, interpretation of cultural heritage, and creative thinking, particularly within the context of Kazakhstan's art education system. This study employed a quantitative research design involving 200 students enrolled in art and art-pedagogical educational programs. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire and analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4. The conceptual model examined the effects of cultural heritage integration and the transdisciplinary approach on artistic perception, interpretation of cultural heritage, and creative thinking, while cultural awareness and educational experience were tested as moderating variables. The findings revealed that cultural heritage integration was positively associated with artistic perception (beta = 0.412, p < 0.001) and interpretation of cultural heritage (beta = 0.365, p < 0.001). The transdisciplinary approach demonstrated the strongest relationship with creative thinking (beta = 0.438, p < 0.001). Interpretation of cultural heritage was also positively associated with creative thinking (beta = 0.327, p < 0.001). Cultural awareness and educational experience showed significant moderating effects, although the moderation effect of cultural awareness was relatively small. The results confirm that cultural heritage functions not only as educational content but also as a pedagogical resource supporting artistic perception, interpretation, and creative development. Transdisciplinary learning expands students' opportunities for creative reinterpretation and original artistic expression. The study highlights the importance of integrating cultural heritage and transdisciplinary approaches into contemporary art education and provides empirical evidence from Kazakhstan to support more reflective, interpretive, and creativity-oriented educational practices.

TI Cultural capital, social capital, and parental support for children's
   out-of-school instrumental study in China

LA English
DT Article

AB This study examines how family cultural and social capital relate to young children's participation in out-of-school instrumental training in urban Chinese city, Chengdu. TI Experimental science of traditional Chinese medicine curriculum design
   based on outcome-based education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION

AB Introduction TCM postgraduates suffer from weak research methodology, innovation and teamwork, restricting their training quality. Outcome-Based Education (OBE) is student-centered and reverse-design oriented, suitable for cultivating TCM postgraduates' research ability. This study constructs an Experimental Science of TCM postgraduate curriculum based on OBE to improve students' research project design capacity. Methods The curriculum integrates OBE and Jolly's technology commercialization model, adopting blended teaching (75% lectures + 25% autonomous learning) across 9 weeks, divided into four modules: feasibility analysis, data mining, experimental design, paper writing. Limitations include single-university small sample; future multi-institutional verification and long-term tracking are needed. The course provides a replicable training mode for TCM postgraduate research literacy.

TI The multi-perspective assessment of pedagogical interaction quality as a
   tool for teaching development: insights from the INTAKT pilot study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom climate; classroom feedback; classroom management;
   multi-perspective assessment; pedagogical interaction; secondary
   education; teaching and learning
ID INSTRUCTIONAL QUALITY; CLASSROOM MANAGEMENT; TEACHERS; STUDENTS;
   DISTURBANCES; RATINGS
AB Effective pedagogical interactions are an important prerequisite for the cognitive, emotional, and motivational development of students and the health of teachers. Yet the dynamics of pedagogical interactions have not yet been sufficiently conceptualized or adequately researched from multiple perspectives. The INTAKT study addresses these gaps by investigating teachers' and students' behaviors and experiences in secondary school classes-from their subjective perspectives (insider view) and by classroom observations (external view). In this paper, we present the INTAKT pilot study, which examined the feasibility of this multi-perspective approach in 16 classes (n = 209 students). Descriptive analyses yielded insightful results on the (perceived) quality of 18 interaction features from the distinct perspectives in each participating class, e.g., visualized by radar charts. Effect sizes suggest substantial differences across perspectives, with the largest and most consistent discrepancy observed for cognitive activation (d ' > 1.0). We exemplify these results with two contrast groups built on observer ratings (low vs. high quality). A comparison of these two groups indicates that the perspective differences were larger in the low-quality group. In addition, we present how we translated the findings into personalized feedback reports for the participating teachers. As an outlook, we document preliminary psychometric diagnostics. In the discussion, we argue that the INTAKT approach is feasible and yields meaningful findings with high face validity. As for the feedback reports, we discuss their potential to support teachers in reflecting on and developing their instructional practice. Beyond that, we critically reflect on the pilot study's sample quality (small number of classes, convenience sample) and outline the main study's strategy to further analyze the scales' psychometric properties and the generalizability of the observed effects.

TI The influence of reinforcement on classroom management and learners'
   performance at secondary schools in South Africa
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE classroom management; discipline; family background; learners'
   performance; misbehaviour; reinforcement
ID SELF-DETERMINATION; PUNISHMENT; REWARDS
AB The influence of reinforcement on classroom management and learner attainment in secondary schools is one of the key components of a conducive teaching-learning environment. Thus, a conducive learning environment is only possible if a teacher is skilled and able to apply different techniques to ensure the required classroom environment. Consequently, this research aimed to identify the influence of reinforcement on effective classroom management and learners' attainment. The research employed a generic qualitative method, and a total of 12 purposely sampled teachers and school heads from six secondary schools were interviewed face-to-face. The study found that positive reinforcement does play a role in classroom management and learners' performance, but that this does not apply in all situations, particularly for learners who come from socioeconomically underprivileged and broken families. However, most teachers did not use positive reinforcement; rather, they used negative reinforcement or punishment to obtain results, contradicting the South African Constitution and the Schools' Act of 1996 that preserve the rights of a child and prohibit corporal punishment. The study therefore recommends that teachers be given mandatory training in necessary classroom management skills and their school's code of conduct to maintain discipline in the classroom for the attainment of educational goals.

TI Generative AI-supported instruction as a cognitive scaffold: effects on
   senior high school students' geometric reasoning and proof construction
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; geometric reasoning; proof
   construction; secondary mathematics education; visualization
AB Difficulties in connecting visual representations with formal deductive reasoning continue to hinder students' success in geometry proof construction. This study examined the association between generative artificial intelligence (AI)-supported instruction and Senior High School students' geometric reasoning and proof construction. A quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test non-equivalent control group design was employed involving 86 students from two intact classes in a public senior high school in Ghana. The experimental group received generative AI-supported instruction, while the control group received conventional instruction. Data were collected using a Geometry Reasoning and Proof Test and a perception and attitude questionnaire. Independent-samples t-tests, paired-samples t-tests, ANCOVA, and descriptive statistics were used for data analysis. The findings revealed that students exposed to generative AI-supported instruction achieved significantly higher geometric reasoning and proof construction scores than students receiving conventional instruction, even after controlling for pre-test performance. Students in the experimental group also reported favorable perceptions and attitudes toward the instructional approach. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI-supported mathematics learning by demonstrating the potential of generative AI to function as a cognitive scaffold that supports the transition from visual intuition to deductive reasoning in geometry. The findings suggest that generative AI-supported instruction may provide a useful instructional approach for enhancing students' geometric reasoning and proof construction.

TI Modelling factors associated with Indonesian fifth graders' English
   learning motivation and task engagement
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL teachers' roles; motivation; peers' roles; socio-economic status;
   task engagement; young learners' views
ID STUDENTS
AB This study examined the roles of teachers, peers and young learners' (YLs) socio-economic status (SES) play from the children's perspective. The theoretical background drew on self-determination theory and YLs' language learning motivation. We collected data with a survey and analyzed them using structural equation modeling involving 598 fifth graders in Indonesia. The model tested direct and mediated relationships between YLs' views of their teachers and peers and their SES (operationalized as parents' educational background, occupation, and income) and task engagement and indirectly with motivation. The results showed that YLs' perceptions of their teachers' and peers' roles significantly and strongly predicted their motivation, whereas their SES showed a significantly weaker relationship with motivation. Parents' income and occupation, however, had a statistically nonsignificant relationship with the children's motivation. YLs' English learning motivation significantly and strongly predicted their engagement with English tasks. YLs' views of their teachers and peers had a small, significant direct relationship with task engagement and a significant indirect relationship via motivation. Additional indirect relationships resulting from parental income, occupation, and educational background were positive but lacked statistical significance. In sum, we found that YLs' perceptions of their teachers' and peers' roles, together with their SES, were positively associated with task engagement through their motivation. Teachers play key roles in creating supportive relationships and positive peer interactions, enhancing motivation and engagement. Extra support is needed for students from less privileged backgrounds.

AB As LSAMP/WiscAMP faces an uncertain future, it is important to document the high- impact practices that have been created through this funding source. Focusing on the STEM Boot Camp (SBC) at the University of Wisconsin- Whitewater, this paper builds on the earlier quantitative evaluation on SBC by extending the analysis across additional cohorts and incorporating a qualitative component to better understand mechanisms underlying student persistence and success. TI Language, academic adjustment, and help-seeking perceptions among Arab
   students from East Jerusalem in Israeli higher education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic adjustment; constrained participation; east Jerusalem students;
   help-seeking; language barriers
AB This study examines the academic experiences of Arab students from East Jerusalem in Israeli higher education, focusing on how language, academic adjustment, and help-seeking intersect under conditions of structural and linguistic inequality. It challenges dominant models that frame adjustment as a linear process of integration and instead introduces the concept of constrained participation to account for the uneven and negotiated nature of academic engagement. Drawing on an interpretive qualitative design, the study is based on in-depth, semi-structured interviews with thirty undergraduate students enrolled in a Hebrew-dominant academic institution. The data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, enabling the identification of recurring patterns across participants' lived experiences. The findings reveal four interrelated dynamics shaping academic involvement: arduous access marked by cumulative fatigue; language as both a cognitive and participatory barrier; help-seeking as a constrained and socially negotiated practice; and adjustment as an ongoing process of self-regulation under psychological strain. Academic engagement is shown to begin prior to classroom entry, shaped by structural demands that affect students' readiness to learn. Language operates not only as a medium of instruction but as a gatekeeping mechanism that structures visibility, participation, and recognition. Help-seeking is often redirected toward informal networks, while formal support remains underutilized. By conceptualizing participation as conditional rather than given, the study offers a procedural account of how students may be formally included yet remain epistemically and socially marginal. It thus provides a refined framework for understanding academic engagement in contexts of inequality.

TI Home and preschool collaboration during and after the COVID-19 pandemic
   - the perspective of Estonian and Swedish preschool teachers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collaboration; ECEC; family; pandemic; preschool; relationship
AB This study aims to describe how a small group of preschool teachers in Sweden and Estonia have perceived changes in collaboration and communication between home and preschool during and after the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions. The results are based on qualitative, semi-structured interviews with 14 preschool teachers from both countries and draw on neo-ecological system theory. The collected data suggest that the participating teachers are experiencing a transition where physical communication is partly replaced by digital communication, at times increasing the distance between parents and teachers and fostering one-way communication. Further, the varying restrictions between the countries and the diverse roles of teachers and principals in these specific preschools illustrate how macro-level decisions can influence home-preschool collaboration at both exo- and meso levels. In this study, teachers from Estonia highlighted their role in supporting parents emotionally, whilst participating Swedish teachers reflected on how the added responsibility of health screenings during COVID-19 restrictions required them to develop a firmer professional approach. Additionally, specific examples from participants illustrate differing approaches to preschool-hosted family events, indicating a shift toward more individualized forms of collaboration within the contexts studied.

TI Navigating ethical collaboration with machine translation: An
   exploratory study on the role of L2 development in GenAI writing
SO COMPUTERS AND COMPOSITION
LA English
DT Article
DE Machine translation; Ethical collaboration; Writing; L2 learners;
   Language development; L2 grammar; Processability theory; GenAI training;
   GenAI guidelines; GenAI acknowledgement
AB We explore how language development, and training informed by development, impact L2 students' navigation of ethical collaboration with machine translation (MT). Our interdisciplinary approach integrated the Writing Studies' concept of 'ethical collaboration' - an ethically guided interface between students and GenAI - with Applied Linguistics, which highlights the need to address GenAI/MT ethics and L2 language. We created a model synthesizing the "Student Guide to AI Literacy" (MLA, 2024) with a theory of L2 development. Data were collected by 1) an established protocol - direct writing in English, self-translation from the L1 and machine translation from the L1, 2) developmentally focused and acknowledgement training, and 3) postediting of self-translation. An emergence (onset) criterion and frequencies measured written development and evaluation of MT output, frequencies measured monitoring after training and a statistical analysis measured impact of the training types. The analysis of development and evaluation demonstrated that development impacted un/ethical evaluation of MT output. The post-edits indicated that developmentally focused training encouraged ethical monitoring when development permitted and had more impact than acknowledgement training. We conclude that guidelines and training on ethical collaboration with GenAI should be informed by L2 development, not only GenAI literacy, and that research on this topic should continue.

TI A community of inquiry perspective on human-AI co-facilitation within
   micro-blended learning
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Micro-blended learning; Teacher-AI collaboration; Community of inquiry
   (CoI) framework; Distributed presences; High school math education
AB This study explores the distribution of teaching, social, and cognitive presences across human teachers and artificial intelligence (AI) systems in micro-blended learning environments for K-12 mathematics education, framed by the Community of Inquiry (CoI) framework. Utilizing a semester-long experimental design in high school Algebra classes, the instruction alternated between teacher-led in-person sessions and AI-facilitated online learning using MathPal, a conversational AI agent. The findings reveal a complementary relationship between teacher-led instruction and AI contributions, where teachers provided foundational conceptual scaffolds, affective support, and responsive guidance, while MathPal extended learning through step-bystep individualized scaffolding, adaptive feedback, and socio-emotional reinforcement. Based on these findings, this study introduces the Distributed Community of Inquiry framework, expanding CoI theory to address emerging dynamics in teacher-AI collaboration. Practical implications include optimizing modality alignment, embedding adaptive relational features into AI systems, and incorporating scalable learning designs that support equitable access to instructional support. This research contributes insights into the synergy between human and AI facilitators within micro-blended learning environments and highlights areas for future research, including broader validation across disciplines and AI platforms.

TI Need satisfaction and need frustration profiles among pre-service and
   in-service teachers: Links with self-efficacy, commitment, and

AB This study used a person-centred approach grounded in Basic Psychological Needs Theory to identify profiles of autonomy, relatedness, and competence need satisfaction and need frustration among pre-service and in-service teachers in Kuwait, and to examine how these profiles relate to self-efficacy, occupational commitment, and intentions to quit. In Fall 2025, 1755 teachers (pre-service n = 780; in-service n = 975) completed an online survey. TI The role of co-parenting in preschoolers' school readiness and an
   exploration of the underlying mechanisms
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE School readiness; Co-parenting; Parent-child relationships; Parenting
   practice; Preschooler
ID FATHER-CHILD RELATIONSHIPS; FAMILY CHECK-UP; ACADEMIC-ACHIEVEMENT;
   AFRICAN-AMERICAN; CONDUCT PROBLEMS; LOW-INCOME; COMPETENCE; QUALITY;
   AGE; MOTHER
AB Co-parenting quality has been closely linked to children's social-emotional competencies, yet few studies have examined its effects on academic and social-emotional domains simultaneously or the underlying mechanisms within the family systems. Drawing on a sample of 320 Chinese preschoolers (Mage = 44.39 months; SD = 3.72; 53% girls, n =170; 71% only child, n = 226) and their mother-father dyads, we investigated the effects of parent-perceived co-parenting on preschoolers' pre-academic skills and social competence as well as the chain mediation effects via parenting practices and parent-child relationships. TI Exploring the heterogeneity of home literacy practices: Profiles among
   Spanish-English bilingual children and their relations with language and
   literacy skills
SO EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH QUARTERLY
LA English
DT Article
DE Home literacy environment; Bilingualism; Reading development; Individual
   differences; Parental concern
ID PARENTAL INVOLVEMENT; SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS; VOCABULARY; ENVIRONMENT;
   GROWTH; EXPERIENCES; LEARNERS; NUMBER; INPUT; COMPONENTS
AB Purpose: This study examined the heterogeneity of home literacy practices in Spanish-English bilingual families using a person-centered approach. The relations between the home literacy profiles and children's bilingual language and early literacy skills and parental concern were examined. Methods: Parents of 127 kindergarten children completed surveys on home literacy practices. Children completed standardized measures of vocabulary, sentence repetition, rapid letter naming, and passage comprehension in both languages. Latent profile analysis was used to examine the profiles of home literacy practices, as well as whether there were differences in children's language and literacy skills across profiles. We also evaluated whether there were differences in parental concern of children's language development across home literacy practice profiles. Results: A three-profile solution fit the data well, including a Limited Conventional Literacy Practice Profile (17%), a Spanish-dominant Literacy Practice Profile (43%), and a Moderately English-dominant Literacy Practice Profile (40%). Profiles' characeristics are described in relation to language exposure, parental education, and self-reported reading ability. Children in the Moderately English-dominant Literacy Practice Profile outperformed those in the Spanish-dominant Literacy Practice Profile on English language and emergent literacy skills. Parents in the Limited Conventional Literacy Practice Profile expressed significantly greater concern about their children's language development than parents in the Moderately English-dominant Literacy Practice Profile. Conclusions: Findings demonstrate the heterogeneity of home literacy practices among Spanish-speaking families in the U.S. and the importance of considering individual differences when investigating the home literacy environment of Spanish-English bilingual children. Implications for theory and practice are discussed.

TI A therapeutic-based professional development model for enhancing
   emotional regulation and positive discipline in early-career teachers in
   Thai schools
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE emotional regulation and positive discipline; integrated therapeutic
   training; school safety; teacher professional development; Thai
   education context
ID MINDFULNESS; STRESS; STUDENT; EDUCATION; INTERVENTIONS; CONSEQUENCES;
   ENGAGEMENT; BEHAVIOR; BURNOUT; TRAUMA
AB Early-career teachers in Thailand often struggle to manage emotions and apply positive discipline, particularly when facing disruptive behavior, heavy workloads, and limited support. These challenges frequently lead to punitive responses that harm classroom relationships, lower student engagement, and heighten teacher stress. Although national policies emphasize safe and supportive schools, professional development rarely provides therapeutic tools to address these issues. This study presents and validates an integrated therapeutic-based professional development model designed to enhance emotional regulation and positive discipline among early-career teachers in Thai schools. Grounded in cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR), trauma-informed care (TIC), and emotion-focused therapy (EFT), the proposed model integrates evidence-based psychological approaches into a culturally responsive training framework. Using a multiphase research and development design with mixed-methods data collection, the study engaged 120 early-career teachers and incorporated expert validation (N = 7), focus group discussions (N = 10), pre- and post-tests, surveys, reflective journals, and interviews. The resulting five-component model consists of core principles, learning objectives, structured therapeutic content, experiential learning activities, and assessment tools, further supported by peer coaching, professional learning communities, and access to mental health professionals. The results indicated that experts confirmed the proposed therapeutic-based professional development model as highly appropriate, theoretically rigorous, and practically feasible. The validated model consists of five integrated components: principles grounded in CBT, MBSR, TIC, and EFT; objectives focused on enhancing teachers' emotional awareness, regulation, and positive discipline; structured content addressing emotions, stress, classroom triggers, and therapeutic communication; experiential learning activities such as mindfulness and role-play; and assessment processes for monitoring teacher development and program effectiveness. Empirical findings further demonstrated significant improvements in teachers' emotional regulation capacities, accompanied by a reduction in reliance on punitive disciplinary measures, thereby confirming the model's effectiveness in promoting supportive, emotionally responsive classroom practices.

TI Beyond institutional boundaries: a model for cross-institutional
   interdisciplinary education
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE cross-institutional; curriculum design; engineering; immunology;
   interdisciplinary; project-based learning; undergraduate
ID STUDENTS
AB Addressing complex scientific and societal challenges increasingly requires collaboration across disciplinary and institutional boundaries. However, most interdisciplinary educational initiatives remain confined within a single course or institution, limiting opportunities for students to engage in learning environments that reflect the distributed and collaborative nature of contemporary research and professional practice. In this perspectives article, we present a design-oriented pedagogical framework for cross-institutional interdisciplinary education that integrates two independent undergraduate courses offered at separate post-secondary institutions. The model enables collaboration between biomedical engineering and immunology students through a shared interdisciplinary project centered on the emerging field of immunoengineering. We describe key design principles underlying this approach, including defining discipline-specific and shared learning outcomes, supporting the development of disciplinary competencies alongside interdisciplinary collaboration skills, and designing project-based assessments that facilitate collaboration across institutional and scheduling constraints. Drawing on two iterations of implementation, we also reflect on practical administrative and curricular challenges encountered and strategies used to address them. Together, this work provides a discipline-agnostic framework and practical considerations for implementing cross-institutional interdisciplinary education, contributing to ongoing efforts to prepare students for collaborative, interdisciplinary practice and problem-solving.

TI Practice-Integrated Research Seedbeds: A conceptual framework for
   embedding inquiry in management education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Management education; Undergraduate research; Research-based learning;
   Communities of practice; Evidence-based management
ID UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH; BUSINESS SCHOOLS; STUDENTS; EXPERIENCES;
   RELEVANCE; PERCEPTIONS; CHALLENGES; KNOWLEDGE; ACADEMICS
AB Business schools prepare students for professional action but often provide limited training on how evidence is produced, evaluated, and used in managerial decisions. This gap weakens the use of evidence in practice and perpetuates a research-practice divide. Although undergraduate research and research-based learning have demonstrated strong benefits across disciplines, their integration into management education remains fragmented and peripheral. This study introduces a conceptual framework for Practice-Integrated Research Seedbeds (PIRS), which repositions inquiry as a core professional competence rather than an academic exercise. PIRS are structured learning communities in which undergraduate students engage in sustained, mentored inquiry while addressing authentic organizational problems. Drawing on scholarship in undergraduate research, communities of practice, and evidence-based management, the framework specifies core components, design principles, and ethical and quality safeguards that enable scalable implementation without undermining the practitioner orientation of business programs. This study further proposes an evaluation agenda that captures students' learning, professional outputs, engagement processes, and institutional and societal impacts. Although developed for management education, the framework offers transferable design logic for other professionally oriented fields seeking to integrate inquiry into practice.

TI Understanding stuttering through the lens of women who stutter: A
   reflexive thematic analysis of the women who stutter podcast
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Stuttering; Women Who Stutter; Reflexive Thematic Analysis;
   Intersectionality
ID QUALITY-OF-LIFE; IMPACT; ADULTS; IDENTITY
AB Despite advancements in stuttering research, the lived experiences of women who stutter (WWS) remain significantly underrepresented. This study explores these multifaceted experiences across educational, professional, relational, psychosocial, identity-related, and personal domains, while also attending to the intersectional dimensions of gender and stuttering that uniquely shape their lives. Drawing on a reflexive thematic analysis of 80 episodes of the Women Who Stutter: Our Stories podcast, the study amplifies women's voices and highlights dimensions of stuttering often overlooked in research and practice. These episodes were recorded between 2010 and 2025. Using reflexive thematic analysis, this study identified four overarching themes: (1) the multifaceted impact of stuttering across life domains; (2) more than fluency: the internal landscape of stuttering; (3) from struggle to strength: women's journey with stuttering; and (4) the power of shared spaces: being a woman in the world of stuttering. Findings highlight how stuttering intersects with gendered expectations, identity formation, social stigma, and mental health. Participants' narratives revealed how disclosure, community connection, and therapeutic validation shaped pathways from concealment to empowerment. This study amplifies the voices of WWS and calls for more intersectional, gender-responsive approaches to stuttering research, therapy, and advocacy.

TI From Savings to Nutrition: How Stokvels Currently Operate and How They
   Could Enable Nutrition-Sensitive Interventions: A Realist Evaluation in
   South Africa
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE stokvels; informal savings groups; food security; dietary diversity;
   South Africa
ID FOOD INSECURITY; HEALTH
AB Objective: We examined how informal rotating savings and credit associations influence food purchasing and nutrition-related behaviors in urban communities with low income, and we explored their potential as platforms for adding nutrition value to purchasing decisions and behavior change interventions. Design: We conducted a qualitative realist evaluation guided by an Initial Programme Theory. We analyzed interview and focus group discussion data thematically to identify context-mechanism-outcome configurations shaping decision-making and food choices. Setting: Two urban communities with low income in Cape Town, South Africa. Participants: Sixty individuals from 20 grocery stokvels participated, including 20 leaders interviewed individually and 40 general members in 4 focus group discussions. Analysis: Thematic analysis examined governance structures, collective decision-making, food purchasing practices, and mechanisms relevant to nutrition-focused education and interventions. Results: Stokvels comprised 10-30 members contributing ZAR200-ZAR1500 monthly. All operated under formal constitutions, with 85% enforcing penalties for rule breaches. Bulk purchasing of staple foods, sugar, and processed meats occurred in 95% of stokvels, whereas only 1 group considered nutritional value. Stokvels were predominantly women-led (95%). Conclusions and Implications: Stokvels are well-governed and socially cohesive groups. While governance and collective systems generate economic leverage, they also shape purchases toward shelf-stable, nutrient-poor foods.

AB Objective: To examine if variation in session format and content of a prenatal obesity prevention program is associated with fruit and vegetable (FV) voucher redemption in Hispanic/Latino pregnant participants. Methods: A secondary analysis of participants who received FV vouchers in a single-arm feasibility trial. TI Food Insecurity, Multilevel Coping Strategies, and Depression among
   Single Female Caregivers: Findings from the It Study
SO JOURNAL OF NUTRITION EDUCATION AND BEHAVIOR
LA English
DT Article
DE food insecurity; coping behavior; depression; women; caregivers
ID NUTRITION ASSISTANCE PROGRAM; MENTAL-HEALTH; FAMILIES; MOTHERS
AB Objective To investigate relationships among food security status severity, multilevel food insecurity coping strategies, and depression in single female caregivers of children. Methods A convenience sample of US caregivers (n = 86) with high poverty rates provided cross-sectional survey data in 2022-2023. We used regression to examine associations among key variables. Results We documented high rates of food insecurity (76%) and depression (78%). More severe food insecurity was associated with more depressive symptoms (P = 0.004) and greater use of community, interpersonal, and individual food insecurity coping strategies (P < 0.05). Food insecurity severity was unrelated to federal policy-related coping strategy use. Greater use of community, interpersonal, and some individual (shopping, tradeoffs) coping strategies was associated with more depressive symptoms (P < 0.05); policy-level strategy use and individual rationing were not. Conclusions and Implications Findings recommend targeted interventions addressing intersections of coping with food insecurity and mental health among high-risk groups, particularly during high-risk times (e.g., coronavirus 2019 pandemic).

TI "The Absence of Criticism Constitutes Sufficient Praise?" Development
   and Implementation of a "Feedback Team Time-Out" in Surgical Training
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE surgical feedback; surgical training; feed-back tool; learning
   environment; feedback culture
ID SAFETY; COMMUNICATION; PERCEPTIONS; SURGEONS
AB INTRODUCTION: Feedback is essential for the assessment of competencies and addressing measures for improvement. It leads to greater satisfaction and maintains high-quality standards in healthcare delivery. Feedback is an integral part of medical education, but structured feedback is rare in surgical training. In Germany, postoperative feedback discussions take place regularly in only 12% of all surgeries. The aim of this study is therefore to improve feedback in surgical training by developing, implementing, and evaluating a feedback tool called "Feedback Team-Time-Out" and to assess the feedback culture before and after the introduction of this tool. METHODS: The feedback tool was developed in a stepwise, iterative process by an interdisciplinary team and is based on the WHO checklist. After the tool was developed, an exploratory pre-post intervention study was conducted in the Department of Visceral Surgery at Kiel University Hospital from February to September 2024 to assess the perioperative feedback culture before and after implementation of the tool. Questionnaires were used to assess the quantity, quality, and content of perioperative feedback, and the feedback tool was subsequently evaluated. The questionnaires were completed by both the trainees and the trainers. RESULTS: Perioperative feedback was documented using questionnaires in 69% of all training procedures before the tool was introduced and in 86% after its introduction. Before the introduction of the tool, intraoperative feedback was given in 72.5% of procedures vs. in 87% after introduction, according to trainees (p = 0.064), and postoperative feedback in 31.4% vs. 42.6% (p = 0.234). According to the trainers, intraoperative feedback was provided to 82.2% of trainees in the pre-intervention phase (p = 0.085) and to 75% in the postintervention phase (p = 0.009). Preoperative discussion of the learning objective increased from 11.5% to 44.4% (p < 0.001) according to trainees and from 26.7% to 70.8% (p < 0.001) according to trainers. In the evaluation, trainers and trainees confirmed that the tool leads to more feedback in surgical training. The most common reasons given for not using the tool and not giving feedback in general were a lack of time, insufficient staffing, and the absence of structured workflows. In an effort to improve the feedback culture and surgical training in everyday surgical practice, both trainers and trainees expressed a desire for more time and the importance of feedback to be strengthened in everyday clinical practice. CONCLUSIONS: Postoperative feedback is rarely given in surgical training. Introducing a feedback tool can be the first step to establish a surgical feedback culture and thereby improve surgical training and outcomes.

TI Understanding coaches' perspectives on sport as a driver of
   employability-related soft skills in athletes with intellectual
   disabilities
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Coach perceptions; Workforce; Learning disabilities; Physical activity;
   Employability skills; Labour market
ID QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; PHYSICAL-ACTIVITY; PEOPLE; WORK; EMPLOYMENT;
   OPPORTUNITIES; PRAGMATISM
AB Background: In an evolving global workforce, soft skills (personal, non-technical) are increasingly essential, yet individuals with intellectual disabilities face employment barriers. Sports participation offers a unique context to foster these skills, but coaches' awareness and strategies to support their development remain underexplored. This study aimed to explore coaches' perspectives on the role of sport in fostering soft skills among athletes with intellectual disabilities and their relevance for employability. Method: Underpinned by a pragmatic paradigm, this study interviewed 30 licensed coaches working with athletes with intellectual disabilities. All from Spain and Andorra with experience in national or international competitions across different sports (i.e., basketball, futsal, swimming). Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis through an abductive lens, iteratively moving between participant narratives and existing frameworks of employability. Results: The analysis revealed that while coaches value soft skills, they demonstrate limited initial awareness of the direct link between sport and employment. Technical training is consistently prioritized over soft skills development, which is viewed as an inherent outcome of sport. Coaches identified athlete strengths and developmental gaps. These results are further analysed through four main themes: (1) sport-employability relationship; (2) soft skill development; (3) key soft skills for employment identified through sport; and (4) athletes' skill progression. Conclusions: Coaches notice soft skill development but rarely apply explicit strategies. The identified gaps in coach awareness suggest that structured training and interventions could support coaches in intentionally cultivating these skills through their trainings, thereby enhancing the employability and social inclusion of athletes with intellectual disabilities.

TI Academic language demands and math-specific demands in test items:
   Relationships and effects on student performance by home language
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Test items; Academic language; Mathematical competencies; Second
   language learners
ID LINGUISTIC COMPLEXITY; MINORITY-STUDENTS; MATHEMATICS; LEARNERS; IMPACT;
   COMPREHENSION; COMPETENCES; ABILITY; MODEL
AB Second language learners are often considered disadvantaged in mathematics assessments due to academic language demands embedded in test items. These demands are frequently treated as construct-irrelevant, yet their relationship to math-specific requirements remains unclear. This study investigated (1) the association between academic language features and mathematical demands in Grade 8 standardized test items and (2) whether these demands differentially affect students depending on home language. We analyzed 153 items from the German VERA 8 assessment using established coding frameworks for linguistic and mathematical competencies. Correlational analyses showed that academic language demands are systematically related to mathspecific demands, with patterns varying across competencies. Linear mixed modeling revealed that students with a non-exclusively German home language had lower solution frequencies. However, performance differences were smaller in tasks with greater demands in representations, problem solving, and technical skills. The findings suggest that linguistic demands are intertwined with mathematical competencies rather than purely construct-irrelevant.

TI Spatial machine heuristic: Effects of agent type and interaction
   environment on foreign language speaking anxiety and willingness to
   communicate
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE MAIN model; Machine heuristic; Spatial machine heuristic; Foreign
   language speaking anxiety; Willingness to communicate
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY; SOCIAL PRESENCE; STUDENTS; PROFICIENCY; IMPACT; ANOVA
AB This study examined how agent type (human vs. AI) and interaction environment (real vs. cyber) independently and jointly shape foreign language speaking anxiety (FLSA) and willingness to communicate (WTC) in speaking practice. Drawing on the MAIN model, the machine heuristic, and an exploratory spatial machine heuristic, a 2 & times; 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted. Results showed that AI agents led to greater reductions in FLSA than human agents, and cyber environments led to greater reductions in FLSA than real environments. No significant main effects of agent type or interaction environment were found for WTC, but interaction effects emerged for both FLSA reduction and WTC, suggesting that the two outcomes may respond differently to combined agent and spatial cues. Moderated mediation analyses further showed that perceived comfort with the environment served as an important psychological pathway linking interaction environment to both outcomes, although this pathway did not differ significantly by agent type. These findings suggest that agent cues and spatial cues shape FLSA and WTC through partly different mechanisms, and that perceived comfort with the interaction environment plays a meaningful role in linking spatial context to affective speaking outcomes.

TI Strategies for enhancing K-12 teachers' competence in outdoor education:
   Insights from a meta-analysis
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Meta-analysis; Enhancement strategies; Outdoor education; Teacher
   competence
ID SELF-EFFICACY BELIEFS; ADVENTURE EDUCATION; PERSPECTIVES; EXPERIENCES;
   ENVIRONMENT; KNOWLEDGE; ACCURACY; PROJECT; FIELD; BIAS
AB Teachers' outdoor education competence is critical to the quality and sustainability of outdoor learning. Although prior research has examined strategies for enhancing this competence, the evidence remains fragmented and heterogeneous. This study synthesized 39 effect sizes derived from 25 empirical studies published between 2014 and 2025. Guided by a strategy-context-competence analytical framework, a three-level meta-analytic model was employed to account for the dependence among multiple effect sizes within studies. The results revealed a positive and statistically significant overall effect of competence-enhancement strategies in outdoor education, while highlighting substantial contextual variability. These findings suggest that strategies for strengthening teachers' outdoor education competence are promising, particularly through coherent, sustained, and contextsensitive professional learning.

TI Professionalism, multicultural preparation, and pedagogical practice: A
   comparative study of pre-service teachers' experiences in Cameroon and
   Indonesia
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Pre-service teachers; Professionalism; Multiculturalism; Pedagogical
   practices; Comparative teacher education; Postcolonial contexts
ID POLICY
AB This article examines how teacher education programmes in Cameroon and Indonesia prepare pre-service teachers for the teaching profession and how their experiences compare across two postcolonial and culturally diverse contexts. Addressing a gap in comparative teacher-education research, the study explores pre-service teachers' perceptions of professionalism, multicultural preparation, pedagogical practice, societal perceptions of teaching and programme-related challenges. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 pre-service teachers and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. The findings indicate that preparedness is shaped through different institutional pathways. Cameroonian pre-service teachers associated preparedness primarily with academic progression and upgrading of qualifications, whereas Indonesian participants emphasised certification, competency-based preparation and structured professional pathways. Across both contexts, participants highlighted the importance of continuous professional development, professional recognition and pedagogical competence, while also reporting theory-practice gaps, infrastructural constraints and policy-related uncertainties. This article provides comparative insights into how contexts, policies and programmes shape equitable teacher preparedness.

ID INSTRUCTIONAL LEADERSHIP; PRINCIPAL LEADERSHIP; CHINA; STRATEGIES
AB Over recent decades, teacher professional learning has gained attention for improving schools and student outcomes. TI How do adolescents understand, analyze, and evaluate misinformation on
   social media? - Chinese students' perspectives from task-based
   interviews
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Adolescent; Fake news; Information evaluation; Media and information
   literacy; Misinformation; Social media
ID INTERPERSONAL-TRUST; CREDIBILITY; DISSONANCE; SCIENCE; AGREEMENT; NEWS
AB Adolescents increasingly rely on social media for information, yet often struggle to discern credible content from widespread online misinformation. Guided by dual-process theory, this study employed a task-based interview design to examine how different cognitive processing modes contribute to adolescents' evaluation of misinformation. Twenty-two students aged 10 to 15 years from the Chinese Mainland completed simulated social media information evaluation tasks designed to elicit either impulsive (time-pressured, intuitive) or reflective (evidence-based, analytical) reasoning. Immediately after task completion, structured task-based interviews were conducted to investigate their decision-making process during evaluation. Thematic analysis revealed that evaluation processes were highly context-dependent, shaped by cognitive factors, content features, and perceived relevance. The findings clarify the interplay between intuition and reflection during adolescents' information evaluation, highlighting how cognitive and motivational factors jointly inform their strategies. This study contributes to media and information literacy research by providing empirical insights into adolescents' thinking and reasoning processes when confronting misinformation.

TI Traditionalist, supplementer, or reformer? medical student use of
   non-official curricular resources
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Non-traditional resources; commercial learning platforms; self-regulated
   learning
ID FACULTY
AB Objectives: The purpose of this study was to explore why and how medical students use non-traditional learning resources relative to the formal curriculum, to inform curriculum development efforts, and support self-directed learning. Methods: A qualitative study grounded in a pragmatic research approach was conducted using semi structured interviews with medical students at the University of Ottawa. Participant recruitment occurred via email/social media, and a pre survey was used to ensure sampling of both low-and high-level resource users. Transcripts were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis in NVivo. Analysis was both deductive, guided by self-regulated learning (motivation, goal setting, feedback, self-monitoring), and inductive to capture unanticipated themes. Results: Twenty-nine students participated (18 pre-clerkship; 11 clerkship). Four themes were developed: two addressing motivations for using non-traditional resources- the traditional curriculum is repetitive and inflexible and non-traditional resources are high-yield and flexible; one addressing goal setting-studying for today's exam or tomorrow's patient; and one addressing how students engage with resources, captured through three archetypes-the Traditionalist, the Supplementer, and the Reformer. Conclusions: This study demonstrates how medical students navigate learning by turning to non-traditional resources, shaped by their motivations, goal orientations, and distinct engagement patterns. These insights highlight opportunities to streamline and modernize curricula, integrate vetted high yield resources, and strengthen students' self-regulated learning skills. Leveraging the three learner archetypes can further guide curriculum planning by recognizing diverse learning approaches, engaging Supplementers as indicators of curricular gaps, supporting Traditionalists with structured pathways, and viewing Reformers' non-attendance as an expression of SRL rather than disengagement.

TI The critical extension framework: making organisational assumptions
   explicit in multilingual writing assessment
SO LANGUAGE TESTING IN ASIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Assessment validity; Critical extension framework; Rhetorical diversity;
   Teacher agency; Epistemological pluralism; Multilingual assessment
ID ASSESSMENT LITERACY
AB At the construct-articulation stage, current ESL writing rubrics quietly pull rhetorical preference into the operational definition of language proficiency. The interpretive consequences reach beyond measurement alone: once scores cannot tell organisational strategy apart from language control, teacher interpretation, feedback, and gatekeeping decisions all lose precision. This framework-development study traces the problem through critical discourse analysis of four major frameworks (TOEFL iBT, IELTS Academic Writing, CEFR, and classroom assessment principles). It shows how descriptor language governing organisation, coherence, and development encodes linear, thesis-first norms. Coding-scheme stability is established through intra-analyst (Cohen's kappa = 1.00) and inter-analyst (81.7 per cent agreement) checks on stratified subsets matched in size and scheme (12 of 34; 35.3 per cent). The Critical Extension Framework (CEF) names this diagnosis explicitly as pattern recognition folded into rhetorical effectiveness at the descriptor level. It responds by inserting a pattern-recognition step before scoring, separating the three inferential layers that current rubrics conflate: pattern recognition, rhetorical effectiveness, and Language Resources. Situated within established validity architecture at the domain-description inference, the framework makes organisational assumptions explicit before they enter later scoring, generalisation, and use claims. A preliminary two-rater pilot suggests that Language Resources scores may converge when raters work from the scoring descriptors and scoring protocol in Appendix B together with the essay texts. Rhetorical Effectiveness ratings on the reader-responsible implicit essay show pronounced, construct-sensitive disagreement. That disagreement locates the framework's heaviest validation burden. The point holds with particular force for multilingual writing assessment in Asian EFL/ESL contexts.

TI Constraints and Strategic Pathways in Cotton Cultivation
SO CASE STUDIES IN THE ENVIRONMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE sustainable cotton farming; DPSIR framework; problems in cotton farming;
   solutions in cotton farming
ID CHALLENGES
AB Cotton farming in India faces socioeconomic constraints and unstable market conditions. The present study assesses the problems and possible solutions in cotton growing in Ahilyanagar, Maharashtra. Insights from 130 cotton growers, supported by the DPSIR (Driver, Pressure, State, Impact, Response) framework and a problem-solution tree, are presented. TI Logical Transformation of University Governance in a Risk Society:
   Evidence From High-Risk Teaching and Research Settings
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE accountability; auditability; China; high-risk laboratories; incident
   reporting; qualitative interviews; risk society; safety governance;
   traceability; university governance
ID RANKINGS; PERFORMANCE
AB Universities are often imagined as epistemic institutions oriented towards experimentation and openness, yet in high-risk teaching and research settings they increasingly operate as risk organizations. Drawing on risk society theory, this study examines how governance rationalities are reshaped in high-risk environments within a university in south-eastern coastal China. Based on 22 semi-structured interviews conducted across the governance chain, including principal investigators and course leaders, technicians and laboratory managers, EHS and safety staff, administrators, and laboratory users, the paper analyzes how manufactured uncertainty and accountability pressures are organized in everyday routines. The findings identify four interlinked mechanisms. First, competence is reformatted from tacit expertise into auditable evidence through training certification, SOP sign-off, access authorization, and formal record-keeping. Second, accountability is organized through 'signature politics', producing traceable responsibility chains that redistribute exposure while encouraging defensive compliance. Third, risk governance operates through temporal regimes-approval lead times, audit cycles, and renewal requirements-that collide with the rhythms of teaching and experimental work, generating informal workarounds. Fourth, governance is also affective and moral: incident and near-miss reporting may support collective learning or reproduce fear, depending on whether disclosure is protected or triggers accountability cascades. Conceptually, the paper advances institutional defensibility as a mechanism through which universities seek legitimacy under conditions of uncertainty. Practically, it shows that effective risk governance depends on aligning auditability with situated judgement, protecting reporting as voice, and matching responsibility with authority in high-risk academic work.

TI The role of comparative continuation tasks in chunk learning
SO ASIAN-PACIFIC JOURNAL OF SECOND AND FOREIGN LANGUAGE EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Chunk learning; Comparative continuation tasks; Alignment effect;
   Dynamic development
ID CHINESE LEARNERS; REPETITION; LANGUAGE; USAGE
AB Chunk learning has been crucial in English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) learning. This study introduces comparative continuation tasks into chunk learning, exploring whether it can promote chunk learning efficiency. This study adopts an experimental approach which collects quantitative data to assess students' chunk learning performance. Sixty-two Chinese college students as EFL learners took part in this research. We compared the impact of different chunk learning tasks on acquiring verbal chunks, nominal chunks, discourse chunks and idiomatic chunks in continual phases. The results indicate that (1) comparative continuation tasks yield better chunk learning output than repetitive translation, cloze and recitation; (2) chunk learning develops in an accumulative and dynamic way, and comparative continuation tasks constantly promote chunk learning after several rounds; (3) comparative continuation tasks provide a scaffold for EFL learners to use and imitate. Comparative continuation tasks successfully trigger an alignment effect which bridges the gap between chunk learning and chunk use, and their interaction is strengthened after several rounds of comparative continuation tasks. The proposed comparative continuation tasks complement the current chunk learning methods.

   discrimination in surgery
ID WOMEN
AB Early obstacles to career progression of women in surgery present a major challenge in a variety of surgical subspecialties. Although there is a variety of literature on the attitudes and needs of female residents and trainees to foster interest in a career as a surgeon, there is a lack of research about the perspectives of female medical students about a possible career as a surgeon. TI Self-Care in Graduate Counseling Students: Examining Personal and
   Academic Predictors Through the Job Demands-Resources Model
SO COUNSELOR EDUCATION AND SUPERVISION
LA English
DT Article
DE burnout; ecological systems theory (EST); graduate counseling students;
   job demand-resources (JD-R); self-care
ID STATISTICAL POWER; BURNOUT; WELLNESS; REGRESSION; EFFICACY
AB Self-care is a critical competency for graduate counseling students (GCS), essential to their wellness and professional functioning. However, intensive academic and clinical demands often impede self-care engagement, elevating burnout risk. Using the job demands-resources model, this study examined how personal resources, academic environmental demands, and academic environmental resources predict GCS' engagement in self-care. Ecological systems theory informed the hierarchical entry of variables into the regression analysis, which drew on survey data from 217 GCS enrolled in CACREP-accredited programs across the United States. Personal resources initially predicted self-care engagement; however, when burnout, an indicator of the cumulative impact of academic demands, was included in the model, personal resources were no longer significant, and burnout negatively predicted self-care engagement. Burnout emerged as the strongest negative predictor of self-care. Findings highlight the persistence of burnout despite the presence of resources, underscoring the need for early interventions and structural changes in counselor education programs to alleviate systemic pressures and promote sustainable self-care practices.

TI Early intervention professionals and spoken language interpreter
   collaboration: Essential knowledge for supporting families of children
   with hearing loss
SO DEAFNESS & EDUCATION INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Children; hearing loss; multilingual; interpreter; culturally and
   linguistically diverse; early intervention educators; speech-language
   pathologists; audiologists
ID DEAF/HARD
AB For parents who speak a language different from the early childhood intervention (ECI) professionals working with their child, an interpreter is a crucial member of the early intervention team. This article considers the perspectives of spoken language interpreters and ECI professionals providing services to the families of children with hearing loss (CHL) about the knowledge needed prior to collaborating in an ECI appointment. The study collected survey responses from 69 ECI professionals who had experience working with interpreters and 23 spoken language interpreters working in Australia. Participants' responses indicated it was important for interpreters to know key terminology in the languages being used, the purpose of the appointment, the language situation of the family, and awareness about communication in CHL and disability. Three themes emerged when examining what ECI professionals need to know: knowledge and skills to have about interpreting (the briefing process, communication, working with interpreters), knowledge and skills to have about interpreters (interpreter competencies, interpreter appropriateness), and knowledge to share with the interpreter (about the appointment, professional knowledge). These findings provide a roadmap of key skill and knowledge areas for which training and materials can be developed to support more effective ECI professional-interpreter collaboration to better support families of CHL who are culturally and linguistically diverse.

TI Understanding ethical dimensions of AI in higher education: insights
   from faculty members and students
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL TECHNOLOGY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Ethics; Higher education; faculty members;
   students; mixed method
ID AGENCY
AB This study, conducted using an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design, aims to examine the views of faculty members and students on ethical issues related to the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education. In the quantitative phase, data were collected via a survey from 971 students and 135 faculty members, followed by semi-structured interviews with 23 students and 14 faculty members to obtain qualitative data. The findings show that both groups generally expressed supportive views regarding the ethical use of AI, but these views took different forms at the individual, technological, institutional, and societal levels. Faculty members emphasized the importance of ethical principles but pointed out the lack of institutional guidelines and support. Students, on the other hand, stated that AI tools were beneficial in their learning processes, but expressed uncertainty about the sharing of ethical responsibilities and the assessment of the ethical appropriateness of the processes. Qualitative findings showed that perspectives were shaped in six themes, revealing a multidimensional ethical structure in the use of AI in education. Participants emphasized that while AI facilitates learning, its excessive use can have negative effects on cognitive skills. The results indicate that, in order for AI to be used ethically in higher education, professional development support should be provided to faculty members, courses covering ethical dimensions should be added to curricula, clear ethical usage guidelines should be established at universities, and these guidelines should be updated through interdisciplinary collaboration.

TI Validation of a School Climate Walkthrough Assessment
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF SCHOOL & EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Assessment; ecological variables; environment; observation; school
   climate; self-report; student voice
ID CLASSROOM CLIMATE; PERCEPTIONS; ACHIEVEMENT; STUDENTS; SUPPORT; SAFETY
AB School climate measurement is an increasingly important component of data-driven school improvement efforts. School climate assessment is enhanced by data triangulation, a process of analyzing school climate via subjective reports from students, staff, and families, observer ratings, and outcome data within the context of school-level variables. The present study involved the development of a school climate observation and student interview tool aligned with data triangulation methods. The School Climate Walkthrough Assessment (SCWA) is a measure for observing environmental indicators and behaviors alongside quantitative and qualitative student reports of school climate for a general snapshot of school quality. The SCWA was developed as a complement the Georgia Elementary School Climate Survey (GESCS), a component of the Georgia School Climate Survey which has been validated, translated, and adapted for use across international settings. Validity evidence for the SCWA is discussed with a focus on practical utility of the SCWA.

TI Universal Screening in Practice: A Comparative Study of the CogAT and
   ACT Aspire for Gifted Identification
SO JOURNAL FOR THE EDUCATION OF THE GIFTED
LA English
DT Article
DE CogAT; ACT aspire; achievement tests; gifted identification; education
   policy
ID COGNITIVE-ABILITIES TEST; LOW-INCOME; REPRESENTATION; EDUCATION;
   STUDENTS; MATHEMATICS; PROGRAMS; SCIENCE; TESTS; STEM
AB Research shows that many academically accomplished students from disadvantaged backgrounds are not identified for gifted and talented programs. This study investigates a large sample of more than 10,000 students that took both the Cognitive Abilities Test (CogAT) and the American College Testing (ACT) Aspire test. We examined test similarities and differences with an eye to widen the net for gifted identification in practice. This study demonstrates that the ACT Aspire and CogAT have a significant overall correlation of r = .59. However, the correlation varies across cohorts noticeably from r = .72 to r = .46. This variation in correlations and inconsistency in the predictive nature of diversity of both tests across cohorts suggests greater caution in the interchangeable use of the ACT Aspire and CogAT as gifted indicators. Our findings support the practice of using more than one test as part of the identification process.

TI InterruptedCase Studies: Engaging Students by ConnectingFood Chemistry
   to Real World Issues
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate; Writing; ProblemSolving; Food Chemistry
ID FOOD
AB The preparation of many foods often involves high temperatures and extended cooking times, which, particularly in the presence of reducing sugars and amino acids, can promote the formation of acrylamide, a potentially carcinogenic compound produced during the Maillard reaction. In educational settings, this reaction is commonly addressed in laboratory courses through food preparation activities that are used to introduce its underlying chemical principles. This study investigated how students engaged with key concepts related to the Maillard reaction and strategies for reducing acrylamide in food through the interrupted case study method. A Descending Hierarchical Classification analysis of 53 students' texts using IRAMUTEQ revealed students' engagement with terminology and discussions concerning acrylamide formation and mitigation in foods such as French fries, toasted bread, and roasted coffee. These findings support the use of case-based learning as a pedagogical approach to connect food chemistry with socioscientific issues and support informed decision-making about dietary practices.

ID BACTERIAL ADHESION
AB Biomaterials used in medical implants are prone to bacterial adhesion and biofilm formation, which can lead to persistent infections. , which is a major cause of prosthesis-associated infections, adheres to biomaterial surfaces and forms biofilms, increasing resistance to antibiotics and immune responses, compromising the osseointegration. Protein adsorption on biomaterial surfaces plays a crucial role in bacterial adhesion. Serum albumin has the capacity to inhibit bacterial adhesion by creating a less favorable surface, whereas fibronectin (FN) promotes bacterial attachment by binding to bacterial fibronectin-binding proteins. This work studies the influence of human serum albumin (HSA) and FN coatings on adhesion of to polycaprolactone (PCL) scaffolds, commonly used in tissue regeneration. TI Evaluating Scoring Mechanisms for Measuring the Stroop Effect in
   Individuals With Down Syndrome
SO JOURNAL OF INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE cognitive inhibition; Down syndrome; Stroop task
ID SCHOOL-AGE-CHILDREN; TEST NORMATIVE DATA; ALZHEIMERS-DISEASE;
   INTELLECTUAL DISABILITIES; EXECUTIVE DYSFUNCTION; YOUNG-CHILDREN;
   AMYLOID-BETA; ADULTS; ASSOCIATION; PERFORMANCE
AB Background The Cat/Dog Stroop task is a modification of the original Stroop task as a measure of cognitive inhibition frequently used in studies of individuals with Down syndrome (DS). There is great heterogeneity in scoring mechanisms for this task and similar Stroop tasks, potentially impacting convergence of and interpretation of study findings. We review scoring mechanisms used with the Stroop task in the general population and those that are used among individuals with DS to evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of these scoring mechanisms in this population.Method We reviewed the literature to identify current scoring mechanisms used for the original Stroop task and for the Cat/Dog Stroop task among individuals with DS. Using a sample of 146 children and adults with DS ages 6-29 years who completed the Cat/Dog Stroop, we independently modelled the identified scoring mechanisms. Scoring mechanisms were assessed for skew, kurtosis and normality as assessed through the Anderson-Darling test with the full sample and by age bands.Results Eight distinct scoring mechanisms were identified that could be used with the conditions present in the Cat/Dog Stroop task. Six of these eight scoring mechanisms had been used in studies of individuals with DS, with the remaining two mechanisms not yet applied to Cat/Dog Stroop in individuals with DS. Of these scoring mechanisms, one mechanism consistently emerged across stratified age groups as approximating normality for the Cat/Dog Stroop task based on skewness, kurtosis and tests of normality in a sample of individuals with DS.Discussion For consistency in how the Cat/Dog Stroop task is scored for children and adults with DS, we recommend that the number of correct responses in the incongruent condition should be divided by completion time in the incongruent condition. Additionally, for adults, incongruent completion time minus the congruent completion time or incongruent completion time divided by congruent completion time may also be appropriate.

TI Try a New Lens: A Pedagogical Framework for Student-Centred Literary
   Criticism Through Role-Play
SO LITERACY
LA English
DT Article
DE creative pedagogy; critical thinking; interpretive lenses; literary
   criticism; multiple perspectives; role-play
ID CRITICAL THINKING; GAMIFICATION
AB Although many teachers aspire to help their students become literary critics, implementing student-centred literary criticism in the secondary classroom remains challenging. Given the potential for critical thinking, literary criticism is an activity that many secondary English teachers aspire to bring to their classrooms. This article begins by reviewing existing research on the topic, which largely includes case-based and theoretical arguments for teaching specific interpretive lenses to secondary English students. It then presents a pedagogical framework for combining interpretive lenses, literary criticism actions and role-play design to facilitate student-centred literary criticism activities. The article proposes that teachers can develop role-play activities in which students try new lenses or ways of 'seeing' and interpreting a text. Drawing on practitioner-based examples, the Pedagogical Framework for Student-Centred Literary Criticism supports teachers in designing multiple-perspective curricula using role-play as a creative pedagogy. This article concludes that this framework offers English teachers an accessible approach utilizing creative pedagogy and facilitating student-centred literary criticism lessons in the English language arts classroom.

AB : Social learning theory posits that students calibrate their ability assessments over the course of secondary school. However, there is limited understanding of the developmental trajectories of subject-specific self-efficacy. Therefore, the present study investigated differences in changes in students' subject-specific self-efficacy within and across two grade levels (sixth and eighth grade) in two subjects (mathematics and English) in a three-wave longitudinal study. TI What is the point of the PhD in this age of uncertainty: Reframing
   researcher education
SO INNOVATIONS IN EDUCATION AND TEACHING INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE PhD education; researcher education; doctoral education; PhD careers;
   researcher careers
ID ENGAGEMENT
AB In contemporary European societies, we are living through increasingly turbulent times characterised by rapid societal shifts driven by new technologies, communication methods, and work practices. Simultaneously, universities face mounting external pressures such as government policies, funding cuts, and reallocation. In this paper, we view these challenges as an opportunity to reconsider the fundamental nature of PhD education. If the PhD, as we currently understand it, did not exist, what should it aim to achieve? We address this question through a research-informed approach that combines our own and others' studies on the PhD and post-PhD experience. We examine the spectrum of meanings associated with research, the variety of post-PhD careers, graduates' and employers' perspectives on graduate preparedness, the participation of non-academic stakeholders in research and PhD training, and the concepts of agency and purpose.

TI Beyond-school collaborations as social learning spaces: thresholds and
   value creation in school improvement
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL CHANGE
LA English
DT Article
DE Beyond-school collaboration; Inter-professional collaboration social
   learning spaces; School improvement; Thresholds; Value-creation cycles
ID NETWORKS; EQUITY; IMPACT
AB Responding to the need for context-sensitive approaches to school improvement, this study examines beyond-school collaborations (BSCs) as social learning spaces (SLSs) in initiatives addressing persistent and complex challenges. Drawing on value-creation cycles (VCCs) as an analytical lens, the study addresses two research questions: (1) What are the defining characteristics of BSCs? and (2) In what ways are these characteristics enabling or constraining collaborative processes for school improvement work within BSCs, as analysed through VCCs?. The empirical material is drawn from 15 Swedish municipalities working in collaboration with a national education agency and includes interviews, observations of project meetings, and field notes. The findings identify three interrelated characteristics-manageability, knowing, and attitudes-that shape how collaboration unfolds across institutional boundaries. Conceptualised as dynamic thresholds, these characteristics operate as practice-based conditions that influence participants' engagement and mediate movement across cycles of value creation. The findings suggest that collaboration across boundaries is not a fixed design feature but an ongoing accomplishment shaped by relational, organisational, and epistemic dynamics. BSCs appear most generative when they are as flexible as possible and as structured as necessary, with sustained attention to enabling and constraining thresholds in the domains of manageability, knowing, and attitudes. Engagement in VCCs supports expanded learning processes, pushes current knowledge boundaries, and contributes to the development of improvement-oriented cultures. In this sense, BSCs function as generative SLSs capable of addressing complex and "wicked" challenges through shared inquiry and capacity-building.
