TI The impacts of educational reform on teachers' emotions in the context
   of Vietnam
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL CHANGE
LA English
DT Article
DE Education reform; Teacher emotions; Vietnam; Professional development;
   Curriculum reform
ID SCHOOL TEACHERS; IDENTITIES; STUDENTS
AB This study was conducted to investigate the impact of the large-scale educational reform 2018 on teacher emotions in Vietnamese secondary education. A mixed methods approach was employed with an explanatory sequential design, utilizing a self-developed and validated survey questionnaire and semi-structured interviews. A total of 564 lower secondary and upper secondary teachers who were teaching subjects in the new curriculum participated in the study, with 21 of them interviewed later. The findings revealed that teachers experienced both positive and negative emotions; however, positive emotions were more prevalent and stronger than negative ones. Teachers expressed interest and curiosity about new teaching methods and were grateful for the reform as it provided professional development opportunities. However, they reported feelings of anxiety and confusion regarding the effective implementation of the reform. Teachers believed that the reform positively influenced their pedagogical knowledge and skills, and they acknowledged that it brought significant changes to the education system. Based on these findings, the study offers several implications for teachers and relevant stakeholders regarding teacher education.

TI Lighting in school environments: participatory design methods through
   workshop explorations at a pre-design phase
SO LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Research methods; Participatory design research; Workshop; Educational
   spaces; Lighting design
ID LEARNING ENVIRONMENTS; PERSPECTIVES; TECHNOLOGY; EDUCATION; PEDAGOGY
AB This study focuses on a workshop exploration based on participatory methods before lighting interventions at a primary school in east-central Sweden. This approach is based on participatory design (PD) principles, aiming to support teachers' and pupils' voices within educational research (ER), lighting design, and architecture disciplines. Two workshops are presented, one addressing teachers (n = 5) and the other addressing pupils (n = 33). The first workshop focused on lighting perception, while the second addressed pupils' choices of space for certain learning activities. Results from teachers' work revealed that higher light levels are evaluated more favorably for on-screen activities. Furthermore, shadow evaluation was the factor that varied the most when comparing the two lighting scenarios. Additionally, pupils' preferred working location depended on their activity, and the proximity to daylight was higher for individual tasks than group discussions. Findings from both workshops were later implemented as design directions to inform a larger research project on school lighting interventions.

TI A Taxonomy of Literacy Practices for Engaging with Artificial
   Intelligence: Reading and Writing in the Age of Generative AI
SO TECHTRENDS
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Generative AI; Digital literacy; Pedagogy; New
   literacies studies; Literacy practices
AB Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming reading and writing practices in and out of educational contexts, yet few frameworks exist to support students' responsible engagement with these tools. This conceptual paper proposes a taxonomy of literacy practices for engaging with AI, grounded in the new literacies of online reading comprehension (Leu et al., , ); Coiro, ). Using Leu et al.'s () five processing practices and Coiro's () multifaceted heuristic as an analytical lens, we identify seven interconnected practices students enact when reading and writing with AI. We conceptualize these not as hierarchical competencies but as socially situated practices enacted differently across contexts and purposes. For each practice, the taxonomy provides a description, an observable indicator, and ethical considerations embedded as intrinsic dimensions. This framework extends established new literacies scholarship into AI-mediated environments, providing educators with language and observable markers for supporting students' evolving literacy practices.

TI Memorable messages, perceived message deficiencies, and advice from
   estranged queer adolescents
SO COMMUNICATION EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Family communication; LGBTQIA+; estrangement; social learning theory;
   theory of memorable messages
ID 1ST-GENERATION COLLEGE-STUDENTS; SOCIAL SUPPORT; COMMUNICATION; FAMILY;
   GAY; SEX; PARENTS; SCHOOL; SOCIALIZATION; EDUCATION
AB This study explores the intersection of education and family socialization through memorable messages reported by adolescents who are estranged from their parents because of their queer identity (estranged queer adolescents [EQAs)]). Using the theory of memorable messages, 40 EQAs aged 13-19 described memorable messages they received during their estrangement process, the deficiencies in those messages, and messages they had for others. We identified five types of memorable messages: four negative (shame, violence, denial of gender, mismatched words and actions) and one positive (acceptance). EQAs reported three message deficiencies of lack of identity validation, emotional support, and protection. EQAs directed advice to parents (unconditional love and emotional responsiveness) and peers (self-acceptance and patience). Thematic co-occurrence analysis revealed a relationship between (a) the memorable message of denial of gender, (b) the perceived deficiency of support, and (c) advice for other EQAs to be patient; revealing how despite the negative memorable messages and lack of support EQAs received from their parents, they still had hope for a better future. These findings illuminate how EQAs make sense of memorable messages they received from their family and offers insights to foster more affirming environments within families and educational contexts.

TI Self-directed learning readiness in preclinical medical education:
   Patterns, variation, and academic outcomes from a mixed longitudinal and
   cross-sectional study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-directed learning; Self-regulation; Mixed-effects model;
   Longitudinal study; Academic performance; Preclinical medical education;
   Lifelong learning
ID STUDENTS; GENDER; COMPETENCE
AB Background The transition from undergraduate education to medical school demands increasing learner autonomy and self-regulation. Guided by Zimmerman's Self-Regulated Learning (SRL) theory and Grow's Staged Self-Directed Learning Model, this study examined how self-directed learning readiness (SDL-R), encompassing learning motivation, planning and implementation, self-monitoring, and interpersonal communication varies across the preclinical curriculum and how these domains relate to academic performance. Methods A mixed longitudinal and repeated cross-sectional study (2022-2024) was conducted among preclinical medical students (N = 807 responses; 434 unique students from three cohorts, Classes of 2025-2027) at an LCME-accredited US medical school. All enrolled first- and second-year students were eligible; recruitment was voluntary via web-based REDCap surveys administered once per semester. Linear mixed-effects models evaluated within-student change in total SDL-R and its four domains across semesters. Ordinary least-squares regression with cluster-robust standard errors assessed the contribution of standardized subscale scores to cumulative grade point averages. Bonferroni correction was applied within each family of comparisons, with effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals reported. Results SDL-R scores varied across preclinical semesters in a pattern consistent with developmental progression, with a modest decline in first-year Spring followed by recovery through year two. Planning and implementation was the strongest positive predictor of GPA in Year 1 (beta = 0.142, p = .004) and in the combined model (beta = 0.154, p < .001). The SDL-R domains collectively explained 22.2% of GPA variance in Year 1 (R & sup2; = 0.222) and 9.0% in Year 2 (R & sup2; = 0.090); the combined model explained 15.0% (R & sup2; = 0.150). Interpersonal communication showed a significant negative partial association with GPA, consistent with a statistical suppressor effect. Second-year students, older learners, males, and higher-achieving students showed higher SDL-R levels. Conclusion SDL-R is a dynamic, context-sensitive competency during preclinical training, with planning and implementation as its strongest academic predictor. Targeted curricular interventions that scaffold metacognitive planning, self-monitoring, and adaptive strategy use may enhance both academic performance and lifelong learning capacity.

TI Perceptions of medical dramas among medical students in the West Bank,
   Palestine: a cross-sectional study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; Medical dramas; Bioethics; Professionalism;
   Palestinian medical students; Hidden curriculum;
   Entertainment-education; Cultivation theory
ID TELEVISION
AB Background Medical dramas are widely consumed by medical students globally and may constitute an informal or hidden curriculum influencing professional identity, empathy, and ethical reasoning. Palestinian medical students represent an understudied population navigating a resource-constrained and geopolitically complex healthcare context. Objectives To investigate the perceptions of Palestinian medical students regarding medical dramas, including viewing habits, assessments of clinical and ethical realism, psychological and behavioural impacts, and the potential role of such media as an informal educational resource. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among 638 undergraduate medical students from five universities in the West Bank, Palestine, using convenience and snowball sampling. Data were collected via an online structured questionnaire adapted and culturally validated from the Czarny et al. (2008) instrument, incorporating forward-back translation, pilot testing (n = 15), and internal consistency assessment (Cronbach's alpha = 0.81). Descriptive statistics and Chi-square tests were applied. Results Mean age was 21.1 +/- 1.65 years; 66.8% were female. Most participants (73.4%) had watched medical dramas, primarily via digital streaming platforms. While 77.3% perceived clinical scenes as only slightly or moderately realistic, 41.9% considered ethical content to be moderately accurately depicted. Approximately 46.6% reported increased empathy and 47.2% reported increased study motivation. Drama viewers were significantly more likely to rate informal sources-family (p < 0.001), friends (p = 0.021), and online news (p = 0.037)-as important for ethical guidance, compared with non-viewers. Conclusions Palestinian medical students engage substantially with medical dramas and appraise their content critically. Associations between drama viewing and increased empathy, study motivation, and reliance on informal ethical guidance sources suggest a potential hidden-curriculum effect. Given the cross-sectional design and convenience sampling, causal inferences cannot be drawn. These findings support cautious integration of medical dramas into bioethics and professionalism curricula as supplementary teaching tools.

TI Nationwide survey of formal mentorship characteristics and perceptions
   among resident physicians in Japan
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Formal mentorship; Postgraduate medical education; Resident physicians;
   Gender diversity; Japan
ID MEDICINE; BURNOUT
AB Background Mentorship is considered essential in residency training, yet its structure and quality in Japan remain unclear.Methods We conducted a nationwide, multi-center descriptive study of postgraduate year (PGY) 1-2 residents who completed both the General Medicine In-Training Examination (GM-ITE) and a formal mentorship survey in 2024. Residents who declined participation, provided no response to the survey, had incomplete survey responses, or did not have a formal mentor were excluded.Results Of 9,179 residents who took the GM-ITE, 3,877 from 570 hospitals were analyzed. Most reported having one mentor (71.6%), and mentors were predominantly male (72.9%). Only 61.0% of programs offered lectures on mentorship. Mentoring interactions were relatively limited, with 60.4% of residents reporting meeting less than once a month.Conclusions Among residents with formally assigned mentors, important gaps remained in mentor diversity, feedback quality, and mentoring engagement. Efforts to strengthen mentor training, improve feedback practices, and promote more structured mentoring interactions may help optimize residents' educational and professional development.

TI Extended reality and web-based imaging in case-based anatomy education:
   a two-year study of knowledge retention on anomalies and variations
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Anatomical variations; Anatomy education; Case-based learning; Extended
   reality; Virtual reality; Educational measurement
ID MOBILE CECUM; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; CT
AB Background This prospective repeated-measures quasi-experimental educational study, conducted across two consecutive first-year medical school cohorts, aimed to develop and implement case-based learning (CBL) modules using three-dimensional (3D) models and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) within an extended reality (XR) environment. The intervention integrated anatomical variations and anomalies to enhance immediate learning and long-term knowledge retention. Methods MRI data from selected donors at the John A. Burns School of Medicine (JABSOM) were used to create XR-CBL modules. First-year medical students from the classes of 2024 (Cohort 2021) (n = 61) and 2025 (Cohort 2022) (n = 67) participated. Before the session, students received an email detailing the activity. During the gross anatomy laboratory, they accessed a website to explore cases featuring learning objectives, clinical and radiological data, 3D models, and MRIs. The XR experience utilized desktop-based XR technology. An assessment was administered before, immediately after, and eight weeks post-intervention. Students also completed a mixed-format feedback survey. Results A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed a significant effect of the intervention on student performance across both cohorts. For Cohort 2021, Wilks' Lambda = 0.384, F (2, 59) = 47.27, p < 0.001, partial eta & sup2; = 0.616. For Cohort 2022, Wilks' Lambda = 0.30, F (2, 65) = 72.72, p < 0.001, partial eta & sup2; = 0.691. Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni adjustments indicated significant improvements from pre-test to post-test and from pre-test to post-post-test for both cohorts (p < 0.01). There was no significant difference between the post-test and post-post-test scores (p = 1.00). In Cohort 2021, mean scores significantly increased from pre-test (3.9 +/- 1.9) to post-test (6.2 +/- 2.6) and were maintained at post-post-test (6.3 +/- 1.7). Similarly, Cohort 2022 demonstrated significant gains from pre-test (4.3 +/- 1.6) to post-test (7.6 +/- 2.2), with high retention at post-post-test (6.3 +/- 2.4). Pairwise comparisons confirmed that improvements from baseline were significant (p < 0.01), while no significant decay occurred between post- and post-post-assessments (p = 1.00). Conclusions Incorporating multimodal resources, including anatomical variations and anomalies through CBL, into the gross anatomy laboratory was associated with significant score improvements and positive student perceptions. Learners reported that the interactive, imaging-based tools helped them better understand complex anatomical relationships, particularly when anatomical variability was highlighted.

TI Competency based medical education: assessment of procedural and
   cognitive skills in gastroenterology residency training
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Competence by design; Entrustable professional activities; Ottawa
   surgical competency operating room evaluation
ID OTTAWA SURGICAL COMPETENCE; O-SCORE; DESIGN
AB Introduction Competence by Design (CBD) was implemented in Canada to assess physician trainees' ability to demonstrate competence via entrustable professional activities (EPAs) utilizing the Ottawa Surgical Competency Operating Room Evaluation (O-SCORE); a score originally validated to assess surgical competence. Our study assessed for differences in O-SCORE utilization between non-procedural (cognitive) and procedural EPA assessments in a real-world setting to inform future critical appraisal of CBD. Methods Adult Gastroenterology subspecialty EPA assessments from 2019 to 2023 at the University of Alberta were reviewed. Evaluator gender, clinical vs. academic practice, advanced training expertise, EPA type, and O-SCOREs were extracted from each EPA assessment. Competence assessments (achieved, neutral, not achieved) were assigned to each EPA assessment based on local competence committee protocols. Chi-squared testing with 95% confidence intervals were calculated. Results 2660 EPA assessments were included (1385 cognitive and 1275 procedural). Approximately 70% of total EPA assessments denote competence, with approximately 20% neutral, and < 10% indicating "competence not yet achieved". Proportionally higher cognitive EPA assessments denoted competence compared to procedural EPA assessments (75% vs. 63%, p < 0.01). Evaluator characteristics associated with EPA achievement were male gender, community (vs. academic), and hepatology (vs. luminal GI) practice. Discussion We report low rates of the full range of O-SCORE utilization and the majority amount of EPA assessments denoting competence. Further the proportion of EPAs assessed as success varied by evaluator characteristics (gender, specialty, and practice type). This stresses the need for continued cycles of critical appraisal to improve faculty assessment and feedback in residency trainee progress.

TI Knowledge, attitudes, practices and clinical preparedness regarding
   porcelain laminate veneers among dental interns
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Laminate veneer; Knowledge; Practice; Attitude; Students; Questionnaire
ID CERAMIC THICKNESS; TEETH
AB Background In recent years, increasing aesthetic expectations have led to a growing demand for porcelain laminate veneer treatments. This study aims to address a gap in the literature by evaluating the knowledge, attitudes, and practices of undergraduate dental students regarding porcelain laminate veneers, within the context of updated dental curricula, thereby providing insight into their current level of theoretical understanding and clinical preparedness.Methods This study employed a descriptive cross-sectional design. The sample consisted of final-year students from the Faculty of Dentistry at Atat & uuml;rk University. A total of 150 students were invited to participate; those who agreed and completed the questionnaire in full were administered a KAP-based survey adapted for porcelain laminate veneer applications.Results A total of 134 dental interns participated in the study, of whom 61.9% were female and 38.1% were male. Based on objective assessments, the level of theoretical knowledge was found to be high, with correct response rates ranging between 85% and 94% for many items; however, lower success rates were observed in technically demanding aspects, such as cement thickness effects on shade selection (28.4%) and preparation classifications (45.5%). Subjective evaluations revealed limited clinical experience and self-confidence; notably, only 32.1% of participants had encountered a laminate veneer case in clinical practice. While no significant difference was found in theoretical knowledge levels by gender (p = 0.083), male participants demonstrated significantly higher self-perceived clinical confidence scores compared to females (p = 0.024). A weak negative correlation was observed between objective knowledge scores and self-perceived clinical confidence scores (r = -0.201, p = 0.020).Conclusions Despite a high level of theoretical knowledge among dental interns, this theoretical knowledge was not reflected in students' self-perceived clinical preparedness and confidence. Furthermore, a weak negative correlation was identified between objective knowledge and self-perceived clinical confidence scores, suggesting these constructs are related but distinct. These findings highlight the need to strengthen simulation-based training, clinical case exposure, and complication management within undergraduate prosthodontic education.

TI A study on the application of the remote multidisciplinary team teaching
   model in clinical postgraduate education of urology
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Remote; Multidisciplinary team (MDT) teaching model; Postgraduate
   education; Clinical competency; Evaluation of teaching model
AB Background Postgraduate medical education increasingly requires learners to develop clinical reasoning, manage uncertainty, integrate heterogeneous clinical information and collaborate across disciplines. Multidisciplinary team (MDT) teaching may provide a clinically situated learning environment in which trainees can observe and participate in complex decision-making. However, evidence on the use of remote MDT teaching in urology postgraduate education remains limited.Methods This randomized controlled study included 76 professional master's students rotating through a surgical standardized residency training base. Students were assigned to a remote MDT teaching group or a conventional teaching group, with 38 students in each group. The remote MDT intervention was delivered as a structured teaching package that included pre-session case preparation, remote multidisciplinary case discussion, expert-guided case analysis, post-session reflection and iterative feedback. Outcomes included theoretical knowledge, clinical decision-making, practical skills, questionnaire-based evaluation of the teaching model and overall competency.Results Students in the remote MDT group achieved higher scores than those in the conventional teaching group in theoretical knowledge, clinical decision-making, questionnaire-based evaluation and overall competency. No significant between-group difference was observed in practical skills. The pattern of findings suggested that the remote MDT model had a stronger effect on outcomes requiring information integration, clinical reasoning and collaborative decision-making than on procedural performance.Conclusions Remote MDT teaching may be a useful component of urology postgraduate education, particularly for learning outcomes related to clinical reasoning and knowledge integration. Its value appears to derive not only from remote delivery, but also from the structured organization of preparation, multidisciplinary discussion, reflection and feedback. Procedural skill development remains dependent on supervised hands-on practice. Future multicentre studies are needed to confirm these findings and to examine which components of the intervention contribute most to learning.Trial registration Not applicable.

TI Students' views about alternatives to traditional dissertation for
   Master in Public Health: results of a virtual focus group
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF HEALTH PROMOTION AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Beliefs; education; employment and skills; educational settings; MPH;
   dissertation
ID PROGRAMS
AB A traditional dissertation remains a component of most Master in Public Health programmes, but there is increasing interest and use of alternatives. A virtual focus group of six students studying an online distance Master in Public Health explored their perceptions about dissertations and preferences for alternatives. Students value the dissertation as a means of consolidating learning and focusing in-depth on chosen topics. Alternatives were viewed as attractive but not always practical. Participants felt that additional options need to be accompanied by guidance to ensure students make the most appropriate choice for their future. Three types of students with different needs emerged; students aspiring to progress to a PhD should do a traditional dissertation, students already employed in a relevant role may choose a work-based dissertation or replace the dissertation with taught units, and students doing the MPH to increase their employability could choose a placement-based dissertation or replace the dissertation with work experience reflection. Innovations that introduce alternatives to the traditional dissertation would be welcomed by MPH students studying online, but they would need to be accompanied by suitable career advice to ensure students choose the most appropriate route for their future aspirations.

TI Sustainability in engineering education: an editorial and interpretive
   synthesis
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sustainability in engineering education; engineering education;
   education for sustainable development; integration; transformation;
   decolonisation
ID DECOLONIZATION; TRANSFORMATION
AB This editorial provides an introduction to and interpretive synthesis of the seventeen contributions to the European Journal of Engineering Education special issue on Sustainability in Engineering Education, and the current state, emerging trends, and future directions of the field. The special issue contributions indicate that sustainability in engineering education is moving beyond early add-on approaches towards broader curricular integration, yet transformative ambitions remain only partially realised and unevenly enacted across institutional, disciplinary, and national contexts. These insights are complemented by two additional perspectives: a reflective insider account of current trends at one European university and a critical challenge to dominant European viewpoints through South African scholarship on transformation and decolonisation. Beyond further curricular integration, the next phase of sustainability in engineering education is argued to depend on enhanced institutional reflexivity, epistemic plurality, and critical engagement with the purposes, assumptions, and societal responsibilities of engineering education and engineers.

TI 'Out into space?' - Engineering students' understanding of the carbon
   cycle and challenges they face while solving atmospheric CO accumulation
   tasks
SO EUROPEAN JOURNAL OF ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Stock-flow failure; Engineering Education; misconceptions; carbon cycle;
   real-world problem solving; mathematical modelling
ID CLIMATE-CHANGE; PUBLIC PERCEPTIONS; MENTAL MODELS; KNOWLEDGE; RISK;
   MISCONCEPTIONS; BELIEF
AB This study examines the challenges faced by engineering students in understanding atmospheric CO2 accumulation, a key concept for climate literacy and sustainable engineering. Through qualitative analysis of task-based interviews with third-year engineering-mathematics students from a Swedish university, we identify and categorise cognitive, metacognitive, and affective challenges in conceptualising the carbon cycle and solving CO2 mass balance tasks. Our findings reveal difficulties in integrating formal mathematical training with real-world environmental issues, underscoring the importance of addressing these multidimensional challenges in engineering education. The study highlights the need for pedagogical strategies - for mathematical modelling and climate education - that not only impart cognitive knowledge but also foster metacognitive skills and address affective factors related to climate change and problem-solving. By integrating sustainability-themed real-world problems into curricula, this research advocates for a holistic educational approach, preparing engineers to effectively contribute to climate change mitigation and sustainability efforts.

TI The Clinical Mentorship Program: a mixed-methods evaluation of a
   community-based medical education pathway program for high school
   students
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical education; Clinical education; Pathway program; Mentorship;
   Shadowing; Underrepresented students; Health equity
AB Students from low-income and underrepresented backgrounds face structural barriers to entering medicine, including limited access to early clinical exposure, physician guidance, and professional networks. To address these disparities, medical students at the Warren Alpert Medical School of Brown University created a year-long Clinical Mentorship Program (CMP) for high school students in Woonsocket, Rhode Island. The intervention combined monthly after-school instruction on basic science content and clinical skills by medical students with structured hospital-based shadowing and guided discussion with resident physicians. Using a mixed-methods pre-post design, the intervention evaluated changes in educational motivation, clinical self-efficacy, medical knowledge, awareness of other academic enrichment programs, and physician access and comfort. High school students demonstrated significant gains in motivation to attend college, understanding of cardiopulmonary anatomy and physiology, understanding of physician roles, comfort interacting with physicians, self-reported physician access, and awareness of local educational opportunities. Qualitative findings highlighted the importance of experiential learning, guided shadowing, a clearer understanding of medical careers, and persistent structural barriers. These findings suggest that community-based programs that leverage local resources, networks, and infrastructure to combine medical education with guided clinical exposure may be feasible entry points into the medical pipeline for students confronting complex socioeconomic disadvantages.

TI Critically engaged and complexity-informed climate education: Or, how to
   face "the end of the world as we know it" without freaking out
SO JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE climate change; climate education; colonialism; complexity
AB This article introduces Critically Engaged and Complexity-Informed Climate Education (CECE), a pedagogical approach that does not aim to "solve" climate change and biodiversity loss, but to compost the habits of knowing, being, desiring, and relating that have helped produce them. Rather than promoting hope in solutions that preserve existing systems, CECE supports people to cultivate intellectual, affective, and relational capacities needed to navigate social and ecological destabilization without becoming overwhelmed, immobilized, or seeking quick fixes. We describe the origins of CECE, outline its guiding compass, and illustrate it through an example of how it supports learners to identify false climate solutions.

TI Climate change education: The shape of curriculum and pedagogy
SO JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE climate change education; curriculum; pedagogy; scoping review
ID REVIEWS
AB This paper presents a two-stage scoping review of 67 studies published between 2010 and 2025, mapping the development of curriculum and pedagogy in climate change education (CCE), and serves as the introduction to a special issue of the Journal of Environmental Education that examines the state of curriculum and pedagogy in climate change education (CCE). The review identifies trends across theoretical framing, policy alignment, curricular design, and teacher and student perspectives. Findings show that CCE research is expanding but remains emergent, characterized predominantly by qualitative, descriptive work situated in formal education, especially university. Limited theorization, scarce policy-focused scholarship, and few evaluative or mixed-methods studies highlight key gaps. The eight papers included in this special issue address some of these gaps by advancing innovative pedagogical approaches, new curriculum designs, and insights into learner and teacher dispositions.

TI A person-centered approach to climate change education: Supporting
   students to align their interests, identities, and inquiry
SO JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE climate change education; identity; interests; inquiry-based learning;
   person-centered instruction
ID KNOWLEDGE; RESPONSES; CHILDREN; ANXIETY; WORK
AB This paper validates a person-centered pedagogical framework for cultivating meaningful student engagement with climate change. The approach fosters alignment between the curriculum and students' personal interests and identities. Using design-based research in a 13-week undergraduate course, we developed and applied the ENDURE framework to analyze this alignment. The framework identifies productive connections where student interest is either 'natural' (pre-existing) or 'stimulated' (sparked by the curriculum). Our analysis revealed that a significant majority of students (21 of 29) achieved these strong forms of alignment. Beyond enhancing knowledge acquisition, this profound connection cultivated a sense of personal relevance and agency. Such person-centered strategies are vital for designing educational experiences that empower students for sustained, meaningful action on the climate crisis.

TI A systematic review on research studies about formal science climate
   change curricula: Insights and implications for elementary contexts
SO JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE elementary climate change learning; constructivist approach to climate
   change; climate change educational research
ID MIDDLE SCHOOL STUDENTS; EDUCATION; ADAPTATION; KNOWLEDGE; CONCEPTIONS;
   MITIGATION; EARTH
AB Climate change presents a global emergency, and formal education plays a crucial role in building students' understanding of climate science. When climate change is integrated into a coherent curriculum, even elementary-aged students can deepen their scientific knowledge and become motivated to engage in community action and activism. Though there is a growing attention to this potential, research in elementary grades remains relatively limited, and there is a need to compare research related to coherent curriculum at the elementary or primary grades across the globe. This systematic review examined research on K-12 climate change curricula, through a constructivist lens, with a particular focus on elementary learning environments. Analysis of 56 peer-reviewed articles from various countries identified three major trends in climate change education research: 1) significantly fewer studies involve elementary grades compared with secondary levels; 2) most research is conducted in high-income countries; and 3) students in elementary grades can develop climate change understanding through locally-informed, student-centered instructional strategies. This review discusses implications for research related to constructivist climate change elementary science curricula, especially in low income and lower-middle income countries.

TI Curricular and pedagogical insights from higher education on eco-social
   transitions and climate change education: mapping student frames to
   design for agency, justice, and action
SO JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE environmental education; eco-social transitions; student perceptions;
   higher education; Iramuteq
ID ENVIRONMENTAL-EDUCATION; SUSTAINABILITY TRANSITIONS; REPRESENTATIONS
AB This article seeks to contribute to understanding how eco-social education in higher education affects how eco-social transitions are understood and problematized by higher education students. Despite recognizing the importance of current discussions on eco-social education, aimed at overcoming the focus on the formative function of higher education institutions through the introduction of active methodologies and the reformulation of university practices toward a transformative agenda, there are questions as to whether the current circumstances of eco-social education in the formative-curricular sphere provide an adequate scenario for these pragmatic approaches. For this purpose, this study takes the senior students at the University of the Basque Country as a case study, examining their perception of eco-social transitions using innovative methods such as the Grid Elaboration Method and automatic text analysis through the IRAMUTEQ program. We ask ourselves whether students' perceptions are consistent with a view of transitions that transcend hegemony or whether, on the contrary, they strengthen it. The study reveals that students value aspects related to the environment, technology, and gender issues. There is evidence of robust environmental awareness and an inclination toward adopting sustainable technologies. However, they see these principles and values more as abstract horizons than as integral components of transition processes. The diagnosis concludes that eco-social transition is perceived from a hegemonic and anthropocentric perspective, focused on economic growth and transformation driven by technological innovation. This diagnosis is of interest for further comparative studies that aim to reconsider the formative-curricular sphere in the field of environmental education at the university level. These findings engage directly with Climate Change Education (CCE) by identifying the curricular and pedagogical factors that enable values to be translated into practice on a larger scale. The study outlines the implications for the design of educational programmes and assessments in higher education, providing actionable evidence for the redesign of CCE curricula at university level.

TI Patchy pedagogies: Networking place-based climate change education
   online
SO JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE place-based education; climate change education; Anthropocene; online
   learning; teacher education; graduate teacher education
ID ANTHROPOCENE; TEMPORALITY
AB Despite significant climate change learning outside of formal education sites, climate change education in post-secondary is still only emergent, particularly in education for teachers and other non-formal educators. Drawing on student coursework from three iterations of online graduate education courses, this paper leans on Anna Tsing and colleagues' insights about the "patchy" Anthropocene to examine how students' localized understanding of climate realities can be collectively woven into a broader understanding of the planetary condition, fostering pathways toward climate action through education. By translating place-based education into an asynchronous, online forum, graduate coursework networked students' grounded realities. Students participated in an extension of artist Xavier Cortada's Longitudinal Installation, where each of them storied both the geographic and temporal elements of their climate experiences as they relate to education, engaged affectively with the stories of others, and reflected on their across global/local scales toward climate action through education.

TI Enhancing climate change understanding through system dynamics tools: An
   empirical study on middle school students
SO JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE systems thinking; system dynamics; climate change education; middle
   school students
ID THINKING SKILLS; ELEMENTARY-SCHOOL
AB This study uses system dynamics tools to investigate middle school students' systems thinking skills in climate change education. A one-group study was conducted with 120 eighth-grade students (62 females, 58 males aged 13-14) at a public school in Turkey during a four-week climate change unit. Students' dynamic, stock-flow, and causal thinking skills were assessed using structured worksheets and evaluated with a four-level rubric. Results revealed varying proficiency levels across the three skills. Students demonstrated the highest level in stock-flow thinking, followed by dynamic thinking and causal thinking. The findings provide insight into how students interact with system dynamics tools in climate education and identify common student challenges in different thinking skills, offering empirically-based considerations for the design of middle school climate change curricula.

TI Comparison of 3D model-based and slide-based teaching for afferent and
   efferent spinal cord pathways: a pre-test/post-test study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Spinal cord; Afferent pathways; Efferent pathways; Neuroanatomy
   education; Three-dimensional model
AB Background Understanding the organization of afferent and efferent spinal cord pathways can be challenging for students due to their complex spatial relationships. This study aimed to develop a three-dimensional (3D) educational model demonstrating these pathways and to compare student learning outcomes between model-based instruction and conventional slide-based teaching. Methods A pre-test/post-test educational study was conducted with second-year dental students (n = 60). Transverse sections of the C4 and T7 vertebrae were designed and 3D-printed at four times their anatomical size. A spinal cord model made of modeling clay was placed within the vertebral canal, and afferent and efferent pathways were represented using color-coded cables. Students completed a 15-item multiple-choice pre-test assessing baseline knowledge of spinal cord pathways and were allocated into two groups. Group 1 (n = 30) received conventional slide-based instruction, while Group 2 (n = 30) was taught using the 3D model. After the instructional sessions, students completed the same test as a post-test. Within-group and between-group comparisons were analyzed using paired-sample and independent-sample t-tests. Results Both instructional approaches resulted in significant improvements in post-test scores. In the slide-based instruction group, mean scores increased from 5.00 +/- 1.98 to 8.47 +/- 2.54 (p < 0.001). In the 3D model group, mean scores increased from 4.77 +/- 2.39 to 10.27 +/- 2.29 (p < 0.001). The mean improvement was significantly greater in the 3D model group (5.50 +/- 3.07) compared with the slide-based group (3.47 +/- 2.70) (p = 0.007). The effect size for the difference between groups was moderate to large (Cohen's d approximate to 0.70).<br /> Conclusion Both instructional methods improved short-term knowledge of spinal cord pathways; however, model-based instruction was associated with greater learning gains. These findings suggest that three-dimensional models may serve as a useful supplementary tool in neuroanatomy education. Further studies using validated assessment tools and evaluating long-term knowledge retention are needed to confirm these findings.

   and Scholarship: Reimagining Student Success

LA English
DT Article
DE school psychology futures; leadership; advocacy; equity; systems change
ID THAYER CONFERENCE; PERSPECTIVE
AB The School Psychology Futures Conference represents a decennial effort to examine the field's evolving responsibilities to children, youth, families, schools, and communities. This special topic section-School Psychology Futures Conference Advancing Preparation, Practice, and Scholarship: Reimagining Student Success-highlights scholarship inspired by the 2023-2024 Futures Conference. This introductory article situates the 2023-2024 Futures Conference within a broader history of future-oriented scholarship and professional self-examination in school psychology. We argue that the conference extended and reoriented long-standing conversations about role expansion, prevention, consultation, systems change, leadership, and advocacy by centering intersectional social justice, anti-oppressive practice, and liberatory education and mental health care. The special topic section is organized around six pillars: Leadership, Science and Scholarship, Practice, Education and Lifelong Learning, Workforce Development, and Advocacy. Across these pillars, the included articles address social change leadership, culturally responsible and community-centered practice, graduate preparation and mentorship, workforce sustainability and diversity, early childhood systems, artificial intelligence, restorative justice, and advocacy for systems transformation. This special topic section offers a forward-looking agenda for school psychology as a visible, necessary, and relevant force advancing equitable and liberatory educational and mental health systems. Impact Statement This special topic section advances a reimagined vision of school psychology grounded in leadership, culturally responsible practice, systems-level advocacy, and liberatory education and mental health care. The contributions offer actionable directions for strengthening graduate preparation, diversifying and sustaining the workforce, expanding equity-oriented scholarship, and promoting practices that are responsive to children's, families', and communities' lived experiences. Overall, this work positions school psychologists as leaders, collaborators, and advocates who can help transform systems so that student success includes not only achievement and mental health, but also belonging, dignity, agency, and opportunity.

TI Exploring Academic Self-Concept, Learning Goal Orientation, and Years of
   Study as Predictors of University Students' Affective Learning Outcomes
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE affective learning outcomes; higher education; university students;
   cognitive-affective assignments
ID FRIENDSHIP QUALITY; ACHIEVEMENT GOALS; SOCIAL SUPPORT; SKILLS;
   TRUSTWORTHINESS; ENGAGEMENT; MOTIVATION; 1ST; COOPERATION; BEHAVIORS
AB Research on learning in higher education focuses heavily on cognitive factors and academic performance. However, affective learning outcomes are crucial for overcoming learning difficulties and for personal development. Consequently, this study explores which personal factors are associated with affective learning outcomes among university students. We consider academic self-concept, learning goal orientation, and years of study as personal factors, and politeness, trustworthiness, cooperation, support, and friendship as affective learning outcomes. TI Developing Authentic LGBTQ+ Leadership Through Identity-Conscious
   Programmes to Foster Inclusivity, Innovation, and Social Responsiveness
   in Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE LGBTQ+ leaders; authentic LGBTQ+ leadership development; LGBTQ+
   leadership development programmes; EDI; UK higher education
ID QUEER; MODEL; GAY; FEAR
AB This paper explores the development of authentic LGBTQ+ leadership through an identity-conscious leadership development programme for LGBTQ+ staff in UK higher education. Focus group data collected eighteen months after programme completion offered longitudinal perspectives into leadership outcomes and programme design. Reflexive data themes are synthesised into a conceptual framework that illustrates how LGBTQ+ authentic leadership developed. The framework shows that authentic mentoring relationships, supported by trust, hope, and positive emotions, reduced identity and minority stress whilst forming and sustaining leadership identities. The research emphasises the importance of identity-conscious leadership development programmes in supporting LGBTQ+ leaders, strengthening leadership capacity, and enhancing institutional effectiveness, resilience, and civic responsibility.

TI Text comprehension across print and audio: a person-centered mixed
   methods study of learner profiles
SO CONTEMPORARY EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE Audio; Comprehension; Mediums; Mixed methods; Mixture modeling; Print;
   Reading
ID READING SELF-EFFICACY; INDIVIDUAL-DIFFERENCES; PRIOR KNOWLEDGE;
   INFORMATION; PERFORMANCE; METAANALYSIS; ACHIEVEMENT; CALIBRATION;
   INTEGRATION; STRATEGIES
AB This explanatory sequential mixed methods study investigated how undergraduate students process and comprehend mixed-genre texts in print and audio mediums. Undergraduate students (n = 130) completed quantitative measures of self-efficacy, reading habits, and prior topic knowledge while their screens were recorded during text processing in print and audio mediums. Observable behaviors (e.g., scrolling, playback adjustments, off-task activities) were coded. Using finite mixture modeling, distinct reader and listener profiles were identified based on affective and behavioral variables, then validated using prior knowledge and comprehension outcomes. In the subsequent qualitative phase, representative participants from each profile (n = 10) engaged in retrospective cued think-alouds that illuminated the cognitive and strategic processes underlying these profiles. Quantitative analysis revealed similar performance on recall and inference items across mediums, with print yielding higher scores on main idea identification and vocabulary gain. Three reader profiles emerged (Distracted Surfers, Labored Harvesters, Fluent Surveyors) alongside three listener profiles (Inconsistently Attentive, Inattentive, Persistently Attentive). Qualitative data revealed these profiles differed in strategies, processing depth, and attention regulation, explaining the quantitative patterns. Integrated findings demonstrated how learner characteristics interact with medium features to influence comprehension outcomes. This research advances theoretical understanding of comprehension across mediums and provides practical implications for educators incorporating audio in instruction and for designers developing educational technology optimized for diverse learner profiles. Educational significance: This study shows how college students comprehend mixed-genre texts across print and audio using a person-centered approach. The investigation uncovered distinct learner profiles based on attention, strategy use, and self-regulation, showing that comprehension success is not uniform but depends on the fit between learner characteristics and medium affordances. These findings help educators select or combine mediums to align with learning goals, design multimodal learning environments that reduce distraction, and guide students in the use of medium-specific strategy use. As higher education increasingly incorporates diverse text delivery methods, understanding these profile-medium interactions is vital for enhancing learning outcomes.

TI Assessing pharmacy student understanding of menopause and hormone
   replacement therapy: A survey study
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Menopause; Pharmacy; Pharmacy student; Education; Survey study; Hormone
   replacement therapy; Student knowledge
AB Objectives: Pharmacists have the potential to take on a leading role in menopause service provision, but this calls for a well-educated workforce. To support this ambition, high-quality undergraduate teaching is paramount so qualified pharmacists are prepared to take on these roles. This study aims find out current confidence and knowledge of pharmacy students on menopause and hormone replacement therapy. Methods: Pharmacy students at eight universities in the United Kingdom were invited by email to complete an online survey on menopause and hormone replacement therapy. Students were asked to self-report their confidence on each topic (0 = not confident at all, 10 = very confident), answer subject-specific questions and specify their preferred teaching methods. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and a thematic approach where appropriate. Key findings: In total 178 students (158 [88.8%] aged 18-24 years, 147 [82.6%] female) in years 1 (59, 33.1%), 2 (35, 19.7%), 3 (28, 15.7%) and 4 (56, 31.5%) completed the survey. Median [interquartile range] self-reported confidence in knowledge on menopause and hormone replacement therapy was 5.0 [4-6] and 4.0 [2-5], respectively. Students had basic knowledge of what menopause is, how long it lasts and common symptoms, but were uncertain about the risks and benefits of hormone replacement therapy. Students most commonly chose lectures (133/176, 75.6%) as their preferred teaching method. Conclusions: Pharmacy students lack confidence in their own knowledge of menopause and hormone replacement therapy. Pharmacy schools must evaluate their current curricula and consider how these topics are taught, specifically the associated risks with hormone replacement therapy.

TI From national green transition awareness to sustainable development
   attitudes: Professional responsibility identity as a mediator among
   polymer materials undergraduates
SO EDUCATION FOR CHEMICAL ENGINEERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Engineering education; Sustainability attitudes; Professional
   responsibility identity; National green transition awareness; Polymer
   materials education
AB This study examines how perceived awareness of China's national green transition is associated with sustainability-related professional attitudes among polymer materials engineering undergraduates, with a focus on the mediating role of professional responsibility identity (PRI). A cross-sectional survey of 371 students was conducted using newly developed, context-specific self-report scales for National Green Transition Awareness (NGTA), PRI, and Sustainable Development Attitude (SDA). Mediation analysis using PROCESS Model 4 indicated that PRI partially mediated the relationship between NGTA and SDA. NGTA was directly associated with SDA, while a substantial portion of this association was indirect and operated through students' internalization of environmental responsibility as part of their future professional role. These findings suggest that sustainabilityrelated policy narratives may become educationally meaningful when they are connected to students' understanding of professional responsibility. This study contributes to chemical and materials engineering education by highlighting an identity-oriented pathway through which perceived policy awareness may be linked to sustainability-oriented professional attitudes.

TI Self-directed learning capability and sustainable innovative behavior
   among human resource management students: The mediating roles of
   artificial intelligence and divergent thinking skills
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Self-directed learning capability; Artificial intelligence skills;
   Divergent thinking skills; Sustainable innovative behavior; Generation Z
   students; HRM education
ID CREATIVITY
AB This study examined the associations among self-directed learning capability, artificial intelligence skills, divergent thinking skills, and self-reported sustainable innovative behavior among Human Resource Management students in Thailand. A quantitative research approach was employed, and data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling. The sample comprised 161 fourth-year Human Resource Management students, and data were collected via an online questionnaire. The findings revealed that self-directed learning capability had significant positive associations with artificial intelligence and divergent thinking skills, as well as with self-reported sustainable, innovative behavior. These findings suggest a potential developmental process in which self-directed learning supports the use of artificial intelligence, expands cognitive capability, and may ultimately contributes to self-reported sustainable innovative behavior. The study suggests that promoting sustainable, innovative behavior among students in the digital era should emphasize the development of self-directed learning capabilities alongside the integrated promotion of artificial intelligence and creative thinking.

TI The role of social anxiety and attentional focus in a virtual reality
   environment on articulatory control in adults who stutter
SO JOURNAL OF FLUENCY DISORDERS
LA English
DT Article
DE Stuttering; Attention; Speech motor control; Articulatory variability;
   Social anxiety
ID INTERPRETATION BIAS; SAFETY BEHAVIORS; COGNITIVE STRESS; EXTERNAL FOCUS;
   MOTOR CONTROL; SPEECH; MOVEMENT; DISORDER; EMOTION; PHOBIA
AB Purpose: Adults who stutter (AWS) show a maladaptive attentional focus when speaking under socially stressful conditions and at the same time, attentional focus has shown to impact articulatory control in this population. The purpose of this study was to determine the predictive factors of social anxiety and attentional focus on articulatory control in AWS compared to a group of adults who do not stutter (ANS), varying in social anxiety levels. Method: Seventeen AWS and 23 ANS repeated sentences in a virtual reality environment under a low-and high-socially stressful condition. Speech motor control was assessed by measuring movement duration (DUR) and lip aperture variability using the spatiotemporal index (LA STI). Conclusion: Results showed social anxiety predicts changes in articulatory variability in AWS when speaking under social stress, while attentional focus plays a lesser, insignificant role.

TI From survey to experiment: How growth mindset and teacher support shape
   online learning engagement in adolescents
SO LEARNING AND INDIVIDUAL DIFFERENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Growth mindset; Online learning; Teacher support; Machine learning;
   Improving classroom teaching
ID RESILIENCE SCALE; SOCIAL SUPPORT; STUDENTS; SCHOOL; TRAJECTORIES;
   ACHIEVEMENT; TRANSITION; MOTIVATION; BURNOUT
AB Improving adolescents' sustained online learning engagement is critical, yet the specific pathways remain unclear. To address this gap, this study conducted two studies to explore how growth mindsets promote online learning engagement among adolescents, specifically examining the mediating role of psychological resilience and the moderating role of teacher support. Study 1 employed a cross-sectional survey design (middle school students, N = 920), utilizing structural equation modeling and machine learning. Results indicated that growth mindsets predicted online learning, mediated by psychological resilience and moderated by perceived teacher support; psychological resilience was identified as the strongest predictor in random forest analysis. These findings provide practical insights for the designing of online learning interventions.

TI The adaptivity of classroom teaching: Comments from a teaching quality
   perspective
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
ID INSTRUCTION
AB This commentary discusses adaptivity from the point of view of classroom teaching. The concept of teaching quality is introduced with a focus on the model of three basic dimensions and two principles: opportunity vs. use, surface vs. deep structure of teaching and learning. Adaptivity is defined by diversity of learning opportunities, differentiation, diagnostics, and suitability, and two major research goals are stated: developing a generic measure of adaptivity and specifying the relationship between basic dimensions and adaptivity. TI Longitudinal and differential effects of differentiated instruction on
   academic achievement and subjective well-being in inclusive secondary
   education
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Differentiated instruction; Academic achievement; Subjective well-being;
   Inclusive education; Competencies
ID READING COMPETENCE; SELF-CONCEPT; QUALITY; ABILITY; METAANALYSIS;
   VALIDATION; DIMENSIONS; CLASSROOMS; FRAMEWORK
AB Background: Differentiated instruction (DI) is a fundamental component of teaching quality, particularly in diverse and inclusive classrooms. While DI has been shown to enhance students' academic achievement, research at the secondary education level remains limited, and its impact on students' subjective well-being-widely recognized as essential for learning-has been largely unexplored. Moreover, effects may differ for students with special educational needs in learning (SEN-L). Aim: This study investigated cross-sectional and longitudinal effects of classroom-level DI practices on students' academic achievement and subjective well-being in lower secondary education, incorporating both student and teacher perspectives. Additionally, it examined whether the effects of DI differ between students with and without SEN-L. Sample: Data were drawn from a longitudinal study with three measurement occasions (Grades 6, 7, and 9). The sample comprised 4654 sixth-grade students, along with 417 German and 398 mathematics teachers. Methods: Multilevel regression analyses with latent variables were conducted to investigate cross-sectional effects. To examine longitudinal effects, latent neighbor change models were applied. Results: Cross-sectionally, DI showed some small positive associations with academic achievement and, particularly student-reported DI, small positive associations with subjective well-being. DI predicted some changes in both outcomes over time, albeit inconsistently and with small-to-negligible effect sizes. The findings indicate only two small differential effects for students with SEN-L compared to other students. Conclusions: The study extends research on DI by focusing on both students' academic achievement and subjective well-being in lower secondary education, while calling for continued research into its longitudinal effects and underlying mechanisms.

TI The Resource Gadgets Pedagogical Framework: A conceptual model for
   lecturer-guided mobile learning in resource-constrained nursing
   education
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Mobile learning; Nursing education; Resource-constrained; M -learning;
   Resource Gadgets Pedagogical Framework; Conceptual framework; LMIC
   nursing; Sub-Saharan Africa; Digital equity; Nurse education; Smartphone
   pedagogy
AB Mobile learning (m-learning) is education delivered anytime, anywhere via pocket-sized, internet-connected devices. M-learning enables nursing students to access clinical guidelines, multimedia resources, and evidencebased knowledge. However, in many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), institutional simulation laboratories, audiovisual equipment, and WiFi remain limited, constraining the implementation of technologyenhanced pedagogy. Paradoxically, smartphone ownership among students is widespread, presenting an underutilized opportunity for structured mobile-assisted learning. This paper presents the Resource Gadgets Pedagogical Framework (RGPF), a conceptual model for lecturerguided smartphone-mediated learning in resource-constrained nursing education. The framework is empirically informed by qualitative data from undergraduate nursing students and theoretically grounded in six complementary learning theories: constructivism, critical pedagogy, andragogy, Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, Activity Theory, and Self-Determination Theory. The RGPF conceptualizes mobile-assisted learning as a structured five-step instructional sequence: (1) Structured Initiation (Frame task), (2) Guided Digital Inquiry (Specify sources), (3) Visual-Multimodal Processing (Time-bound search), (4) Collaborative Synthesis, and (5) Educator-Facilitated Anchoring (Anchor learning). Each component is theoretically grounded and operationalized through practical classroom strategies without institutional technological investment. The Resource Gadgets Pedagogical Framework (RGPF) contributes a replicable pedagogical model that reframes students' smartphones from perceived classroom distractions to structured cognitive learning tools. The framework embeds digital equity safeguards as prerequisite implementation conditions for lecturer-guided mobile-assisted learning and positions m-learning as a gateway toward AI-enhanced nursing education. While analytically generalizable, the framework requires multi-site empirical validation. The RGPF offers educators, curriculum designers, and policymakers in LMICs a foundation for scalable, equitable, and theory-driven innovation in nursing education across resource-constrained settings.

TI Academic overload, ChatGPT use, and resilience: Parallel mediating
   pathways to academic stress among nursing students
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic overload; Academic stress; ChatGPT usage; Nursing students;
   Parallel mediation; Resilience
AB Background: Academic overload is a major contributor to student stress, but its underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood, particularly in the context of emerging AI tools such as ChatGPT. Aim: To examine the direct and indirect effects of academic overload on academic stress through parallel mediating roles of ChatGPT use and psychological resilience among nursing students. Methods: This cross-sectional study involved 409 nursing students from a university in central Vietnam. Participants completed validated self-administered questionnaires assessing academic overload, ChatGPT usage, resilience, and academic stress, along with demographic characteristics. Parallel mediation analysis was conducted using Hayes' Process Macro (Model 4) to examine direct and indirect pathways. Results: Academic overload had a significant total effect on academic stress (B = 0.584, p < .001), with 84.6% attributed to the direct effect and 15.4% to indirect effects. Academic overload was associated with resilience (B = -1.223) and higher ChatGPT usage (B = 0.359). Resilience showed a protective effect (B = -0.042), while ChatGPT usage was associated with higher academic stress (B = 0.108), indicating opposing mediating pathways. Conclusions: Academic overload exerts its effects on academic stress via opposing pathways, with resilience acting as a protective factor and ChatGPT use as a potential risk factor. Educational strategies should strengthen resilience and support guided, effective use of AI tools to mitigate potential negative impacts on learning and well-being.

TI Historical trauma-based education and nursing professional identity: A
   qualitative analysis of reflective essays
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Professional identity; Nursing education; Historical trauma; Holocaust;
   Genocide; Reflective writing; Trauma-informed pedagogy
ID FRAMEWORK; HOLOCAUST
AB Background: Professional identity formation is a central goal of nursing education, yet less is known about how students connect historical trauma-based learning with ethical nursing practice. Holocaust and genocide education may support moral reflection, empathy, advocacy, and professional responsibility when delivered through trauma-informed pedagogical safeguards. Aim: To explore how registered nurses enrolled in a Master of Science in Nursing-Nurse Practitioner program interpreted Holocaust and genocide education and connected this learning to professional identity work and anticipated practice. Design: Qualitative study using reflexive thematic analysis. Methods: Fourteen de-identified reflective essays written after a structured educational unit on the Holocaust and the Rwandan genocide were analyzed. Analysis was primarily inductive and informed by sensitizing concepts from nursing ethics, trauma-informed education, and professional identity formation. Results: Six themes were identified: historical awareness as a moral compass; empathy and cultural humility; recognition of dehumanization and structural violence; resilience and advocacy; leadership and professional responsibility; and reflective self-awareness. Students described historical trauma-based learning as a catalyst for ethical sense-making, emotional processing, and value clarification. They connected this learning to intended professional commitments, including safeguarding dignity, challenging discrimination, attending to trauma histories, and advocating for vulnerable patients. Conclusions: Historical trauma-based education may provide a meaningful reflective space for professional identity work in graduate nursing education. The findings suggest that, when supported by trauma-informed pedagogy and reflective writing, difficult historical content can help students articulate ethical commitments and anticipated nursing responsibilities. Future studies should examine whether these immediate reflective commitments are sustained over time and translated into practice.

TI Short report: Patterns of motor difficulties among autistic, ADHD, or
   Autistic-ADHD youth in Iceland
SO RESEARCH IN DEVELOPMENTAL DISABILITIES
LA English
DT Article
DE Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD); Autism; Youth; Motor
   impairment; Movement Assessment Battery for Children Second - Edition
   (MABC-2)
ID DEVELOPMENTAL COORDINATION DISORDER; CHILDREN; SPECTRUM; ATTENTION;
   IMPAIRMENT; SCHEDULE; VERSION; SKILLS
AB Background: Research indicates motor delays in youth with ADHD or autism, but patterns in cooccurring ADHD and autism remain under-explored. This study compared motor performance in youth with co-occurring conditions with that of single-diagnosis groups.
   Methods: A sample of 122 stimulant medication naive children in Iceland (Mage = 9.06 +/- 1.95 years) diagnosed with ADHD (n = 77), autism (n = 15), or both (n = 30), without intellectual impairment, was assessed using the Movement Assessment Battery for Children-Second Edition.
   Results: Kruskal-Wallis test results showed a significant effect for percentile rank, with post-hoc comparisons revealing the Autism group scored significantly lower than both the ADHD and Autism + ADHD groups. Similarly, for the total test score, significant differences were found, with the Autism group again scoring lower than both the ADHD and Autism + ADHD groups. Across subscales, significant group effects were found for Balance, where the Autism group underperformed both the ADHD and Autism + ADHD groups; Aiming and Catching, where the Autism group scored lower than the ADHD group; and Manual Dexterity, where the Autism group scored lower than the Autism + ADHD group. No significant differences were found between the ADHD and Autism + ADHD groups on any measure.
   Conclusion: Youth with co-occurring ADHD and autism demonstrate motor performance levels similar to those with ADHD only, with both groups outperforming the Autism group. These findings suggest that the presence of ADHD symptoms may relate to distinct motor trajectories in autism.

TI The multimodal organisation of teacher feedback: A multimodal
   (Inter)action analysis
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher feedback; Modal density; Modal coherence; Multimodal
   (Inter)action analysis; Higher-level action
ID LECTURES
AB This study explores the multimodal organisation of teacher feedback during teacher-student interactions in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) classrooms. Drawing on Multimodal (Inter) action Analysis, fourteen higher-level actions (HLAs) constituting feedback were identified, and twenty-four embodied modes involved in their realisation were coded. Building on these annotations, the multimodal organisation of feedback HLAs is examined through two interrelated dimensions: modal density and modal coherence. Modal density analyses the configuration of embodied modes within individual HLAs. It is operationalised through three variables: modal complexity, modal intensity, and modal units (Querol-Julian, 2023). Modal coherence focuses on the dynamic orchestration of embodied modes across HLAs. Two key coherence features are distinguished: hierarchical coordination of modal resources across concurrent HLAs, and temporal offsetting of modal resources for bridging successive HLAs. The findings reveal that feedback HLAs exhibit distinct modal density profiles, underpinned by a structured yet adaptable multimodal organisation. Within and across HLAs, multimodal simultaneity and succession work in tandem, enabling feedback to unfold not as a series of isolated actions but as a hierarchically organised and multimodally coherent trajectory. The findings reveal that feedback HLAs exhibit distinct modal density profiles, underpinned by a structured yet adaptable multimodal organisation. Within this organisation, multimodal simultaneity and succession work in tandem, enabling feedback to unfold not as a series of isolated actions, but as a hierarchically organised and multimodally coherent trajectory.

TI Expanding, persistent, and intermediary conceptions of equity: A
   longitudinal study of prospective mathematics teachers
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION

DE Equity; Equitable mathematics education; Mathematics teacher learning;
   Prospective mathematics teachers; Professional development
ID TEACHING PRACTICES; SOCIAL-JUSTICE; EDUCATION; ACHIEVEMENT
AB This study examines how prospective mathematics teachers (PMTs) developed conceptions of equity in an equity-focused professional development program. Drawing on three rounds of semi-structured interviews with twelve participants, data were analyzed through a combination of deductive and inductive thematic coding using Gutierrez's four-dimensional equity framework: access, achievement, identity, and power. TI The paradox of inclusion: Generative AI and the center-periphery divide
   in language education
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE Generative AI; CALL; Scoping review; Center-periphery; Linguistic
   justice; Paradox of inclusion
AB The emergence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) marks an infrastructural transformation in Computer-Assisted Language Learning (CALL), yet the rapid expansion of the field reveals a fundamental tension between pedagogical optimization and structural inequality. This article presents a theory-informed critical scoping review of 53 studies (2020-2026) to map the uneven landscape of GenAI in language education. Using a Center-Periphery framework, the study analyzes how GenAI functions as a pedagogical accelerator in high-resource, Englishdominant contexts ("The Center") while simultaneously marginalizing low-resource and Indigenous linguistic settings ("The Periphery"). Findings demonstrate that in the Center, GenAI enables process-oriented optimization in L2 writing and significant gains in interactional fluency through rapid feedback loops and low-stakes practice environments. In the Periphery, however, the mechanisms of data scale and statistical generalization result in structural exclusion, which manifests through degraded feedback, dialect leveling, and epistemic bias. This study conceptualizes this dual-edged force as the Paradox of Inclusion: the process by which technologies that appear to democratize access simultaneously reproduce and intensify existing global inequalities. The article concludes by arguing for a shift from purely technical innovation toward a framework of responsibility, emphasizing Indigenous Data Sovereignty and Critical AI Literacy as essential pathways toward achieving global linguistic justice in the digital age.

TI Expectations of independence from the outset? The discourse of
   researcher independence in the pre-application stage of doctoral
   admissions
SO INNOVATIONS IN EDUCATION AND TEACHING INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Doctoral access; doctoral admissions; doctoral education; researcher
   independence
AB This paper explores how the discourse of 'researcher independence' operates in the pre-application stage of doctoral recruitment. Drawing on semi-structured interview data from an institutional case study of pre-admissions practice at a UK Russell Group university, we examine how doctoral programme officers and academic directors of doctoral programmes interact with enquiries from pre-applicants. Our Foucauldian-inspired analysis demonstrates that researcher independence functions as a powerful discursive formation structuring staff expectations of pre-applicants. This paper calls for greater reflexivity among all admissions actors regarding how unspoken ideals like 'researcher independence' govern access to doctoral education.

   independence: A conceptual analysis
SO INNOVATIONS IN EDUCATION AND TEACHING INTERNATIONAL

DE Writing; researcher independence; activity theory; doctoral development;
   mediating artefacts
ID ACADEMIC IDENTITY; STUDENTS
AB The doctorate is a learning process that aims to develop new understanding, with the ultimate goal of acquiring research-related skills and competencies required to become an independent researcher capable of autonomous work within teams. Pedagogical implications for using writing as a mediating artefact are discussed in the paper.

TI A delicate balance: The interplay of supervision, academic context,
   motivation, and emotions in doctoral education
SO INNOVATIONS IN EDUCATION AND TEACHING INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Supervision; research autonomy; academic context; doctoral education;
   emotions
ID KNOWLEDGE; STUDENTS
AB Doctoral education may be experienced as a transformative process through which PhD candidates progressively develop and come to be recognised as autonomous researchers. Supervision relationships can be spaces for the development of autonomy; however, supervisors' support may be complex and multidimensional, drawing on constant struggles for balance. Drawing on a perspectivist approach and adopting a mixed-methods design, this study explored the interplay between the supervisory relationship, the academic/research context, motivation and emotions in doctoral education. TI Reconsidering researcher independence in an era of AI enabled learning
SO INNOVATIONS IN EDUCATION AND TEACHING INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Researcher independence; doctoral education; artificial intelligence
ID EDUCATION; PEDAGOGY; PHD
AB This paper examines researcher independence in doctoral education, particularly in the context of an AI-enabled learning environment. TI Stages of competence in doctoral researcher development: Insights from a
   collective autoethnographic study of Journal Club participation
SO INNOVATIONS IN EDUCATION AND TEACHING INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Doctoral education; journal club; stages of competence; collective
   autoethnography; researcher development
ID STUDENTS
AB This study explores how doctoral scholars' competencies evolve over time through their experiences of Journal Club (JC) participation. Using collective autoethnography and Framework Analysis, Higher Education and Psychology doctoral scholars at a UK research-intensive university produced monthly and summative reflections. Guided by the Stages of Competence theory, we examined how knowledge, skills, and attitudes developed through ongoing engagement in JC discussions and leadership. Findings reveal a spiral trajectory of growth, marked by repeated transitions from conscious awareness of gaps to deliberate practice and eventual intuitive expertise. JC participation supported thesis-specific development, critical thinking, scholarly confidence, and peer mentoring, while also fostering emotional well-being and a sense of community. We propose a novel conceptual framework that explains how competencies evolve through JC across stages of the doctoral journey. These findings refine linear assumptions in competence theory and highlight JC's value as a practical mechanism for scaffolding doctoral development.
