TI Construction and application of an intelligent tutoring system for
   resident physicians' medical record writing based on large language
   models
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Large language model; Medical record writing; Residency training;
   Documentation quality; Intelligent tutoring system
AB Objective To develop and evaluate a large language model (LLM)-based intelligent tutoring system for medical record writing in residency training and to assess its effectiveness in improving documentation quality and documentation-related learning outcomes. Methods: A single-center quasi-experimental controlled before-and-after educational evaluation was conducted from January to December 2025 at a tertiary teaching hospital. Residents (PGY1-PGY3) were allocated to the intervention cohort (LLM-based tutoring system plus conventional teaching) or the control cohort (conventional teaching alone) according to existing teaching arrangements. The system used pseudonymized historical real patient cases to provide structured documentation tasks, automated multidimensional assessment, and personalized feedback. The primary outcome was the overall medical record writing score (0-100). Secondary outcomes included domain-specific documentation scores, documentation error rates, completion time, and resident satisfaction. Statistical analyses included t tests, chi-square tests, effect-size estimation with 95% confidence intervals, and multivariable linear regression. Results: A total of 240 residents were included in the analysis (120 per cohort), with comparable baseline characteristics. After 6 months, the intervention cohort demonstrated significantly greater improvement in overall medical record writing scores compared with the control cohort (between-group mean difference in change, 9.0 points; 95% CI, 7.5-10.5; Cohen's d = 1.56; P < 0.001). Improvements were also observed in documentation domains related to history taking, diagnostic analysis, differential diagnosis, and treatment planning. Documentation error rates decreased significantly in the intervention cohort, and residents reported high satisfaction with the system. Conclusions: The LLM-based intelligent tutoring system was associated with improved medical record writing quality, documentation efficiency, and resident satisfaction in a residency training setting. These findings support its use as a scalable supplement to conventional documentation training while requiring further validation for broader educational outcomes beyond documentation.

TI Development of core competency indicators for emergency medicine
   residents based on the competency model: a Delphi and analytic hierarchy
   process study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Emergency medicine; Standardized residency training; Competency model;
   Delphi method; Core competency
AB Background Standardized residency training in emergency medicine is not well-defined in China. Establishing a core competency indicator system for emergency residency training is essential for standardizing and enhancing the quality of training and emergency care. Objectives This study aimed to develop a core competency indicator system for emergency residency training in China, based on the competency iceberg model. Methods This study employed a multi-step approach, including a literature review, semi-structured expert interviews, to formulate a list of preliminary indicators. A two-round modified Delphi method was utilized to achieve consensus, with 19 emergency experts recruited from 11 tertiary hospitals across four regions of China. Consensus was determined using a 5-point Likert scale, with a mean importance score > 3.5, a coefficient of variation < 0.20, and a full-score proportion > 20% serving as criteria for indicator retention. Results All 19 invited experts completed both rounds of consultation, achieving a 100% valid response rate. The authority coefficient of the consultation was 0.895, and Kendall's W values ranged from 0.566 to 0.634 (p < 0.005), indicating strong expert consensus. The final indicator system includes 34 third-level indicators within 14 s-level indicators, categorized into 5 first-level dimensions: motivation, trait, self-concept, knowledge, and skill. Conclusions This study represents an initial step towards establishing a contemporary competency-based training program for emergency residency training in China, providing a scientific reference for the standardization of emergency residency training.

TI Beyond the Classroom: Analyzing the Gap Between Knowledge and Action in
   Sustainability Within Higher Education Sport Sciences Curricula
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE sustainability consciousness; value-action gap; physical activity; sport
   sciences; nautical activities; active tourism; higher education;
   environmental stewardship; SDGs
AB Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) are increasingly tasked with fostering pro-environmental agency to address the global climate crisis. Within physical activity and sport sciences, future nautical sports managers occupy a unique role as stewards of marine ecosystems. This study investigates the sustainability consciousness of 170 undergraduate university students from a single institution. It focuses on analyzing the knowledge-action gap within the framework of the 2030 Agenda. Utilizing the Sustainability Consciousness Questionnaire (SCQ-S), this work assessed knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors to quantify this dissonance through a robust non-parametric statistical pipeline. Crucially, the frequency of engagement in nature-based sports, encompassing both nautical and terrestrial outdoor activities, does not significantly reduce this dissonance. These contextual findings indicate that physical exposure to nature does not automatically mitigate the knowledge-action gap, highlighting the need for explicit reflective pedagogies in higher education.

TI Positive Leadership as a Transformative Force for Mental Health and
   Quality of Life Among Women University Leaders
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; mental health; leadership; quality of life; women
   leaders
ID EPIDEMIOLOGY STROBE STATEMENT; SOCIAL SUPPORT;
   ORGANIZATIONAL-DEVELOPMENT; PSYCHOMETRIC PROPERTIES; IMPOSTOR
   PHENOMENON; ADVANCE WOMEN; ROLE-CONFLICT; LONELINESS; FACULTY;
   QUESTIONNAIRE
AB Positive Leadership in Higher Education is a key process; however, its connection to the mental health and quality of life of women in leadership roles at universities has been explored only to a limited extent. This study aimed to analyze the structural relationships between positive leadership, positive mental health, and quality of life in women university leaders, and to explore the lived experiences and coping strategies that explain these associations. A mixed-methods explanatory sequential design (QUAN -> qual) was employed. 45 women holding senior administrative positions in Peruvian universities completed three standardized scales. Positive leadership emerges as a key organizational resource that enhances women's mental health and quality of life. Institutional cultures grounded in inclusion, care, and relational leadership are essential for sustainable and transformative women's leadership in higher education. The WISE: Women Integrated for Sustainable Empowerment is presented as a practical action guide for positive female leadership.

TI Equity in medical school interviews: a cross-sectional analysis of
   school type, gender, and widening participation status
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical school admissions; Multiple mini-interviews; Widening
   participation; Socioeconomic status; Educational equality; Gender;
   School selectivity
ID MULTIPLE MINI-INTERVIEW; SOCIOECONOMIC-STATUS; PERFORMANCE; SELECTION
AB Background Multiple Mini Interviews (MMIs) are widely used in medical school admissions to assess non-academic attributes. While MMIs are designed to promote fairness, questions remain about how applicant background may influence performance. In 2015, a single-institution UK study found no significant impact of school background or socioeconomic status on MMI scores. A decade later, this study re-examines those associations in a similar UK context. Methods In this cross-sectional observational study, we analysed data from 545 home applicants to Imperial College School of Medicine during the 2025 admissions cycle. Using multiple linear regression, we explored the relationship between total MMI score and applicant gender, school type, and widening participation (WP) status. Station-level regressions were also conducted. Results The regression model was statistically significant and explained 7.6% of total score variance. Out of a maximum score of 70, female applicants scored on average 3.2 points higher than males (95% CI: 2.1 to 4.2, p < 0.001). Applicants from independent and state-selective schools scored 2.4 (95% CI: 1.0 to 3.9, p = 0.001) and 1.3 points higher (95% CI: 0.0 to 2.7, p = 0.046), respectively, than state non-selective peers. WP status was not a significant predictor. Station-level analyses revealed no consistent disadvantage for WP applicants. Conclusion Our findings suggest that, unlike earlier UK research, school background and gender now show modest associations with MMI performance. WP applicants, however, perform comparably to their peers, indicating progress towards equitable access. Future work should explore the potential impact of coaching and familiarity with interview formats to inform MMI design.

TI Toward a Multi-Dimensional Framework for Mathematical Proficiency in
   Remedial Education Inspired by the Common European Framework of
   Reference for Languages
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE remedial mathematics; proficiency framework; assessment; CEFR;
   placement; developmental education; standard setting; future validation
ID STRUCTURE SENSE
AB This conceptual paper proposes Math-CEFR, a reference framework for describing postsecondary mathematical readiness in the context of remedial and gateway placement. Single-score placement tests frequently misclassify students and offer little guidance for instruction. Drawing on the architecture of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), Math-CEFR separates global decision bands (M0-M5) from a multi-dimensional diagnostic profile covering procedural fluency, conceptual understanding, structural awareness, and transfer. The framework treats readiness as non-linear and pathway-sensitive, distinguishing two common course pathways in postsecondary mathematics: a quantitative reasoning/statistics route and an algebra-to-calculus route. It is accompanied by illustrative descriptors, task-family specifications, and an alignment and local standard-setting protocol. Because no validity evidence yet exists, transparency and defensibility are design goals whose attainment depends on the validation agenda outlined here-they are not established properties of the framework. Math-CEFR is offered as a structural proposal intended to make placement interpretations more transparent and future empirical evaluation feasible, rather than as a finished testing instrument.

TI Yearly Trends in Preschoolers' Cognitive and Affective Outcomes in a
   Multimedia-Assisted Theme-Based English and Chinese Learning Program
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE early foreign language learning; cognitive development; affective
   development; multimedia-assisted theme-based integrated learning; trend
   analysis
AB Long-term analyses of year changes in preschoolers' cognitive and affective development are limited. This field-based study examined yearly trends in a multimedia-assisted, theme-based English and Chinese program in South Korean daycare centers (2022-2024). Participants included 112, 120, and 124 children aged 3-5 annually. Changes were analyzed for cognitive (vocabulary/sentence comprehension and expression) and affective (learning interest, confidence, and motivation) domains. Group differences based on duration of enrollment (three years vs. less than three years) were examined among five-year-old children. Significant cognitive gains occurred for both languages across all three years. Affective development was significant for both languages in 2022 and 2023; however, in 2024, significant positive changes persisted for English across all subdomains, while for Chinese, only confidence improved. Correlation patterns varied by year and language; notably, English motivation was significantly associated with selected cognitive domains in the third year. Furthermore, group comparisons indicated that children enrolled for three years demonstrated better performance in both English and Chinese than those enrolled for less than three years, with statistically significant differences particularly evident in sentence expression. These findings underscore the value of developmentally appropriate and engaging learning contexts that foster both the cognitive and affective dimensions of early learning.

TI Participation, Feedback, and Academic Adjustment Across Reported
   Classroom Practices: Korean Exchange Students in U.S. Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE short-term study abroad; feedback literacy; academic help-seeking;
   Korean exchange students; qualitative case study; repertoire expansion;
   peer feedback
ID INTERNATIONAL STUDENTS; FORMATIVE ASSESSMENT; EXPERIENCES; ADAPTATION;
   ENGAGEMENT; LEARNER
AB One-semester exchange programs place students in university courses within compressed, credit-bearing mobility timelines. This qualitative case study examines how eight Korean undergraduate exchange students described academic learning and adjustment during a one-semester exchange at a U.S. university. Drawing on online written interviews, the study analyzes students' reported classroom experiences rather than formal course design or enacted instructional practice. The analysis focuses on how students navigated unfamiliar classroom expectations at the level of reported classroom practice. The findings show that participation became visible as academic work when students prepared texts, engaged in discussions, managed language risk, and judged what counted as an appropriate contribution. This study contributes to higher education and international student mobility research by showing how temporary exchange students made classroom expectations workable through targeted strategy additions rather than through a shift from one national learning culture to another. TI Antecedents and Consequences of AI Misuse Among University Students: An
   Empirical Investigation
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE AI misuse; fraud triangle theory; policy deterrence; academic
   self-efficacy; innovation ability
ID SELF-EFFICACY; HIGHER-EDUCATION; DETERRENCE
AB AI misuse has become a significant challenge and concern in higher education. Existing research has focused separately on either antecedents or consequences of AI misuse and has relied on a single theoretical perspective. There is a notable lack of empirical research investigating the antecedents and consequences of AI misuse among university students. To address this gap, this study constructs an integrated research model for the antecedents and consequences of AI misuse based on the fraud triangle theory, deterrence theory, and social cognitive theory. Data were collected from 493 university students through a questionnaire survey and analyzed using structural equation modeling (SEM) to test the proposed hypotheses. The results indicate that ease of use, academic pressure, and peer influence significantly promote AI misuse. Policy deterrence and academic self-efficacy can effectively inhibit AI misuse. Furthermore, AI misuse impairs students' innovation ability. This study advances the systematic understanding of AI misuse and consolidates its theoretical and empirical underpinnings. It enables universities to better govern AI misuse and foster students' innovation ability.

TI Bridging the digital divide: online learning experiences of
   disadvantaged students in South Africa
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE developing country; digital divide; digital inequality; disadvantaged
   students; non-traditional students; online learning; student agency
ID EDUCATION
AB This study examines the benefits and challenges experienced by disadvantaged students participating in online learning within a professional accounting education context, using the digital divide as an analytical lens. The rapid shift to online learning during the COVID-19 pandemic exposed persistent disparities in access and use of information and communication technologies (ICTs), disproportionately affecting students from disadvantaged backgrounds. As higher education institutions continue to integrate online and blended learning beyond the pandemic, understanding how disadvantaged students navigate these environments is critical for developing inclusive digital education. The study employed an open-ended questionnaire, followed by focus group discussions with students participating in a transformation-focused support programme. Qualitative data from both stages were analysed thematically using the digital divide framework, focusing on the interconnected layers of structure, cultural practice, and agency. The findings reveal a multifaceted digital divide in which structural, cultural, and individual factors interact to shape students' online learning experiences. Structural conditions, such as access to appropriate devices and reliable digital infrastructure, influence students' ability to engage with online learning platforms. Cultural factors, particularly financial constraints related to internet access and digital resources, further limit equitable participation. At the same time, the agency dimension highlights students' capacity to adapt to online learning through self-regulation and autonomy when adequate institutional support is available. The study underscores the importance of holistic institutional strategies to support disadvantaged students in digital learning environments. These include improving internet infrastructure, providing financial support for digital devices and connectivity, and adopting flexible teaching approaches that accommodate diverse access conditions.

TI Gender equity in Peruvian higher education: discipline-specific barriers
   in working conditions and academic careers
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic careers; academic promotion; gender inequity; higher education;
   organizational culture; women; working conditions; workload
ID UNIVERSITY; STEM
AB Background: Gender inequities in Latin American academia persist despite increased female enrollment, as traditional career structures presume uninterrupted availability and undervalue caregiving responsibilities. Objective: To examine women faculty perceptions of working conditions, promotion opportunities, and institutional support at a private university in southern Peru, identifying discipline-specific barriers to gender equity. Methods: This case study employed an anonymous cross-sectional survey administered to all 217 women teaching staff, achieving an 84% response rate. An eight-item Likert scale assessed perceptions of working conditions, workload, promotion equity, access to training, and institutional support. Internal consistency was acceptable (Cronbach's alpha = 0.740; McDonald's omega = 0.766). Analyses included Spearman correlations, Kruskal-Wallis tests by academic area, and thematic analysis. Workload intensity was negatively associated with perceived promotion opportunities (rho = -0.228, p < 0.01). Overall perceptions did not differ significantly across academic areas; however, Science and Engineering faculty reported significantly lower access to training (H = 10.324, p < 0.05). Conclusion: Gender equity requires discipline-sensitive interventions addressing workload distribution, transparent promotion criteria, and equitable professional development access.

TI Cloud-based structural biology and drug discovery training module on
   google cloud platform
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE docking; drug discovery; Google Cloud; Jupyter notebook; NIGMS-Sandbox;
   protein structure; protein-protein interaction
ID CRYSTAL-STRUCTURE; TOOLS
AB Training in structural biology and structure-based drug discovery commonly requires specialized software, local high-performance computing resources, and a complex technical setup - conditions that exclude many learners. We present a cloud-based Structural Biology and Drug Discovery curriculum implemented on the National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS) Sandbox platform, giving users browser-native access to research-grade computational workflows without local installation. The course is organized into four modular subunits covering protein structure analysis, protein-ligand docking, protein-protein interactions, and structure-guided drug design, delivered through interactive Jupyter notebooks running on Google Cloud's Vertex AI Workbench and integrate widely used tools including AlphaFold, PyMOL, AutoDock, and ClusPro. Both workshops demonstrated reliable deployment of the cloud-based environment, and participant surveys indicated high satisfaction across clarity of instruction, relevance of activities, and technical robustness (mean scores approximately 4.1-4.4 on a 5-point scale). Together, these results show that cloud-native, reproducible computational environments can substantially reduce the technical barriers that limit access to structural biology training, making such curricula scalable across institutions and equipping learners with the computational skills now expected in modern drug discovery research.

TI Impact of ESG integration in STEM and non-STEM master's programmes:
   evidence from Kazakhstan
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competency development; ESG integration; global competence; higher
   education; Kazakhstan; STEM education; sustainability education
AB This study examines the integration of Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) concepts in selected master's-level programmes in Kazakhstan, with a focus on differences between STEM and non-STEM disciplines and their relationship to student competency development. In the context of science education and global learning, ESG-related competencies can be understood as an important component of global competence, enabling students to engage with complex sustainability challenges. The study adopts a comparative mixed-methods design, combining curriculum analysis with student survey data. A structured ESG Integration Index was developed to assess the extent and depth of ESG-related content across programmes, while self-reported competencies were measured across five dimensions. The sample includes 90 master's students from STEM and non-STEM programmes. The findings indicate that ESG integration is present across all analysed programmes but varies significantly in structure and depth. Non-STEM programmes demonstrate more explicit and multidimensional integration, particularly in social and governance domains, whereas STEM programmes focus more narrowly on environmental and technical aspects. At the same time, students in STEM programmes report higher levels of self-perceived ESG competencies across all dimensions. No statistically significant relationship was found between curriculum-level ESG integration and competency development. These results suggest that ESG integration in higher education may not operate as a linear process (curriculum to competencies), but rather as a mediated system in which learning outcomes depend on pedagogical practices, disciplinary contexts, and student engagement. In the context of science education, this highlights the importance of approaches that support critical reflection, interdisciplinary thinking, and application-oriented learning. Overall, the study provides exploratory empirical evidence on ESG integration in an underexplored Central Asian context and contributes to understanding the complex relationship between curriculum design and sustainability-related competency development.

TI Explainable artificial intelligence for educational decision-making: a
   LightGBM leaf-embedding neural blender for interpretable major course
   prediction using SHAP
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE LightGBM; machine learning; major selection; under-graduate students;
   XAI
ID STUDENTS
AB Introduction Selecting an undergraduate major is a crucial academic decision that significantly influences students' long-term learning trajectories and career outcomes. Despite policies promoting flexible curriculum design and informed major-minor combinations, students often make suboptimal choices due to limited guidance and external influences.Methods To address this challenge, this study proposes a LightGBM Leaf-Embedding Neural Blender (LENB) framework that integrates gradient-boosted tree representations with neural embedding layers to predict major-course selection.Results Using a comprehensive dataset of 19,921 undergraduate students across multiple academic streams- Arts, Commerce, Science, Language, and Other-the proposed model achieves high predictive performance with accuracies up to 87.50% and strong cross-validation stability. The framework incorporates class balancing (SMOTE with class weighting), AdamW optimization with early stopping, and dropout-based regularization to ensure robustness and generalization. Furthermore, SHAP-based interpretability analysis provides clear insights into the factors influencing major selection, revealing that MINOR, CGPA, and Programme are the most dominant predictors, reflecting the importance of academic background and curricular structure. In contrast, socio-demographic attributes such as Gender and Religion exhibit relatively lower influence compared to academic features, indicating reduced reliance on sensitive attributes rather than complete bias neutrality.Discussion Comparative evaluation against RandomForest, XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, and TabNet demonstrates that the proposed LENB framework achieves competitive performance across multiple streams and outperforms baseline models in several cases, particularly in the Arts and Commerce streams. However, in the Language stream, Random Forest achieves slightly higher accuracy, indicating that the effectiveness of hybrid models may vary depending on the underlying data structure. By integrating explainable artificial intelligence with a hybrid learning architecture, the proposed framework delivers transparent, data- driven insights that can support educators, policy-makers, and career counselors in guiding informed academic decision-making.

TI EDI governance and the limits of neutrality in university responses to
   Gaza
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE EDI; Gaza; higher education; Palestine; university governance
AB Universities are often positioned as spaces of critical inquiry, civic responsibility, and global engagement. Yet responses to Gaza have raised important questions about whether these commitments are enacted consistently across geopolitical contexts. In Gaza, universities and educational institutions have been severely damaged or destroyed, with students and staff killed and educational infrastructures profoundly disrupted. Focusing on UK higher education, this Perspective article examines how university responses to Gaza are shaped by university governance, discursive norms, and the institutionalisation of equality, diversity and inclusion (EDI). Drawing on critical scholarship on higher education, decolonisation, institutional silence, and the politics of knowledge, the article argues that appeals to neutrality, the linguistic framing of crisis, and EDI governance can impact the conditions under which Palestinian suffering is recognised, marginalised, or rendered difficult to name. The argument is not that universities lack commitments to equity, inclusion, academic freedom, or global responsibility, but that these commitments are mediated through institutional structures that may constrain the forms of critique they claim to support. By examining how neutrality, balance, wellbeing, and reputational risk are operationalised in practice, the article considers how institutional silence can become a mode of governance. It argues that meaningful engagement requires more than symbolic concern or procedural inclusion. It requires sustained attention to the conditions through which responsibility is organised, critique is managed, and the labour of naming violence is unevenly distributed.

TI The effect of the frequency of use of an intelligent tutoring system on
   learning gains in mathematics in schools in challenging social
   circumstances
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE educational measurement and assessment; Germany; ITS; longitudinal
   study; mathematics education
ID TECHNOLOGY; METAANALYSIS; ACCEPTANCE
AB Intelligent tutoring systems (ITS) are characterized by their ability to provide direct, adaptive feedback and to assess students' knowledge in order to assign exercises matched to their current proficiency. Nevertheless, research on the effectiveness of ITS in mathematics presents an inconclusive picture. To address this, the present study examined the use and effectiveness of an ITS implemented in Grade 8 and 9 mathematics classrooms in schools in challenging social circumstances in Germany. The dataset comprised achievement tests, student and teacher questionnaires, and detailed log data from 587 students in 60 classes; additional analyses used subsamples of ITS users and classes with teacher questionnaire data. We investigated which students and classes engaged with the ITS and whether system use was associated with greater learning gains. Results showed uneven and delayed implementation: only 41 classes used the ITS at least once, and average use among users was low. Multilevel models indicated no class-level effect of mean ITS usage on learning gains. At the individual level, students who used the ITS more than their classmates, particularly during school time, showed small positive associations with post-test performance, whereas home use was not related to gains. Predictors of ITS usage included students' work ethic, gender, and their rating of the ITS as well as teacher experience. Overall, the findings indicate that ITS use does not automatically translate into higher learning gains. Future research should therefore focus on identifying the instructional conditions and usage practices under which ITS use becomes learning-effective, particularly in socially disadvantaged settings.

TI LLM use during exam preparation and student performance in university
   mathematics: a quantitative observational study
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE academic performance; exam preparation; generative AI; large language
   models; mathematics education; mixed-effects model; self-regulated
   learning; university students
AB The integration of large language models (LLMs) into student study practices raises important questions about their association with academic performance, yet empirical evidence from authentic university settings remains scarce. This observational study examined whether self-reported LLM use during exam preparation was associated with performance in a first-semester university mathematics course focused on discrete mathematics and mathematical logic. Data were collected from N=197 students who completed two midterm tests and indicated after each test whether they had used an LLM during preparation. A linear mixed-effects model with a random intercept for student was applied to account for the repeated measurement structure and unbalanced participation in the second test. Reported LLM use was associated with an average score increase of approximately 11 points (95% CI [3.82, 19.12], p=.003), with no significant interaction between LLM use and test (p=.907), indicating a consistent association across both assessments. Participation in the second test was strongly predicted by first-test performance (d=0.97), while LLM use was not a significant independent predictor after controlling for prior achievement. These findings contribute quantitative evidence to ongoing discussions about the role of generative AI in university mathematics education.

TI Temporal trends in engagement with asynchronous e-learning: a
   longitudinal observation
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE asynchronous e-learning; learning analytics; longitudinal study; medical
   education; motivation; post-pandemic education; student engagement
AB The rapid adoption of asynchronous e-learning during the COVID-19 pandemic has raised questions regarding the sustainability of student engagement in digital teaching formats over time. The objective of this study was to examine the trends in participation over time in a mandatory asynchronous course within the domain of preclinical medical education. A longitudinal observational design was applied across multiple cohorts from summer term 2020 to winter term 2025/2026. The course structure, consisting of a video based learning module, a mandatory quiz for participation validation, and an optional synchronous consultation, remained unchanged throughout the study period. Participation, quiz completion, performance, and consultation attendance were assessed descriptively. A total of 703 students participated, of whom 628 completed the quiz. The number of participants per course ranged from 5 to 85, while the number of eligible students ranged from 398 to 745. Quiz completion among participants remained consistently high across all cohorts. Mean quiz scores ranged from 7.20 to 10.00 points. Participation in optional synchronous consultation ranged from 0 to 7 students. Over time, participation decreased, whereas quiz completion and performance among participating students remained stable. These findings indicate that temporal changes primarily affected initial engagement rather than learning outcomes among active participants, highlighting the importance of distinguishing between participation and performance when evaluating asynchronous digital teaching formats.

TI The ethical foundations of professional resistance
SO MEDICAL TEACHER
LA English
DT Article
DE Professionalism; professional resistance; bioethics; advocacy; freedom
AB Issue Although it has long been present in medicine and medical education, the growth in the number of instances of resistance by medical trainees around the world, the visibility thereof, and the resulting disruption of medical education have made the grounding of professional resistance a critical concern for all involved. Position The authors argue that professional resistance needs to be understood as being subject to the principles of bioethics that underpin medical professionalism: beneficence, non-malevolence, autonomy, and justice. Argument The authors consider the implications of this position in terms of three issues: 1) that becoming a professional and pursuing a professional career requires individuals to yield something of themselves, 2) that a profession should aspire to have and to hold to standards that are higher than those required of it, and 3) the issue of the separation of professional and personal lives. Conclusion All acts of resistance by professionals need to align with the foundational ethical principles of their profession to be legitimately considered professional and they cannot simply be set aside when anger or outrage precipitates acts of resistance.

TI Wielding Magic Without Mastery: The Illusion of Competence in the Age of
   AI
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; Illusion of competence; Metacognition; Critical
   thinking; Cognitive offloading
ID DIFFICULTIES; FLUENCY
AB Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can make learners feel they understand more while actually learning less. As these tools become embedded in pharmacy education, students gain instant access to coherent, easy-tounderstand outputs, often without the effortful thinking that builds durable understanding. This commentary argues that GenAI's most consequential educational risk is not inaccuracy, but the illusion of competence: a metacognitive error in which readily available, coherent answers inflate confidence while genuine understanding lags behind. Drawing on cognitive science, the commentary explains how GenAI enables learners to bypass generative processing (the effortful work of retrieving, organizing, and explaining information in one's own words on which durable learning depends). When this work is offloaded, learners increasingly mistake the ease of processing an artificial intelligence-generated output for mastery of the material. This miscalibration is especially dangerous for novice learners who lack the expertise to detect errors or recognize what they have not yet learned, and it threatens the reasoning and judgment at the core of pharmacy practice. The central question is, therefore, not whether GenAI should be used but how. Educators must move beyond permissive or restrictive policies toward intentional design that preserves cognitive effort, calibrates learners' self-assessment, and makes expert reasoning visible. The commentary offers concrete strategies (structured, inquiry-driven GenAI use; assessments that expose the gap between assisted and independent performance; and deliberate modeling of expert vs novice use) to help educators develop competent, reflective practitioners rather than confident learners who cannot think without the tool.

TI The Need for Unification: Assessing Variability in Top 200/300 Drug
   Lists at 7 Schools of Pharmacy
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Top 200; Top 300; Drug list; Brand; Generic
AB Objective: To assess the variability of Top 200/300 drug lists used by pharmacy programs and commonly used resources. A secondary objective was to compare educational assessment procedures for information from Top 200/300 drug lists between institutions. Methods: The Top 200/300 drug list from 7 schools of pharmacy and 4 resources were compared to determine the variability in content. Using generic names, drug lists were analyzed by 2 investigators who independently completed the comparison and met to reach a consensus. Information on formative and summative assessment processes was also gathered from 7 schools of pharmacy. Descriptive statistics were used to report the findings. Results: After combining all school and resource lists, 572 unique generic medications were included; of these, only 36 medications were included on all 7 school lists and all 4 resource lists. There were 89 drugs on resource lists that were not included on any school's list, and an additional 125 drugs were included on 1 or more school lists but not on any resource list. The majority of schools used AccessPharmacy and faculty input to create their Top 200/300 drug lists. Comparing assessment processes, all schools evaluated brand and generic names, with some schools evaluating additional items. Assessment frequency varied from once weekly to once a semester. Conclusion: Significant variation among Top 200/300 drug lists was demonstrated across a sample of pharmacy programs and resource lists. Establishing a single, unified drug list would enhance educational alignment across the pharmacy academy.

AB writing is a common write-to-learn strategy in undergraduate STEM education, particularly for pre-class learning. Yet producing summaries that demonstrate deep comprehension is demanding and often requires instructional support. TI Enhancing domain adaptation of LLM via model composition in solving
   medical exam questions
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
LA English
DT Article
DE Medical question answering; Domain adaptation; LLM composition;
   Augmenting model
AB The advent of large language models (LLMs) has sparked interest among educators across various fields, partic ularly in medical education. However, general-purpose pretrained LLMs may perform inadequately on medical examination questions without domain adaptation. Full fine-tuning of a pretrained LLM requires substantial computing resources, making it impractical for resource-constrained settings. In this work, we investigate a Composition to Augment Language Models (CALM) framework for medical domain adaptation in answering real-world medical examination questions. Specifically, we fine-tune a small pretrained language model on an open-ended medical question-answering dataset to inject medical domain knowledge, and then develop MedCALM by composing this medical-specialized augmenting model with an anchor LLM. In addition, the selection of connected layers significantly affects the effectiveness of composition between the anchor and augmenting models. Our experiments suggest that cross-attention between the last few layers of the two models achieves promising performance.

TI Exploring issues in education regarding the provision of reasonable
   accommodations for persons with intellectual disabilities in pharmacy
   education
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Pharmacy education; Intellectual disability; Communication skills;
   Experiential learning; Reasonable accommodation
ID HEALTH; COMMUNICATION; ATTITUDES; CONTACT; PEOPLE
AB Background: Providing reasonable accommodations for persons with intellectual disabilities (ID) is increasingly recognized as an essential competency for pharmacists. However, pharmacy education in Japan often lacks training that reflects real-world interactions with this population. Objective: To explore practicing pharmacists' experiences and educational needs regarding support for persons with intellectual disabilities, and to identify implications for pharmacy communication education. Methods: Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 11 pharmacists working in community pharmacies and hospitals in Japan. Interviews focused on their experiences supporting persons with suspected ID and their perspectives on education. Transcripts were analyzed thematically using Braun and Clarke's six-phase approach. Results: Two overarching themes-"Educational Gaps" and "From Practice to Pedagogy"-and six subthemes were identified: (1) Experiential Learning and Educational Gaps, (2) On-the-Job Learning Through Imitation, (3) Personalized Communication Adaptation, (4) Removing Prejudice and Respecting Individuality, (5) Building Trust Through Repeated Interaction, and (6) Setting Boundaries and Staying Resilient. Participants emphasized the importance of adjusting communication to patient needs, reducing stigma, and learning through direct experience. Many reported a lack of educational exposure to ID during pharmacy school and developed their skills through informal, workplace-based learning. Conclusion: Pharmacists' narratives highlight the need for communication education that goes beyond standardized assessment to foster empathy, adaptability, and patient-centered care. Pharmacy curricula should incorporate experiential learning opportunities with persons with disabilities and promote collaboration with practicing pharmacists.

TI Enhancing Clinical Reasoning in Surgical Education: A Randomized
   Crossover Trial on AI-Generated Individual Feedback for Key Feature

DT Article
DE medical education; surgical education; large language models; testing
   effect; key feature questions
AB BACKGROUND The positive effect of self-testing has been proven extensively, and past research suggested that feedback could further enhance this effect. This study compared the effectiveness of 2 types of feedback for student entries into an app on learning outcomes regarding clinical reasoning in surgery (RQ1). Additionally, we investigated the effect of general app usage (RQ2) and more intensive app usage (RQ3). METHODS Fourth-year medical students at a German university participated in an entry exam and were then invited to participate in the intervention, which consisted of a self-developed app sending daily notifications with key feature questions throughout the semester, aligned to lecture topics. RESULTS There was no difference in exit exam score between the feedback conditions (p = 0. 454). Lastly, we found that higher intensity of app usage was associated with significantly higher scores and therefore a larger learning benefit over time, manifesting in a significant main effect for group (p = 0.003) and a significant interaction effect (p < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS Our results provide further evidence for the testing effect and demonstrate the successful use of key feature questions in surgical education. Since the results regarding the effect of the feedback types are mixed and the relationship between the constructs seems more complicated, further investigation is needed.(c) 2026 The Authors. TI Disaster risk perception and disaster preparedness beliefs of nursing
   students, and related factors: A cross sectional study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; Disaster risk perception; Disaster preparedness;
   Disaster
ID HAZARD
AB Background Disasters pose serious challenges to health systems, and nurses play critical roles in disaster preparedness and response. Determining nursing students' disaster risk perception and preparedness beliefs is essential for evaluating the readiness of future healthcare professionals. Nurses who accurately perceive disaster risk and believe in the necessity of preparedness are better able to deliver effective intervention and care before, during, and after disasters. Aim This study aimed to examine socio-demographic and disaster-related factors associated with disaster risk perception and disaster preparedness beliefs among nursing students. Methods This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among 862 undergraduate nursing students enrolled at a university in T & uuml;rkiye during the 2022-2023 academic year. Data were collected using the Personal Information Form, the University Students Disaster Risk Perception Scale, and the General Disaster Preparedness Belief Scale through face-to-face administration in classroom settings. Results Nursing students demonstrated a moderate level of disaster risk perception and generally positive disaster preparedness beliefs. Disaster preparedness beliefs were significantly associated with gender, year at school, having received disaster training, owning a bug-out bag, and awareness of local disaster risks. A weak but statistically significant positive correlation was found between disaster risk perception and disaster preparedness beliefs (r = 0.131, p < 0.001). Conclusion Disaster risk perception and preparedness beliefs are related yet distinct constructs among nursing students and are influenced by different factors. These findings suggest that strengthening disaster preparedness in nursing education requires comprehensive strategies that extend beyond raising risk awareness alone to include structured disaster training, skill development, and readiness.

TI Garden path processing in children with Autism Spectrum Disorders:
   Evidence from eye-tracking
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Autism Spectrum Disorders; Garden path sentences; Eye-tracking; Reading;
   Executive functions
ID AMBIGUITY RESOLUTION; READING-COMPREHENSION; WORKING-MEMORY;
   LEXICAL-BIASES; LANGUAGE; ADULTS; MISINTERPRETATIONS; SENTENCES;
   MOVEMENT; AGE
AB Though comprehenders use thematic fit to predict upcoming materials in discourse, the processor does not always select a felicitous parsing pathway. Syntactic processing models claim that multiple parses compete for selection at points of incremental ambiguity, and early parsing decisions often need to be overridden by engaging executive functions. Though previous studies investigated lexical and pronominal ambiguity in Autism Spectrum Disorders, there is a dearth of research on garden path sentence processing in autism. The objective of this study was to assess garden path sentence processing in autistic and age-matched typically-developing (TD) children by employing an eye-tracking-while-reading task. The task included sentences with temporary subject-object ambiguity stemming from either case syncretism or overt case marking of determiner phrases following optionally transitive verbs. Children's executive functions were also assessed to investigate interactions between cognitive control and garden path resolution skills. We found that the autistic children experienced larger costs than their TD peers in integrating overt case cues in garden path sentences. These costs were mainly reflected in the autistic children's significantly longer dwell time and more fixations in the determiner of the critical DPs. Also, autistic children's garden path repair processes were modulated by their executive functions not before the wrap-up of the sentences, which is indicative of delayed cognitive control adjustment. The overall findings show that structural ambiguity resolution was more challenging for the autistic children, and that this weakness stemmed from cognitive control deficits and difficulty with the mapping of morphological cues to argument features, rather than competing syntactic representations per se.

TI The effect of STEM applications based on the OCIPSE learning model on
   primary school students' academic achievement and scientific creativity
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE OCIPSE; STEM education; Scientific creativity; Academic achievement
AB The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of STEM-based teaching practices structured around the OCIPSE learning model on the academic achievement and scientific creativity of fifthgrade primary school students. The study was conducted using an embedded mixed methods design, in which the quantitative strand constituted the main component and the qualitative strand was used to support the interpretation of the intervention process. In the quantitative dimension, a quasi-experimental pretest-posttest control group design was employed, while in the qualitative dimension, a phenomenological approach was adopted to explore students' experiences of the implementation. The research was carried out with a total of 58 students enrolled in a public school in Antalya. In particular, significant differences were observed in favor of the experimental group in the fluency, flexibility, and originality dimensions of scientific creativity. The qualitative findings further indicated that students generally experienced the process as engaging, collaborative, and supportive of idea generation and active participation. Overall, the findings suggest that the OCIPSE learning model may offer a promising and structured framework for STEM teaching at the primary school level; however, these results should be interpreted within the contextual boundaries of the present study.

ID EDUCATION
AB Once primarily serving expatriate elites, the international school industry has increasingly turned its attention to affluent host-country clientele, following trends of marketisation and commercialisation. Promotion on social media has become a necessary effort for student recruitment in a competitive market. Employing Goffman's dramaturgical theory and Bourdieu's theory of social fields, this research compared the promotional strategies employed by two types of international schools and contrasted them with those of Chinese public schools. Findings revealed differences in promotional approaches across the three school types and exposed unexpected divergences within the school types. The study identified four key promotional themes visible in the schools' WeChat posts: enhancing status and visibility, student recruitment efforts, fostering school-home relationships, and reporting about student life and achievements. A trend of commercialisation became evident in all the sampled international schools, with a strong emphasis on student recruitment efforts and paid extracurriculars. The study addresses gaps in research on marketisation, commercialisation, and parental choice within the international education sector. Its focus on social media promotion and student recruitment through WeChat reveals an unexplored side of the international education business.

TI What school communities say-and what it predicts: A discourse-based

DT Article
DE School dropout; Automated text analysis; Machine learning; School
   climate; Educational risk prediction
AB School dropout remains a critical educational and societal issue, particularly in contexts where systemic challenges hinder student retention. Traditional methods of identifying at-risk schools rely on quantitative indicators such as attendance records, academic performance, or socio-demographic data, often offering only retrospective insights. This study explores a novel, scalable approach for early identification of schools with high dropout risk, based on the automated analysis of stakeholder language rather than numeric data. TI Sense of belonging and professional identity in first year students'
   peer networks
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Sense of belonging; Professional identity; Social networks; Peer
   relationships; Higher education
ID POLITICAL-SCIENCE; HIGHER-EDUCATION; PSYCHOLOGY; ENGAGEMENT;
   TRAJECTORIES
AB Background: Students' sense of belonging in higher education (HE) and professional identity can support adjustment and academic success during the challenging transition to HE. However, little is known about how these constructs co-develop over time, and how peer networks play a role in this process. Aims: This study investigates the dynamic and reciprocal development of students' sense of belonging, professional identity, and peer networks during their initial semester in HE. Sample: The sample consisted of a near-complete cohort of 247 first-year psychology students. Methods: Students completed surveys at three time points. Sense of belonging and professional identity were assessed through validated scales. Friendship and help-seeking networks were mapped using sociometric nominations. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models and stochastic actor-oriented models were used to examine reciprocal relations and network co-evolution. Results: Early sense of belonging predicted later professional identity, but not vice versa. Students with higher belonging were more likely to initiate friendships and help-seeking ties. Over time, students became more similar to their friends in belonging. Being asked for help increased students' sense of belonging, while asking for help decreased it. Professional identity was unaffected by peer relationships. Students preferred helpers with similar professional identity. Conclusions: Our findings emphasise that sense of belonging is both a driver and outcome of peer relationships and contributes to professional identity development. This indicates that belonging is a key condition for students to benefit from developmental opportunities and supportive resources in HE learning environments, and that its' development should be supported by HE institutions.

AB Teacher quality is regarded as one of the most important school-related influences on student learning, yet there is limited agreement on which observable teacher characteristics matter most for students' academic progress and how teacher quality is distributed across classrooms. Much research relies on cross-sectional data and singlecountry designs. This study addresses these limitations by examining teacher quality using multilevel modeling with TIMSS Longitudinal data. TI A multilevel meta-analysis of student evaluations of teaching and
   academic achievement
SO STUDIES IN EDUCATIONAL EVALUATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student evaluations of teaching; Teaching effectiveness; Student
   achievement; Validity; Multilevel meta-analysis; Moderator analysis
ID ROBUST VARIANCE-ESTIMATION; LEARNING OUTCOMES; META-REGRESSION; RATINGS;
   VALIDITY; PERFORMANCE; QUALITY; SATISFACTION; INSTRUCTION; PERCEPTION
AB Student evaluations of teaching (SETs) are widely used to judge instructional quality, yet their relationship with student learning remains contested. Drawing on a synthesis of correlational evidence, this study re-examines the association between SETs and student achievement (SA) using a multilevel meta-analytic framework that accounts for statistical dependence among effects. Across 57 studies with 241 correlations, the results show a statistically significant but modest positive relationship (r = .30). This suggests that student ratings are neither arbitrary nor definitive indicators of learning outcomes, but reflect a detectable yet limited association that should be interpreted with caution. Robust variance estimation and sensitivity analyses for small-sample moderator categories were applied to strengthen inference. By providing an updated and methodologically refined estimate of the SET-achievement relationship, this study offers a more balanced empirical perspective on the validity and appropriate use of student evaluations in educational decision-making.

TI Can creative imitation with SCAMPER scaffolding foster creativity in
   Japanese as a foreign language writing? A mixed methods study
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Creativity in writing; Foreign language writing; Creative imitation;

ID GENRE EXEMPLARS; THINKING; STUDENTS; PEDAGOGY
AB In foreign language writing instruction, model texts are frequently treated as normative templates for replication rather than as resources for creative exploration. Creative imitation addresses this tension by guiding learners to analyze and transform model texts to generate original expression, yet research on scaffolding this process remains limited and concentrated in English-language contexts. This study integrates SCAMPER as cognitive scaffolding for creative imitation through a 16-week mixed methods classroom intervention in a Japanese writing course at a Chinese university. TI Diversity climate and discrimination at German universities: a
   cross-sectional study among students in health-related degree programs
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Diversity climate; Discrimination; Student; Health care; Education;
   University
ID SUPPORT SERVICES; ENGAGEMENT; MATTERS
AB Background Diversity is essential in higher education, particularly in health-related programs (e.g., medicine, psychology, and other health professions). Inclusive and non-discriminatory learning environments are crucial for promoting equity and preparing future health care professionals to care for diverse populations. However, empirical evidence on students' perceptions of diversity in German universities remains limited. This study aimed to 1) assess students' perceptions of the diversity climate in their health-related degree programs and university contexts and 2) examine differences in psychosocial and academic variables between students with and without experiences of discrimination.Methods A national cross-sectional online survey was conducted between January and April 2024 among students in health-related degree programs at German universities. Measures included sociodemographic and educational characteristics, students' perceptions of diversity climate (across three dimensions: age, ethnicity, gender), experiences of discrimination, diversity- and equity-oriented beliefs, sense of belonging to the university, study engagement, general and academic self-efficacy, and general and study-related stress. Descriptive analyses were conducted as well as independent t-tests to examine differences between groups.Results A total of 987 students from 83 universities across all 16 federal states participated. Students' perceptions of the diversity climate were moderately to highly positive across age (M = 3.91/5, SD = .59), ethnicity (M = 3.63/5, SD = .65), and gender (M = 3.83/5, SD = .59). While the majority reported no personal discrimination at their university, 28% experienced discrimination within the past two years, most commonly due to gender (42%), physical appearance (23%), mental health (20%), or racial reasons (13%). Additionally, 45% had witnessed discrimination. Students with personal experiences of discrimination reported significantly less positive perceptions of the diversity climate, lower academic self-efficacy, study engagement, and sense of belonging at the university, higher stress, and stronger diversity- and equity-oriented beliefs. Across the full sample, 61% indicated that teaching materials do not adequately represent diverse groups, and 50% perceived lecturers as insufficiently responsive to discrimination.Conclusion Despite generally positive attitudes toward diversity, the students' high rates of experiences of discrimination and their associations with psychosocial and academic variables highlight the need for systematic efforts to promote inclusive learning environments. Targeted interventions, such as diversity training for staff and students, improved representation in teaching materials and curricula, and stronger institutional policies, are essential to promote equity and well-being in health-related education. By using a nationwide scope, focusing on health-related degree programs, and conducting a multidimensional assessment of students' perceptions of diversity climate, this study offers important evidence to inform such efforts and addresses a notable gap in the literature.

TI Experience, awareness, attitudes and ecological worldviews related to
   sustainable development among physiotherapy students in Sweden: a
   cross-sectional survey
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Consciousness of sustainable development; Education; Health professions
   education; New Environmental Paradigm; Physiotherapy; Sustainable
   development; Sustainability Attitudes in Nursing Survey
ID HEALTH; EDUCATION
AB Background To achieve a transition toward sustainable development, education is an essential driver of change. Factors like learners' attitudes, cultural beliefs and social communities may influence the learning process. In the field of physiotherapy, there is limited knowledge regarding students' understanding of and attitudes toward sustainable development.Aim This study aimed to investigate students' perceptions related to sustainable development.Method All eight undergraduate physiotherapy programs in Sweden were invited to participate. An anonymous online survey was sent out to collect data about (i) Students' experiences of sustainable development in the curriculum, (ii) Attitudes toward sustainability and climate change in physiotherapy and physiotherapy education, (iii) Ecological worldviews, and (iv) Consciousness of sustainable development.Results A total of 116 students responded to the online survey.    Educational Measurement
SO EDUCATIONAL MEASUREMENT-ISSUES AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE communication; foundational competencies; score reporting; testing
   purposes; validity evidence
AB I provide evidence and arguments for increased investment in communication competencies in educational measurement. Building on the 2024 framework for Foundational Competencies in Educational Measurement, I emphasize communication as both a distinct domain and an interactive amplifier of collaboration, technical, and measurement competencies. TI From reflection to design: a plurilingual research team's ecological
   approach to cross-linguistic mediation research in icelandic and german
   primary schools
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RESEARCH & METHOD IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Plurilingual research; cross-linguistic mediation; reflective practice;
   ecological systems perspective; multilingual education
ID EDUCATION
AB This study examined how a plurilingual research team (N = 7) drew on reflections from two exploratory workshops in Iceland (Reykjav & iacute;k) and Germany (Berlin) to shape the philosophical, theoretical, and methodological foundations of a longitudinal study on cross-linguistic mediation (CLM) in multilingual primary school settings. Drawing on twenty hours of recorded reflective discussions, the analysis traces how the researchers' philosophical and theoretical positions evolved through encounters with classroom practices and subsequently impacted the design of their research study. Applying Farrell's (2015, 2024) framework and its five dimensions of reflective practice, the analysis highlights a shift toward an ecological understanding of CLM, which emerged from complex interactions among learners, teachers, materials, school cultures, and policy contexts. This shift informed key methodological decisions in the final proposal of the research project, including the adoption of an ecological systems perspective, a pre-intervention mapping phase, the selection of contrasting instructional ecologies, and the design of a collaborative, teacher-oriented professional development model grounded in lived classroom ecologies. The study contributes to research on systematic reflexivity in multilingual education by demonstrating how researchers' reflective practices can serve as a methodological tool, shaping their stances and directly informing decisions about classroom research design.

TI Boxed Thermodynamics: Agent-Based Visualization of Chemical Equilibrium,
   Kinetics, and Free Energy Landscapes
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Physical Chemistry; Computer-Based
   Learning; Thermodynamics; Kinetics
ID CHEMISTRY
AB This paper introduces an agent-based simulation framework in NetLogo for exploring core principles of chemical thermodynamics and kinetics. The approach centers on the behavior of noninteracting particles in compartmentalized boxes whose geometry and energy barriers are explicitly linked to reactions' enthalpy, entropy, and activation energy. By simulating particles within boxes of tunable floor levels and widths, abstract thermodynamic concepts become immediately visible and measurable. The visual logic of the simulations allows users to examine how temperature, chemical potentials, and free energy relate to chemical equilibrium and kinetics, using both multiparticle averages and single-particle traces. The framework supports Master Equation-based predictions, offering a bridge between microscopic dynamics and macroscopic observables. The model provides a conceptually transparent and computationally grounded tool for illustrating the behavior of chemical systems, which can be readily used by students both during class demonstrations and as part of homework exercises.

TI An Industry-Engaged Project-Based Learning Module for Undergraduates:
   Polyimide Films as a Case Study in Scientific and Engineering Thinking
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Problem Solving/DecisionMaking; Materials
   Science
AB Undergraduate laboratory and project-based learning (PBL) activities can be effective for skill development, yet they often lack sustained industry engagement and explicit structures that connect scientific reasoning with engineering-oriented decision making. This paper reports an Open Innovative Experiment model that integrates Science-Industry-Education collaboration into a course-level PBL framework for undergraduate training. Using polyimide films with tunable branching as a representative case study, students completed a structured workflow that combined laboratory preparation/characterization with simulation-assisted interpretation to examine how structure and testing configurations influence dielectric breakdown behavior. Implementation of the model through an industry-engaged, dual-mentor structure enabled authentic problem contexts and constraints while maintaining nonproprietary boundaries. Student and industry-partner feedback, together with course-level outcomes, indicated strengthened experimental competency, improved awareness of reliability/quality considerations, and enhanced ability to translate classroom knowledge into practice. The model provides a transferable approach for incorporating industry engagement into undergraduate experimental curricula in applied chemistry and related disciplines.

TI Are Bioimpedance Parameters Altered in Adults With Down Syndrome? A
   Cross-Sectional Study
SO JOURNAL OF INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE BIA; BIVA; body composition; Down syndrome; health
ID FAT-FREE MASS; BIOELECTRICAL-IMPEDANCE; BODY-COMPOSITION; PERCENTAGE
AB Background Individuals with Down syndrome (DS) exhibit altered body composition that could be assessed through bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA). This study aims to compare the BIA measures and bioelectrical impedance vector analysis (BIVA) between individuals with and without DS. Methods We evaluated 46 individuals with and 46 without DS through BIA and BIVA. We employed generalized linear models (GLM) to assess the effects of group and sex on BIA, adjusting by age and height. Results Individuals with DS had lower whole-body resistance/height (DS: 332.1 +/- 51.1; non-DS: 349.0 +/- 57.5 Omega/m), reactance/height (DS: 36.4 +/- 5.0; non-DS: 41.9 +/- 4.9 Omega/m) and impedance/height (DS: 334.1 +/- 51.2; non-DS: 351.4 +/- 57.6 Omega/m), while men with DS showed lower phase angle (DS: 6.4 +/- 0.7; non-DS: 7.0 degrees +/- 0.5 degrees) and lower bioimpedance index (DS: 50.8 +/- 6.1; non-DS: 55.2 +/- 6.5 Omega/m2); men and women with DS had higher total body water (males p = 0.030; females p = 0.006) and intracellular water (males p = 0.020; females p = 0.010) compared with individuals without DS; women had lower extracellular water (males p = 0.090; females p = 0.004) compared with individuals without DS; the bioelectrical vectors for individuals with DS were different from the population ellipses (p < 0.050), and showed overhydration compared with non-DS. Conclusions Adults with DS showed a distinct hydration pattern in comparison with non-DS adults, as shown in BIA and BIVA analysis.

AB While educational policy can be a lever to drive change in university assessment practices, it needs to be transparent to all stakeholders. This paper explores transparency related to time in Australian university assessment policies, examining techno-rational, socio-cultural, and socio-material discourses to make visible assumptions about students from diverse equity backgrounds and how they are assumed to experience time in assessment. The study presented here adopted an innovative multi-method analysis of public-facing Australian university policies drawing together four approaches: (1) accessibility analysis of time-related policy; (2) corpus analysis of time-related terms and their co-location in meaning making about time in policy documents; (3) socio-critical analysis of What the Problem is Represented (Bacchi, 2009) to be in constructions of participants and time in assessment policies; (4) thematic analysis of policy leaders' and educators' accounts of policy enactment and practice. Findings indicated that, while time was a salient concept, high levels of variability in provisions relating to time were evident between policies. There was also significant variation in how universities talked about time and how students could access more time. Some policies assumed that adjustments give certain students unfair advantages. Others acknowledged students' entitlement to adjustments but had ableist overtones, with students expected to self-advocate within existing assessment systems. This paper demonstrates how multiple analyses can complement each other and bring to the surface the inner workings of assessment policy and practice. We argue that the methodology makes possible a temporal awareness that provides for temporal justice, that is, recognition and transparency around time and its powerful role in the lives of students from equity backgrounds, as a foundation for action directed at access, inclusion, and academic success.Context and implications Rationale for this study: Australian universities increasingly implement assessment policies designed to provide students with equitable access to time. However, the transparency and accessibility of these provisions remain underexamined. This study employed multiple methods to analyse policy and interview data describing policy leaders' and educators' efforts to enhance transparency during implementation. Why the new findings matter: The findings provide evidence that current assessment policies undermine equity for students by utilising hidden deficit discourses and creating inaccessible processes. This research reveals previously unexamined ways transparency is compromised, offering critical insights for universities to begin addressing barriers that perpetuate disadvantage for diverse students in assessment policy and practices. Transparency serves equity when all students are supported to understand, access, and complete assessment on an equal basis. Implications for policymakers, educators, and researchers: For policymakers, this study highlights the need to review existing assessment policies for discourses that obscure the processes and expectations around assessment and in practice serve to disadvantage students from equity backgrounds. It also foregrounds the importance of including diverse stakeholders, including equity students, in policy ideation/drafting rather than just review.
   Analyses suggest that educators have a significant role in trying to mediate and make policies transparent for students who may need access to additional time to demonstrate what they know and can do. For researchers, the novel combination of research methods for policy analysis led to a more complete picture of policy transparency. Future research must include diverse students' voices to investigate their experiences relating to assessment policy and time. Consideration of temporal awareness and temporal justice as theoretical standpoints in interrogating equity in relation to time will strengthen approaches to transparency in assessment policy.

TI Universal Design in Distance Higher Education Institutions: The Path to
   Inclusion
SO ADULT LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE neurodivergent students; students with disabilities; distance higher
   education; adult learners; online learning; universal design
ID STUDENTS; AUTISM; CHALLENGES; LEARNERS
AB The number of Neurodivergent students and students with disabilities has been growing within higher education institutions. There still exists a disparity in admission and graduation rates between students with diverse learning needs and those in the neuromajority. This paper examines the main barriers that contribute to this disparity and, through the lens of Universal Design (UD) and the social model of disability, offers recommendations to prevent and overcome those barriers. Particularly relevant to online higher education contexts that tend to be favored by students with diverse learning needs, UD-aligned considerations are discussed. Those include environmental design (e.g., setting clear expectations and outcomes, embedding bidirectional feedback systems, among others) and social connectedness and support (e.g., building community, fostering supportive relationships, valuing diversity of communication, and creating a sense of belonging) that focus on promoting student well-being and increase their likelihood of completing their educational programs successfully.

AB The success of educational institutions depends on the retention rate of their students. It is a key factor that determines whether these institutions receive accreditation, ratings, or rankings. Retention also influences the placement of students. Students are categorised as being above average, average, or below average according to academic achievement. TI Dispositional Predictors of Counselor Impostor Phenomenon: Vulnerability
   Traits and Coping Resources Among Counselors-in-Training
SO COUNSELOR EDUCATION AND SUPERVISION
LA English
DT Article
DE counselor development; counselor impostor phenomenon;
   counselors-in-training; perfectionism; self-compassion
ID SELF-COMPASSION; PERFECTIONISM; VALIDATION
AB Counselor impostor phenomenon (CIP) is characterized by persistent self-doubt and the dismissal of evidence of competence and is prevalent among counselors-in-training (CITs). Although prior research has examined individual correlates of CIP, no study has examined the relative contributions of vulnerability traits, broad personality dimensions, and coping resources within a single model, or whether CIP and its dispositional correlates differ across training stages. This cross-sectional study examined relationships between CIP and dispositional traits among 172 CITs enrolled in CACREP-accredited counseling programs. A three-step hierarchical regression entered evaluative concerns, striving, and procrastination in the first block, the Big Five personality traits in the second block, and self-compassion and grit in the third block. Evaluative concerns was the strongest predictor in the first block. Among the Big Five, only openness contributed unique variance. In the full model, self-compassion and evaluative concerns were the strongest predictors, contributing nearly identical unique variance in opposing directions, followed by openness and striving, which emerged as a negative predictor once self-critical evaluation was held constant. Procrastination, neuroticism, extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and grit did not contribute unique variance. A one-way MANOVA found no significant differences in CIP or dispositional traits across pre-practicum, practicum, and internship stages. Implications for counselor education and supervision are discussed.
