TI Translanguaging-to-learn: Evidence from a L2 Chinese classroom
SO LINGUISTICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Translanguaging; Output hypothesis; Cognitive; L2 learning; Conversation
   analysis; Classroom observation; Language Pedagogy
ID LANGUAGE; IDENTITIES; L1
AB This study looked into the naturally-occurred translanguaging behaviors gleaned from video recordings of an introductory L2 Chinese class both quantitatively and qualitatively. The participants included 41 college-level learners of Chinese who engaged in communicative tasks and were encouraged to use both their shared dominant language and second languages (L2). Audio recordings of around 400 min of interactions between peers during collaborative tasks were transcribed. Qualitative analysis of the data was based on the framework of Conversation Analysis (Sacks et al., 1974), while particular attention was paid to learners' turn-taking, repair, translanguaging instances, and their chunk disassemble and assemble behaviors in output. Two bottom-up coding schemes built upon existing analytical frameworks (Swain, 1985, 1998; Myers-Scotton, 1993; Poplack, 1980) were used to analyze the learners' translanguaging behaviors quantitatively. The data revealed that learners did not translanguage randomly. Instead, there was abundant evidence linking translanguaging to cognitive processes that might facilitate syntactic processing. Notably, Chinese, a non-inflected language heavily reliant on word order, provided a clear lens for observing how learners analyze and reassemble chunks through multilingual practices. Linking linguistic research to classroom practice, the study moved beyond endorsing translanguaging in language classrooms, and toward more function-specific claims grounded in evidence.

   adapting to facilitating nature-based learning

DT Article
DE A B S T R A C T

AB Benefits of nature-based learning are well documented. However, there are many challenges and open questions in preparing teachers to facilitate nature-based learning. We take a cultural-historical activity theoretical (CHAT) approach to analyzing the dilemmas faced by 14 fifth-and sixth-grade teachers and one principal as they prepared for and facilitated a week-long, nature-based learning experience for students. TI Implementation of a Novel Group-Based Entrustable Professional Activity
   Model During Early Experiential Placements
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF PHARMACEUTICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Entrustable professional activities; Work-integrated learning; Feedback;
   Peer observation; Reflection
ID MEDICATION RECONCILIATION
AB Objectives: This study aimed to evaluate the implementation of a group-based entrustable professional activity (EPA) model embedded within early work-integrated learning placements for pharmacy students. Methods: Early-learner pharmacy students participated in 5 structured hospital-based placement visits focused on obtaining a best possible medication history (BPMH) for patients. A group learning approach was used, where students rotated between performing and observing the activity. The EPA tool was integrated to guide observation, self-reflection and supervisor feedback. Preactivity self-reported confidence and supervisor-assigned entrustment ratings were collected at each visit and aggregated to assess change over time. An end-of-semester survey captured students' perceptions of the EPA framework's utility. Summative performance was evaluated via an objective structured clinical examination, with scores compared with the previous year's cohort, which had not used the EPA tool. Results: A total of 95 students participated in the study. Supervisor-assigned entrustment ratings increased progressively across the 5 visits, whereas student self-reported confidence improved significantly overall. Students who performed the BPMH in later visits reported higher initial confidence and received higher entrustment ratings after observing multiple peers. Objective structured clinical examination performance showed statistically significant improvements in BPMH documentation and total scores compared with the pre-EPA cohort. Students valued the EPA for providing structure, clarifying expectations, enabling targeted feedback, and supporting peer-based learning. Conclusion: A group-based EPA model embedded within early work-integrated learning placements effectively enhanced student confidence and competence developed through structured reflection, targeted feedback, and observational learning while remaining resource-efficient and scalable for undergraduate programs.

TI "Eye" do not understand! Analyzing the roles of negation and reading
   comprehension ability in comprehension difficulties with questionnaire
   items using eye tracking
SO DISCOURSE PROCESSES
LA English
DT Article
ID COGNITIVE-PROCESSES; MOVEMENTS; MISRESPONSE; READERS; METACOMPREHENSION
AB To mitigate response biases, some questionnaires contain negated items. While previous findings suggest that negated items may increase processing difficulty compared to affirmative items, this has not yet been analyzed among participants with varying reading comprehension abilities. Additionally, it is unclear whether questionnaire respondents are aware of these difficulties. This study investigated the roles of item polarity and reading comprehension ability in item processing using eye tracking and cued-retrospective interviews. Forty-nine adults read and responded to 16 affirmative and 16 negated items while their gaze was recorded. These findings underscore the importance of considering item and reader characteristics when designing questionnaires.

AB Learning route descriptions are associated with the formation of spatial mental models. TI Drivers of Professional Satisfaction in Emergency Medicine Residency
   Training in the US
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID QUALITY
AB Background Physician wellness discussions often center on burnout and negative aspects of clinical practice. Less is known about what brings professional satisfaction to physicians, particularly among emergency medicine (EM) residents. Understanding drivers of professional satisfaction is important for the future of the specialty as they may influence residents' career decisions. This study aimed to identify drivers of professional satisfaction among a national cohort of EM residents.Methods We conducted a mixed methods study using a survey administered following the 2024 ABEM In-Training Examination to EM residents in ACGME-accredited programs. The single-item, free-text survey question asked: "List the top 3 drivers of your professional satisfaction in EM." Responses were linked to resident demographics, year in training, and program length. Using an exploratory, sequential mixed methods design, we developed a codebook via team-based thematic analysis. We subsequently quantified theme prevalence, summarized the top 10 themes, and compared the top 5 themes across strata by demographics and program characteristics.Results 3914 of 9820 eligible residents (39.9%) responded. Our team identified 41 unique themes from these responses. The top 10 drivers of professional satisfaction by frequency were: (1) EM community/team culture, (2) positive impact on patients, (3) work-life balance, (4) bedside patient interactions, (5) clinical variety, (6) shift work flexibility, (7) financial compensation, (8) opportunities for procedures, (9) EM clinical skill set, and (10) critical care opportunities. The most prevalent themes did not vary by resident demographics.Conclusion In a national cohort of EM residents, we identified a list of key drivers of professional satisfaction that clustered into a small number of highly prevalent themes. The most important factors were related to the people and culture of the program and making a positive impact on patients. These findings may inform strategies to strengthen EM resident professional fulfillment and support the future of the specialty.

TI Resonance, Education, and adolescence: introducing the special issue
SO ETHICS AND EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Resonance; Hartmut Rosa; philosophy of education; ethics; adolescence
AB This essay introduces the special issue 'Resonance, Education, and Adolescence.' The special issue brings together a diverse set of papers focused on drawing out the educational and ethical implications of Hartmut Rosa's thinking on resonance. We believe these papers demonstrate the importance of Rosa's work for education, and we hope that this issue serves to jumpstart a range of conversations that will become of central importance to educators, parents, policymakers, researchers, and school leaders. TI Exploring AI-assisted methods and acoustic analysis in finding epistemic
   emotions in learning discussions
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF RESEARCH & METHOD IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Acoustic analysis; methodological study; transcript; epistemic emotions;
   epistemic content; AI tools for research
ID COGNITIVE NEUROSCIENCE; VOICE; FAMILIARITY; STATE
AB When studying learning, transcribing verbal and nonverbal information can be highly time-consuming and laborious. AI methods can speed up this process but reviewing data remains essential. This study examines two approaches that could make learning research less laborious to the researcher. First, it was explored whether acoustic analysis is suitable for picking out possible moments of learning from audio recordings, and second, whether possible moments of learning can be picked out from AI transcribed data of audio recordings. Two pre-service physics teachers' audio recordings in classroom peer learning sessions were used as source material. The audio was transcribed by a human and an AI tool. From the transcripts, speech turns indicating epistemic emotions and content were picked. With acoustic analysis of the audio, speech turns with high pitch and/or intensity were marked. The results showed that the AI tool experienced multiple challenges in identifying speakers and speech correctly, leaving a vast need for ensuring the content of the speech turns. However, acoustic analysis picked the speech turns indicating epistemic emotions and content with considerable likelihood. This study suggests that acoustic analysis is a very promising method for locating possible learning moments for further study even from real-world audio data.

AB Paraeducator support is often crucial in the education of students with emotional and behavioral disorders. TI Back to Basics: Supporting Growth in Mathematics Fluency in
   Developmental General Chemistry and the Regulation of Calculator Use
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First Year Undergraduate/General; Chemical Education Research;
   Testing/Assessment; Nonmajor Courses; Stoichiometry
ID CONFCHEM CONFERENCE; SUCCESS; STUDENTS; SKILLS; IMPACT
AB Traditional paper and pencil activities are valuable for assessing, predicting, and improving student performance in general chemistry, particularly when related to mathematical automaticity-what students can do without a calculator-because graders can gain insight into student understanding. This study tracks the changes in the mathematical fluency of 725 students taking a developmental general chemistry course in the fall of 2025. Two instructors taught the course using similar teaching strategies including paper and pencil exams. One instructor implemented a calculator-free exam on stoichiometry, while the other allowed calculators on all exams and activities. Students in the calculator-free condition also participated in calculator-free recitation sections and calculator-free homework and received practice exams that did not require calculators. The validated Math Up Skills Test (MUST) was administered to both groups on the first day of the course and again during the 11th week after the stoichiometry exam. Students in both conditions started and ended the course with concerning levels of mathematical automaticity. However, both treatment and comparison conditions improved substantially, showing average MUST score gains of 13-14 percentage points (+2.7 item improvement). The calculator-free group outperformed the comparison group on several MUST items at a statistically significant level, particularly for items related to course topics. Results show that the use of mathematical concepts within the developmental general chemistry course enhances mathematical fluency regardless of the calculator use condition, although calculator-free activities may provide small benefits. It is recommended that the reader have a copy of the MUST available to appreciate the context of this study.

TI Taking Bragg's Law to a Higher Cognitive Level: Using Sketches to Assess
   Misconceptions of X-ray Diffraction Orders
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Analytical Chemistry; Physical Chemistry;
   Inquiry-Based/Discovery Learning; Laboratory Equipment/Apparatus; X-ray
   Crystallography
ID POWDER XRD
AB Undergraduate textbooks covering X-ray diffraction and Bragg's Law typically show diagrams with only one diffraction order. As a result, students often incorrectly visualize X-ray diffraction orders as beams scattered from different crystalline planes rather than beams scattered at distinct angles. I argue that this misconception arises because the labels for crystalline planes, beams, and diffraction orders all share the same integers (1, 2, ...) and because students typically do not analyze the diagrams carefully. Solving Bragg's Law problems is straightforward and typically does not produce learning at higher cognitive levels. In contrast, sketching different diffraction orders in real space demands a higher level of cognitive skill and is the main theme of my article. This task serves to assess students' understanding and identify those students who can translate the Bragg's Law formula into the physical process in real space. Here, I highlight common student misconceptions and propose hint-based questioning to help students apply critical theoretical concepts. When students see and think about an X-ray diffraction pattern with multiple orders, they experience an "aha!" moment and begin to correctly visualize these beams. I find that showing students a real XRD pattern with diffraction orders is more effective in helping them visualize the physical process than drilling Bragg's Law problems.

TI From Waste to Wealth: An Integrated and Green Chemistry Experiment on
   Fabricating Smartphone-Based Fluorescent Sensors for Tetracycline

AB This comprehensive experiment presents an innovative, multidisciplinary project designed for undergraduate students, integrating the principles of analytical chemistry, environmental protection, and digital literacy. AB This laboratory activity introduces solvent polarity through the visually engaging phenomenon of negative solvatochromism using Brooker's merocyanine (MOED). SO JOURNAL OF INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY RESEARCH

DT Article

AB Background Children with rare genetic conditions are more likely to experience neurodevelopmental challenges requiring additional educational support. Although the governments in the United Kingdom and Ireland are committed to providing such support, securing it can be challenging for parents, with potential adverse implications for their mental health. Children who do not receive the educational support they need are at greater risk of poorer educational outcomes. TI Belonging in Reduced-Size Classrooms: Student Outcomes Among Chinese
   Upper Secondary Students With Intellectual and Other Documented
   Disabilities
SO JOURNAL OF INTELLECTUAL DISABILITY RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE academic achievement; documented disabilities; inclusive education;
   intellectual disability; mixed methods; reduced-size classrooms;
   structural equation modelling; subjective well-being
AB Background International debates on inclusive education often position reduced-size or specialized classrooms as either supportive provision or potentially segregating placement. Student-perspective evidence remains limited, particularly for upper secondary students with intellectual and other documented disabilities.Methods This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study examined associations between reduced-size classroom (RSC) placement and academic and socio-emotional outcomes among 153 upper secondary students with documented disabilities in Wuhan, China. Students were enrolled in RSCs of no more than eight students (n = 47) or mainstream classrooms with resource-room support (n = 106). Structural equation modelling estimated direct and indirect associations involving social integration, teacher support and academic self-efficacy, with prior special education experience treated as a key covariate. Semistructured interviews with nine RSC students explained and contextualized the quantitative patterns.Results After adjustment, RSC placement remained statistically associated with social integration, teacher support and academic self-efficacy, although estimates were attenuated. Bootstrap estimates supported indirect associations with subjective well-being through social integration and teacher support, and with academic achievement through teacher support and academic self-efficacy. Interviews highlighted belonging, personalized instruction, teacher closeness, reduced anxiety and academic confidence, while showing that students valued support quality more than placement labels.Conclusions Reduced-size placement was associated with more favourable student-reported outcomes when students perceived stronger relational security, individualized instruction and teacher support. Because placement was nonrandom and the quantitative data were cross-sectional, findings should be interpreted as associational rather than causal. The study shifts attention from a simple inclusion-versus-segregation binary toward placement quality and support processes that may be especially relevant for students with substantial support needs in upper secondary education.

Methods Data from 5 waves of the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health (Waves I [1994-95] - V [2016-2018]) were used to examine the covariate-adjusted association between adolescent school connectedness (6 items, Wave II) and 6 indicators of adult social connection (Waves IV-V). A one unit increase in school connectedness was associated with significantly higher odds (95% CI) for 5 social connection indicators: weekly activities with relatives/friends or neighbors, 1.23 (1.10-1.37); having > 2 close friends, 1.36 (1.22-1.51); high perceived social support, 1.28 (1.14-1.44); never feeling isolated, 1.20 (1.07-1.36); and high relationship satisfaction with partner, 1.15 (1.002-1.321). The association for the 6th indicator (very close with either parent figure) was 0.98 (0.86-1.13). Implications Schools are foundational social communities for developing relational capacities with benefits extending into adulthood. Conclusions Adolescent school connectedness may promote adult social connection.

TI Pilot Study and Evaluation of a Sleep Health Education Program for Early
   High School
SO JOURNAL OF SCHOOL HEALTH
LA English
DT Article
DE adolescents; education; evaluation; schools; sleep; sleep ninja
ID ADOLESCENT SLEEP; CONSEQUENCES; INSOMNIA; UPDATE
AB Background Sleep education remains largely absent from high school health curricula, despite widespread insufficient sleep in adolescents. This pilot study evaluated Sleep Ninja for the Classroom, a curriculum-aligned sleep health education program for Australian high schools. Methods Participants were teachers (N = 12) and students in Year 7-8 (N = 428). Using a single-arm pre-post design, all students received the three-lesson program during regular health classes. Student sleep knowledge and behaviors were assessed, and a program evaluation examined student- and teacher-rated acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility. Results Improvements were observed in students' sleep knowledge, satisfaction with current sleep pattern, frequency of daytime napping, earlier weekend rise time (mean = 25-min), and weeknight bedtime (mean = 6-min). No changes were found in other sleep behaviors. Students spending < 8 h in bed at program commencement showed the most significant changes in bedtimes (mean = 54-min earlier on weeknights and 39-min earlier on weekends). Acceptability was high, with most students reporting the program was relevant and engaging, and all teachers rating the program as appropriate and feasible to implement. Implications for School Health Policy, Practice, and Equity Sleep Ninja for the Classroom is a brief, acceptable sleep education program that could be considered for inclusion in high school health curricula. Conclusions This study provides preliminary evidence for an Australian curriculum-aligned sleep education program. Controlled studies are needed to evaluate longer-term outcomes and sustainable implementation.

   cyberbullying in Norwegian primary schools
SO SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article

ID PEER-VICTIMIZATION; DIGITAL-AGE; FRAMEWORK; IMPACT
AB This study examines students' perspectives on stakeholder cooperation to address cyberbullying in Norwegian elementary and middle schools (grades 7-10). Q methodology was employed to reveal adolescents' subjective perspectives on what they expect stakeholders to help them with to prevent and stop cyberbullying. Participants were presented with a hypothetical scenario in which their peer was subjected to cyberbullying. Findings also indicate that children value their autonomy and peer relations, which may influence their perception of cooperative efforts.

TI How Should Learners be Socially Embedded in Virtual Learning
   Simulations? Effects on Problem-Solving Performance, Perceived
   Authenticity, Enjoyment, and Social Presence
SO TECHNOLOGY KNOWLEDGE AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Social embedding; Social interaction; Virtual learning simulation;
   Authenticity; Enjoyment; Social presence
ID TEACHER PERCEPTIONS; IMMERSION; STUDENT; REALITY
AB Virtual learning simulations (VLS) are increasingly employed in education for their potential to replicate real-world environments and support authentic, action-oriented learning. Given that learning is fundamentally socially constructed, an important question concerns how varying degrees of social embedding within VLS, particularly through the inclusion of artificial players, affect learning outcomes. This study investigates how varying degrees of social embedding within VLS affect problem-solving performance and learners' perceptions of authenticity, enjoyment, and social presence. A problem-solving task was adapted into four variants, each representing a distinct level of social embedding, based on a predefined taxonomy. In a randomized controlled experiment, 296 postsecondary learners from academic and vocational education tracks were randomly assigned to one of the four variants. To examine the effects of social embedding, a one-way MANOVA was conducted, followed by ANOVAs with planned contrasts. In addition, learners evaluated all four variants based on their preferences. Higher levels of social embedding significantly increased perceived authenticity, enjoyment, and social presence, whereas no significant effects were observed for problem-solving performance. Notably, while learners viewed social embedding as essential for enhancing authenticity, enjoyment, and social presence, a subset preferred individual work in socially enriched yet non-collaborative environments. The findings emphasize the importance of designing socially enriched VLS to enhance learner experience and engagement. While problem-solving performance may remain unaffected, the results highlight the pedagogical value of social embedding for fostering affective learning outcomes. These insights offer practical implications for educators aiming to design more engaging simulation-based environments.

AB This study examined the relationship between intelligent-technological pedagogical and content knowledge (I-TPACK) skills and artificial intelligence literacy (AIL) among pre-service primary school teachers, focusing on the mediating role of general attitudes towards artificial intelligence (GAAI). TI Rate-disabled versus accuracy-disabled subtypes of dyslexia: A
   longitudinal study from preschool to grade 1
SO ANNALS OF DYSLEXIA
LA English
DT Article
DE Dyslexia; Subtypes; RAN; Phonological awareness; Morphological
   awareness; Reading accuracy; Reading rate
ID READING-DISABILITY DYSLEXIA; AUTOMATIZED NAMING RAN; DEVELOPMENTAL
   DYSLEXIA; DUAL-ROUTE; ACQUISITION; FLUENCY; INTERVENTION; PERFORMANCE;
   CHILDREN; INSIGHTS
AB This longitudinal study investigated subtypes of dyslexia based on the distinction between word reading accuracy and word reading rate. Building on prior cross-sectional research, we inquired whether the cognitive profiles of these subtypes can be identified before children learn to read. A large sample of Hebrew-speaking children were assessed on phonological awareness (PA), morphological awareness (MA), and rapid automatized naming (RAN) in preschool and then followed into first grade to evaluate their reading accuracy and rate. In preschool, findings revealed two distinct subgroups: one with selective deficits in PA and MA but intact RAN (PA + MA-disabled) and another with impaired RAN but preserved PA and MA (RAN-only disabled). In first grade, as predicted, the PA + MA-disabled group demonstrated significantly lower reading accuracy compared to both the RAN-only disabled and control groups. The RAN-only subgroup exhibited slow reading but intact accuracy. However, contrary to predictions, the PA + MA-disabled group also exhibited slower reading rates. These results suggest that at the beginning of reading development, low levels of reading accuracy limit reading rate. Our study (i) supports accuracy-rate subtyping of dyslexia, (ii) reinforces the role of both PA and MA in achieving early word reading accuracy, and (iii) highlights the existence of a highly specific RAN-rate dyslexia subtype. These findings have significant implications for early diagnosis and intervention as well as the definition of dyslexia.

TI Virtual Simulation of Intelligent Production Lines Using Unity3D:
   Development and Educational Evaluation
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE engineering education; flexible production control; intelligent
   production lines, manufacturing systems learning; virtual simulation
ID CONFIGURATION
AB As intelligent manufacturing systems become increasingly complex, effective instructional tools are critical to support learners' understanding of intelligent production and operational control concepts. This study presents an educational virtual simulation system for teaching the operation and control of intelligent production lines. Developed around real industrial workflows, the system provides an interactive three-dimensional learning environment that facilitates comprehension of production line structure, process planning, workflow design, and motion control. TI Metric Thinking: Contributions to Its Characterization from a Multilevel
   Perspective
SO TRENDS IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE mathematics education; metric thinking; measurement; mathematical
   thinking; problem solving; design-based research
AB This article develops a local theory for characterizing metric thinking in the measurement of spatial properties from a multilevel curricular perspective, understood as an analytic lens for scaling measurement processes across curricular complexity rather than as empirical evidence from all educational levels. The study adopts a qualitative, explanatory approach and articulates grounded theory with educational design research. The methodological process was organized into four broad moments, operationalized in five phases: an initial literature-based characterization; the design of learning activities involving length, area, volume, center of mass, and angular measure; implementation with engineering students enrolled in integral calculus; analysis of projected and emergent abilities through grounded performance levels; and refinement of the characterization. The findings propose a robust characterization of metric thinking composed of five cognitive processes: perceiving, recognizing, and distinguishing measurable properties; selecting, using comprehensively, and refining measurement instruments; formulating, operationalizing, and optimizing measurement strategies; applying measurement; and developing a critical perspective on measurement. These processes are interpreted as cyclic and mutually connected rather than hierarchical or linear. Within the university engineering tasks analyzed, they also show how measurement can mediate connections between advanced mathematical domains and STEM-related problem contexts. The article concludes by offering a definition of metric thinking that may guide research, curriculum design, and instruction while requiring further validation beyond the university context examined in this study.

TI Artificial intelligence literacy, rather than artificial intelligence
   anxiety, is associated with career optimism in physiotherapy and
   rehabilitation students: a cross-sectional study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence literacy; artificial intelligence anxiety;
   career optimism; physiotherapy and rehabilitation students; health
   professions education
AB Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping health professions education, but its relationship with students' future career outlook remains insufficiently understood, particularly in professions where human interaction remains central to practice. This study examined whether career optimism in physiotherapy and rehabilitation students was more closely associated with AI literacy than with AI anxiety. Methods This cross-sectional study included 438 undergraduate physiotherapy and rehabilitation students from universities in Ankara and Konya, T & uuml;rkiye. Data were collected online between 27 February 2026 and 10 March 2026 using Turkish versions of the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, and the Career Optimism subscale of the Career Futures Inventory. Pearson correlations, subgroup comparisons, and hierarchical multiple linear regression analyses were performed. HC3 robust standard errors were used in sensitivity analyses. Results AI literacy was positively associated with career optimism (r = 0.396, p < 0.001), whereas AI anxiety showed a weaker negative association (r = - 0.147, p = 0.002). In hierarchical regression analyses, AI literacy was the only variable independently associated with career optimism in both the crude model (B = 0.281, beta = 0.384, p < 0.001) and the adjusted model controlling for age, gender, class year, grade point average, formal AI-related training, and weekly AI use frequency (B = 0.284, beta = 0.388, p < 0.001). AI anxiety was not independently associated with career optimism in either model. Sensitivity analyses using HC3 robust standard errors supported these findings. Conclusions Among physiotherapy and rehabilitation students, career optimism was more strongly associated with AI literacy than with AI anxiety. Even in a strongly human-centered health profession, students' career-related expectations appear to be linked more closely to perceived AI-related competence than to AI-related anxiety. Educational strategies may therefore benefit from supporting AI literacy as part of future professional readiness. Trial registration Not applicable.

TI Development and evaluation of a digital simulation tool for teaching
   gynecological cytology: a pilot study with nursing students
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital simulation; Nursing education; Gynecological cytology;
   Educational technology; Emotional engagement; Student perceptions
AB Background Training in gynecological cytology within nursing education presents challenges, including limited opportunities for practical experience and a lack of empirically evaluated educational tools. Digital simulation may offer a structured and safe approach to support learning, learner engagement, and practical preparation. This study aimed to develop and evaluate PapSim, a digital simulation tool for teaching gynecological cytology to nursing students. Methods A pilot educational study was conducted with 40 second-year nursing students following a theoretical session on gynecological cytology. Participants engaged with the PapSim prototype in a supervised laboratory setting. Emotional engagement was assessed using a structured questionnaire based on the Pleasure Framework. Participants rated each emotional dimension on a six-point (0-5) ordinal response scale. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively and through Spearman's rank correlation analysis. Qualitative responses were examined using thematic content analysis. Results: Higher mean scores were observed in the categories of Simulation (4.63), Discovery (4.60), and Exploration (4.48), indicating strong engagement with immersive and task-oriented dimensions. Lower scores were reported in Danger (0.78) and Subversion (1.23), reflecting perceptions of safety and appropriateness. Significant positive correlations were identified between Discovery and Competition (rho = 0.69, p < 0.001), as well as between sensory and empathic dimensions. Qualitative findings reinforced participants' perceptions of realism, cognitive stimulation, and spontaneous peer interaction during the simulation. Conclusions The PapSim prototype was positively perceived and well accepted by nursing students, supporting its use as a complementary educational tool for teaching gynecological cytology. Further studies involving larger and more diverse samples are warranted to evaluate educational outcomes.

TI Evaluation of structured training in osteotomy and splitting for BSSO
   using a 3D-printed mandibular model
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE 3D-printing; Medical education; Orthognathic surgery; Bilateral sagittal
   split osteotomy
ID 3-DIMENSIONAL PRINTED MODELS; MEDICAL-EDUCATION; ORTHOGNATHIC SURGERY;
   SIMULATION; SKILLS
AB Background The teaching of bilateral sagittal split osteotomy (BSSO) requires the utilisation of practical training methods to optimise the surgical result and prevent complications such as bad splits or damage to the inferior alveolar nerve. The objective of the present study was to evaluate a structured training program using a cost-effective, 3D-printed mandibular model to improve osteotomy and splitting performance in BSSO. Material & methods The study was registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00034369, registration date: 20/11/2024). A lower jaw model was fabricated using a semi-professional Prusa XL Multi-Tool 3D printer and a combination of colours and materials. The model also incorporated the inferior alveolar nerve, which was fabricated from a flexible material. The model was modified to facilitate its dynamic integration into a phantom head by modification of the condyles. Twenty participants performed two repetitions of the osteotomy and splitting steps of BSSO. The participants received feedback after the first run and during the second run. The experiments were recorded and assessed using a validated questionnaire (OSATS). Furthermore, the distance between the inferior alveolar nerve and the fracture surface, as well as the number of bad splits, was determined. Results Participants significantly improved their surgical skills as measured by the OSATS between the first and second run from 23.7 points +/- 4.3 (mean +/- sd) to 27.2 points +/- 3.9 (p < 0.001). In addition, the minimal distance between the nerve and the fracture surface increased from 0.2 +/- 0.38 mm to 1.12 +/- 1.04 mm (p = 0.012). The number of bad splits decreased from 15 to 4 (p = 0.044). The estimated material cost of the lower jaw is approximately US$4 with a printing time of an estimated 9.5 h. Conclusion It is possible to develop a cost-effective and realistic training model, that can be used within structured repeated practice sessions for BSSO training and is associated with improved performance in this setting. Further studies are needed to validate the simulator and assess its impact on real-life surgical outcomes.

TI Supporting Feedback, Not Replacing It: University Supervisors'
   Perceptions of Generative AI in Preservice Teacher Field Experiences
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE GenAI; artificial intelligence; feedback; higher education; preservice
   teachers; university supervisors; field experience; teaching
   competencies; teaching; observations
ID FOCUS
AB Artificial intelligence is increasingly shaping educational practices; however, its use by university supervisors (USs) to provide feedback to preservice teachers (PSTs) during field experiences remains underexplored. This collaborative action research study examined USs' perceptions of implementing a generative AI (GenAI)-supported feedback protocol during classroom observations. Supervisors used a researcher-developed protocol in which observational notes, lesson objectives, and teaching competencies were input into ChatGPT to generate draft feedback for post-observation conferences. Data sources included annotated protocol documents, individual interviews, and a focus group, supplemented by existing PST interview data. Inductive thematic analysis indicated that GenAI supported alignment with teaching competencies and enhanced the structure and specificity of feedback. At the same time, findings highlighted important limitations, as AI-assisted feedback required careful human interpretation to ensure contextual accuracy and relevance. Supervisors noted that, while GenAI provided objective-aligned instructional guidance, it did not fully capture the complexity of classroom interactions. These findings suggest that GenAI functions as a support tool rather than an autonomous feedback mechanism, underscoring the importance of human judgment in AI-assisted supervisory feedback within teacher education.

TI Middle School Girls' Attitudes and Engagement in Generative AI
   Cybersecurity Summer Camp
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative artificial intelligence; cybersecurity education; informal
   learning; STEM teaching and learning
ID LEARNING-ENVIRONMENT; SELF-EFFICACY; STUDENTS
AB Informal science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) learning settings can provide early and accessible opportunities for students who have been historically underrepresented in computing to engage with cybersecurity concepts and emerging technologies. This one-group pretest-posttest mixed-methods study examined a week-long, GenAI-integrated informal cybersecurity summer camp for 33 underrepresented and underserved racial and ethnic minority (UUREM) middle school girls. The study investigated pre-post patterns in perceived cybersecurity knowledge, domain-specific self-efficacy, interest, utility value, career aspirations, and selected AI-literacy practices. These findings suggest that informal GenAI-integrated cybersecurity programs may support selected aspects of perceived learning and cybersecurity self-efficacy, while highlighting the need for more rigorous designs, validated AI-literacy measures, and longer-term follow-up.

TI Equity and leadership: examining how socio-economic diversity shapes
   leadership potential in scholarship applicants
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE equity in education; leadership potential; refugee students; scholarship
   programs; socio-economic vulnerability; Sub-Saharan Africa
ID RESILIENCE; ACCESS
AB Higher education participation in Sub-Saharan Africa remains low due to limited transitions from secondary school, driven by financial constraints, socio-economic inequality, gender disparities, and conflict-related displacement. Scholarship programs increasingly target disadvantaged students with leadership potential, yet evidence on the relationship between socio-economic vulnerability and leadership capability remains limited. This study examined relationships between socio-economic vulnerability and leadership potential among 672 final applicants from a pool of 6,407 applicants to a higher education scholarship program implemented across 12 African universities. Composite vulnerability indices and four leadership domains were used in the analysis. Results revealed that vulnerability was not associated with leadership potential across any domain. Refugees and Displaced Persons reported significantly greater vulnerability yet scored higher on transformational leadership and entrepreneurship capacities. No systematic gender or disability differences were found, though the representation of persons with disabilities dropped sharply from undergraduate (21.0%) to postgraduate (7.3%) levels. The findings demonstrate that leadership-related capabilities are may be distributed independently of socio-economic background, while refugee status may paradoxically be associated with distinctive leadership capabilities. Scholarship selection models could prioritize equity-driven approaches that recognize diverse pathways to leadership development, alongside targeted support addressing the structural barriers that constrain educational progression for persons with disabilities in school.

TI Negotiated technological consciousness: a process model of technological
   literacy transfer in technology teacher communities
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE digital learning; education for sustainable development; global
   citizenship; negotiated technological consciousness; teacher
   qualification; technological literacy; technology teacher communities;
   technology-enhanced learning
ID DIGITAL LITERACY; EDUCATION; PEDAGOGY
AB Introduction This study examines technological literacy transfer within technology teacher communities in Thailand, arguing that technological literacy should be understood not merely as technical competence, but as a socially mediated and pedagogically negotiated process shaped by structural conditions, teacher agency, and critical reflection. Methods A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was employed. Phase 1 used constructivist grounded theory to explore how teachers negotiated technological literacy practices within educational contexts. Data were collected through semi-structured in-depth interviews and classroom observations with 21 purposively selected technology teachers, while Phase 2 applied structural equation modeling (SEM) to validate the relationships among the identified constructs using data collected from 246 teachers across multiple educational sectors in Thailand. Results The findings indicate that technological literacy transfer emerged through the interaction between structural conditions, teacher identity, pedagogical processes, and collaborative practices within technology teacher communities. The structural equation model demonstrated acceptable fit with the empirical data (chi(2)/df = 1.53, RMSEA = .047, CFI = 1.00). Professional learning networks significantly influenced teacher identity (beta = .81, p < .01) and the technological literacy transfer process (beta = .34, p < .01). The study developed the "Negotiated Technological Consciousness" model, which explains how teachers and learners critically interpret and reconstruct the social, ethical, and political dimensions embedded within technological systems. Discussion The findings suggest that technology teacher communities function as collaborative and reflective spaces that support critical pedagogical practices and negotiated forms of technological literacy. The dominant path coefficient (PLN -> TID, beta = .81) constitutes a major policy finding: a teacher's critical orientation toward technology is shaped far more by organic peer communities than by top-down mandates, implying that governments must prioritize funding professional learning networks over static certification programs. Technological literacy is therefore better understood as a dynamic process of meaning-making and critical engagement rather than the transmission of technical skills alone.

TI A competence-oriented framework for music teacher education: conceptual
   model and empirical validation of students' perceived self-efficacy
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE competence-oriented approach; higher education; methodological
   foundations; music teacher education; professional competence
AB Introduction: The transition to a competency-based approach in higher education requires theoretically grounded and empirically tested models, but this process in music pedagogy remains fragmented. To address this gap, this study aimed to theoretically substantiate the methodological foundations of competence-oriented teaching in music pedagogy, and to develop and empirically validate a conceptual model of perceived professional competence formation in future music teachers. Methods: A quantitative quasi-experimental design was employed with 194 participating students (N = 194), divided into an experimental group (n = 98) and a control group (n = 96). The experimental intervention combined project methods, master classes, ensemble interaction, digital tools, and reflexive practices. Assessment was conducted across a five-component model (cognitive, activity-based, interpretive, value-based, and reflexive components) using a validated instrument (S-CVI = 0.94; Cronbach's = 0.88). Following the intervention, a statistically significant increase in self-assessment indicators (p < 0.001) was recorded in the experimental group, particularly within the activity-based, interpretive, and reflexive components. Discussion: The study supports the effectiveness of the integrated architectonic system in developing students' perceived professional readiness. These findings suggest that the proposed conceptual model offers robust, practical solutions for the modernization of curricula and the advancement of competence-oriented training in contemporary music education.

TI A custom-configured large language model for Arabic academic feedback: a
   case study within the SSDEC curriculum
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE AI assessment; Arabic; feedback; LLM; social studies
AB Despite the increasing adoption of large language models (LLMs) in higher education, empirical evaluation of their suitability for Arabic academic feedback remains limited. This study presents a case-based feasibility evaluation of a custom-configured Arabic LLM designed to generate rubric-aligned academic feedback for the course Emirates Studies (EMS100) within the Safety, Security, Defense, Emergency Preparedness, and Crisis Management (SSDEC) curriculum, an interdisciplinary framework integrating civic education, digital literacy, and ethical reasoning. Design, AI-generated feedback was systematically compared with instructor-generated feedback across six anonymized student submissions within this instructional context. Descriptive concordance analysis was employed to examine rubric-level alignment between AI and instructor evaluations, supported by qualitative thematic analysis of feedback content. The analysis focused on identifying patterns of alignment and divergence within a structured, rubric-constrained environment rather than establishing formal statistical reliability. Results indicated substantial rubric-level alignment, with the majority of comparisons classified as exact or close matches. The AI system demonstrated strong performance in procedural and rule-governed domains, including APA compliance, structural organization, citation accuracy, and adherence to assignment requirements. Lower alignment was observed in interpretive and culturally contextual domains, particularly in leadership analysis and heritage-related interpretation. Qualitative findings showed that instructors engaged with AI-generated feedback as an assistive resource, selectively refining and contextualizing outputs rather than adopting them uncritically. These findings support a hybrid model of academic feedback in which AI systems enhance efficiency and consistency in procedural evaluation while instructors retain responsibility for interpretive and pedagogical judgment. This case-based study contributes to the emerging literature on Arabic-language AI applications in higher education by demonstrating that rubric-constrained LLMs can generate pedagogically meaningful feedback within structured institutional contexts. The findings provide a foundation for future research on large-scale validation, reliability, and the pedagogical impact of AI-assisted feedback in Arabic academic environments.

TI Metacognitive awareness, epistemological beliefs, and mathematical
   resilience as predictors of perceived mathematical problem-solving
   ability among Ghanaian university mathematics education students: the
   mediating role of student engagement
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE epistemological beliefs; mathematical resilience; metacognitive
   awareness; perceived mathematical problem-solving ability; student
   engagement
AB The purpose of this study is to examine the structural relationships between metacognitive awareness, epistemological beliefs, mathematical resilience, student engagement, and perceived mathematical problem-solving ability among university students. A cross-sectional research design survey was used to examine the research objectives. A total of 350 participants from a population of 2,950 undergraduate students, selected using the Krejcie and Morgan table, were included in the analysis. Exploratory factor analysis with reliability analysis in SPSS software version 27 and hypothesis testing in AMOS software version 23 were used for the analysis. The results indicate that epistemological beliefs, metacognitive awareness, and mathematical resilience are indirectly associated with perceived mathematical problem-solving ability through student engagement. The results indicate that student engagement plays a critical role in mediating the relationship between internal learner characteristics and perceived mathematical problem-solving ability. Practical implications: Mathematics educators should design instructional strategies that strengthen students' metacognitive awareness, epistemological beliefs, and mathematical resilience while creating learning environments that promote active student engagement. Such approaches may help improve students' perceived mathematical problem-solving ability. Teachers can design the learning environment to promote student engagement to improve the students' perceived mathematical problem-solving ability. Although previous studies have examined metacognitive awareness, epistemological beliefs, and mathematical resilience separately or in different combinations, little is known about how these constructs jointly relate to perceived mathematical problem-solving ability through student engagement within a single structural model. To the best of our knowledge, no previous study has simultaneously examined these relationships among university mathematics students in the Ghanaian context.

TI Advising Through the Noise: Medical Student Advisor Perspectives on How
   Preference Signals Have Influenced Surgical Residency Recruitment
SO JOURNAL OF SURGICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE general surgery; medical student advising; preference signaling;
   residency recruitment
ID SURGERY
AB OBJECTIVE: The implementation of preference signals in the general surgery match added another layer of complexity to an already intricate system, challenging medical student advisors in effectively guiding their students. This study aimed to explore advisors' experiences counseling applicants about signaling to inform improvements to the signaling process and improve applicant advising. DESIGN: Qualitative analysis of de-identified transcripts from semi-structured interviews of medical student advisors was performed. SETTING: All interviews were conducted using a video conferencing platform. PARTICIPANTS: Eleven formal medical student advisors to general surgery applicants in the 2024 to 2025 application cycle were interviewed. Participants (55% male) included deans (n = 4), clerkship directors (n = 4), and program directors (n = 3) from across the US. RESULTS: Overall, advisors perceived signaling positively, believing that signaling improved applicant equity by decreasing interview hoarding and prestige bias. Advisors recounted common applicant mistakes, including applicants only signaling reach programs, signaling based on prestige instead of "fit," and misjudging their competitiveness for a program. Advisors felt that applicants should focus on signaling programs they are both interested in and competitive for, which requires an individualized strategy based on a balance of professional goals, geographic preferences, and program fit. Advisors noted several challenges they faced, including a lack of transparency regarding how programs use signals, uncertainty in advising students without clear data, and difficulty judging an applicant's competitiveness. CONCLUSIONS: While advisors generally acknowledged the positive influence of signals on residency recruitment, the lack of information about the purpose and use of signals limited their ability to provide actionable advice to their students. To effectively guide their students, advisors seek clear communication and evidence-based guidance from national organizations regarding both how signals are supposed to be used by applicants and how signals are used by programs. AB Objective: To measure the impact of a skills-based laboratory simulation on students' self-assessed skills and confidence in using best practices for communication through a medical interpreter. Methods: This retrospective, single-institution study was conducted at the Ohio State University College of Pharmacy. Subjects included third-year Doctor of Pharmacy students enrolled in a skills-based laboratory course from 2022 to 2024. Students received a recorded lecture on best practices for using medical interpretation services, followed by a presurvey. Students then completed a simulated encounter involving a standardized patient with limited English proficiency and a live simulated interpreter. After the simulation, the volunteer interpreter and standardized patient completed an evaluation of the students' performance, and the students completed a postsurvey in which they self-assessed their knowledge and performance of best practices on a 4point Likert scale and their level of confidence in doing so on a 3-point Likert scale. Facilitator evaluations of student performance were compared with the students' self-assessed competence to assess agreement and differences in perceived performance, and the variance was analyzed. Descriptive and inferential statistics were performed to describe the change in self-assessed skills before and after the live simulation. Results: A total of 353 students in their third professional year across 3 graduating classes completed the simulation. Across all 3 classes, there were statistically significant improvements in self-assessed competency and in self-assessed confidence in using best practices for interpreter use after the simulation. Conclusion: Simulated patient encounters that incorporate a live interpreter increase students' self-assessed confidence and competence in the appropriate use of language interpreters during patient care.

TI Measuring task-level behavioral learning engagement during text revision
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Process measures; Learning engagement; Validity; Technology-enhanced
   learning
ID STUDENT ENGAGEMENT; ACHIEVEMENT; FEEDBACK; TAXONOMY; SCIENCE
AB Learning engagement (LE) is a crucial mechanism of successful learning. Log data from technology-enhanced learning environments offer numerous opportunities to assess learner behavior unobtrusively, reflecting learning processes, and thereby to understand why learning opportunities work. In the context of constructed response, keystroke logging can be used to obtain process measures that reflect task-level behavior, which could serve as potential indicators of behavioral LE during tasks that require learners to submit written text. However, before measures derived from keystroke logging data can be interpreted in terms of their assessment of LE, it is necessary to validate them. This study aimed to validate two process measures (i.e., the number of keystrokes and the typing time) that have already been used in previous research as potential indicators of behavioral LE during revision, based on a sample of N = 472 English-as-aforeign-language (EFL) learners. In line with expectations, the process measures were positively correlated with the three dimensions of LE (i.e., behavioral, cognitive, and emotional) as assessed with self-reports, whereby the correlations with behavioral LE were the strongest, supporting the construct validity of the process measures as indicators of behavioral LE. The power of the process measures in predicting revision performance was in support of their criterion validity. Contrary to expectations, there were inconsistent effects of an experimental manipulation (i.e., feedback) to increase behavioral LE on the process measures and self-reported LE, limiting the interpretability of the findings. The manipulation had a positive effect on process measures and self-reported cognitive LE, but no significant effect on self-reported behavioral LE. The findings contribute to future research that aims to investigate task-level LE in contexts where learners produce written text. The inconsistent effects on the different measures are discussed.

TI Mapping teacher education strategies to develop digital competence
   targets: A cross-framework analysis
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Digital competencies; Pre-service teachers; Teacher education; Digital
   pedagogy; Curriculum design; DigCompEdu; Network analysis
ID PRESERVICE TEACHERS; TECHNOLOGY; KNOWLEDGE
AB Rapid technological developments are reshaping expectations regarding teachers' digital competence targets, challenging teacher education programmes to design learning experiences that systematically support its development. This study examines how digital competence targets and teacher education strategies intersect within authentic teacher education practices. Drawing on the European DigCompEdu Framework and the second Synthesis of Qualitative Data (SQD2) model, the study analyses 33 documented teacher education practices implemented across five universities. Using quantitative content analysis combined with co-occurrence and network analysis, the study maps (1) the digital competence targets addressed, (2) the SQD2 strategies enacted, and (3) the patterns of association between digital competence targets and teacher education strategies. The findings further underscore the importance of curriculum coherence and pedagogical orchestration in supporting the development of pre-service teachers' digital competence targets.

TI Coordination of a team-taught pharmacy course: Reflection on a
   coordinator's task diary
SO CURRENTS IN PHARMACY TEACHING AND LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Reflective practice; Self-reflection; Course coordination; Team-taught;
   Task analysis
AB Purpose: There is little detailed information available in the literature about the day-to-day workload associated with pharmacy course coordination. A task diary kept by a clinical faculty member coordinating a required pharmacy course was therefore analyzed using the What? So What? and Now What? reflective model. Description: This course coordinator diary for a one-semester team-taught pharmacotherapy course at a public university spanned 425 days. The diary recorded 3063 tasks, of which the most common type of task was email, which constituted 61.5% of tasks. Other common task types were document creation and meetings. The most common task purpose was management of student absences. Other common task purposes included management of the electronic assessment platform, management of the electronic learning platform, and supervision of teaching assistants. Only forty tasks (1.3%) required doctoral-level training. Analysis/interpretation: The large number of tasks may have ramifications for pharmacy faculty in terms of distraction from duties such as scholarship, service and patient care. The volume and administrative nature of tasks also have implications for faculty job satisfaction and burnout. For the institution and for students there are direct costs to fund doctoral-level coordinators as well as opportunity costs regarding faculty productivity and morale and availability of faculty to share doctoral-level knowledge with students. Conclusions/implications: There may be opportunities to assign administrative coordinators to reduce the direct and opportunity costs identified in the reflection. Non-doctoral staff with skills in administration and educational theory may be well-suited to optimizing efficiencies across multiple courses and offering student guidance.

TI Asthma management in schools: A tool for reducing absenteeism?
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE School health programs; Asthma; Absenteeism
AB Asthma is a leading chronic condition among school-aged children and a major driver of absenteeism. Since attendance is linked to academic success, graduation, and earnings, interventions reducing asthma-related absences may improve educational trajectories. We evaluate a program that placed asthma case managers in New York City public schools to engage directly with students and families. Using novel linked health-education data and a triple-differences design exploiting staggered rollout and asthma targeting, we find significant gains in school-based asthma management: absenteeism among children with asthma fell by 5%, narrowing the asthma/ no-asthma gap by 20%, and active asthma prescriptions rose by nearly 10%. These results show that schoolembedded supports can improve children's health while also boosting educational outcomes.

TI Closer in sound, better in learning: linguistic similarity and early
   literacy in Cameroon
SO ECONOMICS OF EDUCATION REVIEW
LA English
DT Article
DE Mother tongue; Language of instruction; Phonetic similarity; Listening
   comprehension skills; Cameroon
ID COGNITIVE SKILLS; LANGUAGE; EDUCATION; OUTCOMES; ORIGINS
AB This paper examines how linguistic similarity between students' mother tongue (L1) and the language of instruction (LOI) affects early literacy skills in Cameroon, a multilingual country with over 270 living languages. Using data from the 2019 Early Grade Reading Assessment (EGRA) and lexicostatistical methods, I construct two continuous measures of phonetic similarity between 15 major local languages and the two official LOIs, French and English. Identification relies on a two-stage least squares strategy that exploits geographic variation in longrun linguistic diffusion. The results show that students whose L1 is phonetically closer to the LOI perform better in listening comprehension, partly offsetting the learning loss associated with linguistic mismatch. The effects are larger within the Francophone education subsystem, in rural areas, among students who receive parental support with homework, and among younger learners, with estimates declining with age. A complementary provincial analysis shows that the predicted gap between low- and high-similarity scenarios varies across provinces and is larger in several low-performing areas. These findings underscore the importance of linguistic alignment in language-in-education policy for improving early learning and promoting equity in multilingual settings.

TI Paths to dropout: Barriers to school continuation for girls in rural
   Malawi
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL DEVELOPMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Girls' education; School dropout; Secondary education; Longitudinal
   mixed methods; Malawi; Adolescent pregnancy
ID LIFE-COURSE; EDUCATION; ENROLLMENT; OUTCOMES
AB Rural Malawi has achieved near-universal primary enrollment under free education, yet few girls complete primary school or transition to secondary. This study investigates why, drawing on a four-year longitudinal panel (2018-2021) of 1823 students in Standards 5-8 across two rural districts, combined with qualitative data from focus groups and interviews. Quantitative analysis reveals stark gender disparities: by endline, nearly half of girls had dropped out compared to one-third of boys. These mixed-methods findings highlight multiple, gendered pathways to dropout and identify key points of intervention. Reducing grade repetition, building more secondary schools in underserved areas, and strengthening re-entry and support for adolescent mothers are critical to helping more girls in rural Malawi stay in school and realize their educational goals. By integrating longitudinal and qualitative data across the primary-secondary transition, this study offers new insight into the timing and compounding nature of dropout risks for adolescent girls in low-resource settings.

AB Objective: To describe and compare how undergraduate general practice (GP) is taught across medical school programmes in selected high-income countries, to inform curriculum redesign at the University of Auckland, New Zealand. Methods: International observational cross sectional comparative study. Study participants were academic leads responsible for undergraduate general practice curricula in medical schools in Australia, England, Ireland, Canada, Norway, Iceland. Forty-four medical schools. The findings demonstrate multiple approaches to embedding general practice beyond traditional block placements. Medical schools facing placement constraints may consider earlier GP engagement, increased GP led campus teaching, and selective use of simulation or digital learning. Further studies should examine educational and workforce outcomes.

Participants were 651 children and their parents. Latent growth mixture modeling identified four trajectories for each emotion type. Positive emotions: High-Level Increasing (8.1%), High-Level Slightly Increasing (28.5%), Moderate-Level Slightly Decreasing (50.7%), Moderate-Level Decreasing (12.7%). Negative emotions: Moderate-Level Highly Increasing (6.7%), Moderate-Level Increasing (25%), Low-Level Stable (36.3%), Low-Level Decreasing (32%). Repeated-measures ANOVA showed task persistence increased when parental positive emotions increased, while academic performance declined in the Moderate-Level Decreasing trajectory. Negative emotion trajectories showed no significant effects. Findings highlight the importance of sustaining parental positive emotions during homework help for children's motivation and achievement. Educational relevance statement: Supporting children with homework is one of the most common ways parents become involved once their children enter primary school. During this process, parents experience a range of emotions that not only can differ between families but also can change over time. The present study confirms that parents' experiences of positive and negative emotions while helping with homework evolve as children progress through primary school. Results showed that 36.6% of parents followed trajectories of increasing positive emotions, while 63.4% reported a decrease over time. For negative emotions, approximately one third of parents (31.7%) experienced an increase, one third (36.3%) remained stable, and one third (32%) reported a decrease across the primary school years. Importantly, these emotional trajectories were differentially related to children's learning. Children demonstrated greater task persistence when their parents experienced increasing positive emotions. In contrast, a decline in academic performance was observed among children whose parents began with moderate levels of positive emotions that subsequently decreased. Notably, trajectories of parents' negative emotions were not associated with children's learning outcomes. These findings highlight the importance of understanding parents' emotional trajectories in homework situations. Monitoring and supporting positive emotions-particularly joy and satisfaction-throughout primary school may help create a more supportive homework environment and strengthen children's learning.

TI Professional vision and medical education: dividing diagnoses into
   categories to support more effective learning in dermatology
SO LEARNING AND INSTRUCTION
LA English
DT Article
DE Perceptual learning; Professional vision; Medical education; Dermatology
ID EXPERTISE; STUDENTS
AB Background: Proficiency in interpretation of visual findings, professional vision, plays an essential role in the doctor's profession. Thus, learning visual features from images is a key curricular component of medical education, for example, in radiology and dermatology. Nevertheless, there is scarcity of research on professional vision in dermatology. Aims: The aims of this study were to 1) measure how professional vision differs before and after a dermatology course, and if there are differences across diagnoses, 2) cluster different diagnoses based on learning patterns, 3) investigate the development of students' accuracy, decision times and confidence within different categories. Sample: Participants were 394 medical students and 7 experts. Methods: Participants completed an online perceptual learning module at three timepoints (pre, mid and post) during a course. Results: Diagnostic accuracy, decision times and confidence improved in most, but not all, pre-mid and mid-post comparisons. There were major differences in learning patterns (amount and pace of improvement) across the eight categories. Conclusions: The differences between diagnosis categories were larger than differences between individual participants. This finding can be utilized in medical education by focusing teaching resources on diagnoses that are difficult to learn.

TI The complementary effects of virtual reality and traditional simulation
   in nursing education: A qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing education; Virtual reality; Scenario-based simulation;
   Experiential learning; Simulation training
AB Background: Simulation-based education plays a pivotal role in bridging the gap between nursing theory and clinical practice. Although traditional scenario-based simulation is effective in enhancing clinical skills, it is often limited by its lack of situational fidelity. Conversely, virtual reality (VR) simulation provides highly immersive learning environments but is challenged by its inability to support genuine interpersonal interactions. There is a paucity of empirical evidence regarding the integration of the complementary strengths of these two modalities and the understanding of nursing students' authentic learning experiences within an integrated model. Objective: Guided by Kolb's experiential learning theory, this study aimed to explore undergraduate nursing students' learning experiences within a dual-track simulation teaching model integrating VR simulation, traditional scenario-based simulation, and guided feedback. The objectives were to identify the perceived strengths and limitations of each modality and to generate evidence-based insights for optimizing simulation teaching design. Methods: Guided by Kolb's experiential learning theory, this study explored undergraduate nursing students' learning experiences within a dual-track simulation teaching model integrating VR simulation, traditional scenario-based simulation, and guided feedback. Specifically, the study aimed to identify students' perceived strengths and limitations of each modality and to generate evidence-based insights for optimizing simulation teaching design. Results: Four primary themes were identified: (1) The dual dimensions of role immersion, encompassing environmental and interpersonal immersion. VR facilitated environmental immersion through its audiovisual effects, although technical issues occasionally detracted from the experience. In contrast, scenario simulation promoted relational immersion via authentic interpersonal interactions, thereby enhancing role identity, albeit limited by the acting abilities of peers. (2) The complementary construction of nursing competence, characterized by cognitive framing and dynamic adaptation. VR was particularly effective in developing systemic cognitive frameworks and rehearsing high-risk scenarios, while scenario simulation was indispensable for nurturing clinical operational skills, dynamic decision-making, and humanistic care. (3) The dual pathways of emotional experience, involving low-anxiety learning and empathy-driven reflection. VR offered a low-anxiety environment but provided mechanical emotional feedback, whereas scenario simulation elicited genuine emotional resonance and moderate anxiety, which in turn facilitated profound reflection. (4) Integrated Teaching Pathway: From Cognitive Rehearsal to Practice Internalization. Students appreciated an integrated teaching pathway that advanced from VR rehearsal to scenario simulation practice accompanied by guided feedback, thereby establishing a comprehensive experiential learning cycle. Conclusion: The dual-track simulation teaching model, which leverages the synergistic effects of virtual reality and scenario-based simulation, provides nursing students with a holistic learning experience encompassing both cognitive development and practical application. It is recommended that nursing educators strategically Today incorporate these pedagogical methods, utilizing the cognitive rehearsal benefits of virtual reality while maintaining the distinct advantages of scenario-based simulation for skill acquisition and the cultivation of humanistic qualities.
   This integrative approach has the potential to produce nursing professionals who exhibit both clinical proficiency and humanistic awareness.

TI Short memory-training can improve inhibition functions in children with
   autism spectrum disorder: Preliminary evidences using an eye-tracker
SO RESEARCH IN AUTISM
LA English
DT Article
DE Memory training; Children; ASD; Memory-guided saccades; Inhibition
   functions
ID EXECUTIVE FUNCTION; ATTENTION; INDIVIDUALS; MATURATION; REFLEXIVE;
   CHILDHOOD; MOVEMENTS; SACCADES; DEFICITS
AB Background: Children with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) often exhibit atypical oculomotor behavior and deficits in executive functioning, particularly in tasks involving inhibition and working memory. Eye-tracking paradigms provide objective markers for assessing these functions. Objective: To assess whether a brief memory-based cognitive training can modulate saccadic eye movements and improve executive functioning in children with ASD. Method: Fifty-four children with ASD were randomly assigned to a training group (G1) or a control group (G2). All participants completed oculomotor tasks before and after the intervention. These tasks included prosaccades (reflexive responses to peripheral stimuli) and memory-guided saccades (requiring inhibition of reflexive responses and spatial memory). G1 underwent 10 min of visuospatial memory training, while G2 had a 10-minute rest period. The main outcome measures included saccadic latency, anticipatory saccades (indicative of impulsivity), and error rate in memory-guided saccades (indicative of working memory performance). Results: No significant change in prosaccadic latency was observed in the two groups. In contrast, the occurrence of anticipatory saccades and error rates in memory-guided saccades decreased significantly in G1 only, while G2 showed no change. Conclusion: A brief memory training significantly improved oculomotor markers of inhibition and working memory in children with ASD. These findings suggest that memory training may enhance attentional engagement and inhibitory control in this population.

TI From form to substance: Rethinking teacher professional development in
   Vietnam
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Teacher professional development; Teacher agency; TPD effectiveness;
   PLC; Education reform; Vietnam
ID LEARNING COMMUNITIES; AGENCY
AB Collaborative Teacher Professional Development (TPD) is a cornerstone of educational reform, but its mandatory, top-down implementation in centralised systems like Vietnam creates a paradox: mandated collaboration coexists with constrained teacher agency and superficial learning. This study explores how school stakeholders in northern Vietnam perceive the effectiveness of compulsory nationwide TPD and how structural and contextual conditions shape their agency within these programmes. We drew on 35 interviews with teachers, lead teachers, and school leaders. Findings reveal a system in transition, struggling to align progressive ideals with entrenched norms of compliance, hierarchy, and face-saving. Teacher responses include adaptive compliance, collective action when trust is high, and achievement-oriented agency negotiating integrity and compliance. These dynamics demonstrate that meaningful TPD reform requires institutional cultures grounded in trust, respect, and professional empowerment.

TI More than just teaching: A group concept mapping study on classroom
   management challenges in higher education
SO TEACHING AND TEACHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Classroom management; Higher education; Teacher behaviour; Engagement;
   Group concept mapping
ID SCHOOL ENGAGEMENT
AB Classroom management (CM) is a key determinant of teaching quality and student learning, yet research has focused mainly on primary and secondary education. Far less is known about how higher education (HE) teachers experience CM in increasingly diverse and technology-rich contexts. This exploratory study identified CM challenges specific to HE and examined how they align with or differ from those in school settings. Using Group Concept Mapping, 93 HE teachers from multiple Dutch institutions generated, sorted, and rated statements describing CM challenges in terms of perceived importance and control. Teachers emphasized behavioural and ecological concerns over relational or didactic ones. We conceptualize CM in HE as relational regulation; the ongoing alignment of interpersonal, instructional, and environmental factors that sustain engagement and learning.
