TI Protecting students from harm: how teachers' experiences of violence
   influence reporting
SO EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Violence; victim; child abuse; school; teacher; reporting practices
ID CHILD-ABUSE
AB Background Schools play a central role in child protection, with teachers on the front line in identifying violence against children. Despite mandatory reporting obligations, many identified situations remain unreported. While institutional barriers to reporting are well documented internationally, the influence of prior victimisation experiences on reporting practices remains underexplored.Purpose This article explores the effects of the experience of violence during childhood or adolescence on teachers' professional practices in protecting students who are victims of such violence. Based in France, the study aims to answer the following research question: To what extent do teachers' experiences of familial violence influence their propensity to report familial violence of which their pupils may be victims?Method The study adopted an explanatory sequential design combining data from a questionnaire sent to teachers from kindergarten (pupils aged from 2.5 years) to high school (pupils aged 18 and older) and answered by 640. Teacher testimonials were also collected during semi-structured interviews with a subset of questionnaire respondents (n = 39).Findings Cross-analysis of results revealed that reporting of concerns of child abuse took place independently of victimisation experience. The practice was largely subject to collective institutional dynamics, in which professional legitimacy, power relations and organisational norms determined the conditions for expression and the scope of teachers' action. Even those with expertise in identification found that their vigilance could be neutralised or their words delegitimised in decision-making processes.Conclusion This research shows that institutional constraints, rather than personal histories of violence, shaped these teachers' protection practices. It makes a case for the training, recognition and legitimacy of teachers to be strengthened so that their expertise can fully contribute to the protection of children who are victims of violence.

TI Students' assessment literacy in quality assurance of higher education
   institutions in Sweden: the perspectives of students, teachers and
   administrators
SO QUALITY IN HIGHER EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Student engagement; students' assessment literacy; internal quality
   assurance; Sweden
AB Student engagement in higher education quality assurance is promoted globally, yet implementation varies and questions remain about how students contribute meaningfully. This study examines student assessment literacy, defined as the knowledge and skills required for participation in quality assurance processes. Drawing on interviews with students, teachers and administrators at Swedish universities, it explores how this literacy is enacted. The findings suggest that student assessment literacy includes understanding the institutional context, representing peers, preparing for and contributing to meetings and adopting a partnership-oriented stance. These competencies develop through participation, supported by training and institutional encouragement and build on the inherent expertise that students bring, namely their perspective on teaching and learning. The findings further indicate that student engagement enhances the quality of education and supports student development. Challenges include hierarchical dynamics, balancing cooperation with critique, ensuring credible peer representation, managing language barriers and a declining willingness among students to engage.

TI Implementation and effectiveness of an interprofessional educational
   intervention on patient safety in perinatal care: a multi-method,
   prospective evaluation study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Interprofessional education; Patient safety; Implementation;
   Interprofessional collaboration; Perinatal care; Obstetrics
ID HEALTH-CARE; TEAMWORK
AB Background Interprofessional collaboration is fundamental to high-quality and safe care - particularly in perinatal care. Interprofessional education (IPE) for students in healthcare professions has significant potential for enhancing interprofessional competencies and patient safety. However, current evidence on effectiveness of IPE is limited, particularly due to various methodological constraints in evaluation studies such as a lack of prospective data, structured outcome measures, and student involvement.Methods In our project SiGerinn, students from nursing, midwifery, and medicine received IPE on patient safety. We employed a prospective, multi-method evaluation study over a two-year implementation period. Structured surveys on self-reported competency levels among program participants were collected at baseline and follow-up, complemented by in-depth interviews with stakeholders to assess the project's implementation status.Results Prospective statistical analyses revealed highly significant improvements in competency levels for interprofessional collaboration, communication with patients and relatives, and interprofessional communication techniques. Competency gains varied across student groups, being highest among midwifery students. Moreover, survey and interview statements revealed strong acceptance and perceived benefits from the IPE patient safety intervention. Interview findings further emphasised the uptake of a disseminating role among participating students by peer knowledge sharing.Conclusion Our results show positive effects on skill development and encouragement through an IPE intervention on patient safety in perinatal care. Despite several methodological limitations such as small sample sizes, consensus-based outcome measures, and self-reported skill level assessments, our findings provide a starting point for future IPE attempts on patient safety education in clinical settings. Furthermore, obtained insights suggest the value of integrating IPE into health professionals' curricula to initiate sustainable learning.

TI Ontologies of risk in research with young people: interrogating research
   practices and de-centring 'risk' in youth digital media research
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF QUALITATIVE STUDIES IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Risk; practice theory; digital media; social media; research methods;
   youth studies
ID SOCIAL MEDIA; QUEER YOUTH; AFFORDANCES; CHILDREN; PRIVACY; POLICY
AB Research practices can be framed by ontologies that position the very people and practices we aim to make sense of (and with) in our research. Research examining young people's digital media experiences can often start from positions of risk that conflate marginality, risk, harm and vulnerability. We question this framing, examining how risk emerges in research practices. Focused on digital research, where new (and older) forms of risk have (re)emerged, we interrogate research practices that centre risk in youth lives. We argue practice theory and its development in media studies offers tools to de-centre risk. Drawing on two case studies we show how research practices are embedded within research infrastructures that situate youth as risky, conflating risk, media and harm, obscuring broader practices and situated experiences of risk. We provide a 'toolkit' to locate how and when ontologies of risk slip into research projects, and how we might disrupt such framing.

TI A Classroom Demonstration of Red Nylon Dyeing with Japanese Madder
   (Rubia Akane) for Teaching Intermolecular Forces and Acid-Base
   Equilibria
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE First-Year Undergraduate/General; Demonstrations; Hands-On
   Learning/Manipulatives; Bronsted-LowryAcids/Bases; Dyes/Pigments;
   Equilibrium; Green Chemistry
ID MOLECULAR-BASIS; CHEMISTRY; EDUCATION
AB This paper reports a rapid classroom demonstration and instructional activity based on nylon dyeing with Japanese madder (), designed to support integrated learning of intermolecular forces and acid-base equilibria at the introductory undergraduate level. Using roots of home-cultivated madder, nylon fabric can be dyed a vivid red within approximately 10 minutes, providing an immediate and visually engaging starting point for discussion. The instructional focus then shifts to the molecular structure of the major dye component, purpurin (1,2,4-trihydroxyanthraquinone), enabling students to connect macroscopic color changes with otherwise invisible microscopic interactions. Compared with previously reported demonstrations of blue nylon dyeing using alizarin (1,2-dihydroxyanthraquinone), the present approach improves classroom safety by eliminating the need for strong bases. When implemented in a 50 minute session in a first-year engineering course, the activity led to improved student understanding of the mechanisms of intermolecular attraction and the concept of acid dissociation constants. From the perspective of sustainability and green chemistry, the use of naturally derived and locally grown materials represents a small-scale yet feasible approach to addressing the utilization of Earth's limited material resources in individual classroom settings. This work aims to broaden access to chemical education by providing a classroom activity that can be implemented without specialized facilities, thereby offering learning opportunities to a wide range of students worldwide.

TI An empirical investigation of contextual barriers and academic
   achievement disparities for students with disabilities in South Gondar
   primary schools, Ethiopia
SO JOURNAL OF RESEARCH IN SPECIAL EDUCATIONAL NEEDS
LA English
DT Article
DE academic disparity; contextual barriers; disability; Ethiopia; primary
   schools; students with disabilities
AB This study assessed contextual barriers and academic achievement disparities for students with disabilities (SWDs) in South Gondar Primary Schools, Ethiopia. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design with an ex post facto quantitative component was employed. A sample of 544 participants (227 SWDs, 317 students without disabilities) was selected from five primary schools. Quantitative data from continuous assessment scores were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews and focus group discussions were analysed thematically. A statistically significant academic achievement disparity was found between SWDs (M = 33.22, SD = 34.44) and their peers (M = 70.55, SD = 12.53), t(542) = -12.02, p < 0.001, Cohen's d = 1.48. SWD achievement also varied significantly across schools, F(4, 222) = 6.24, p < 0.001, eta(2) = 0.10. Key barriers reported included a severe shortage of special needs teachers, inaccessible physical infrastructure, lack of teaching materials and assistive technology and pervasive negative attitudes. The large academic achievement gap is strongly associated with systemic and attitudinal barriers rather than individual incapability. Improving outcomes for SWDs requires targeted investment in teacher training, accessible infrastructure, learning resources and attitudinal change.

TI Enhancing Pretest Item Calibration in Multistage Adaptive Testing Using
   Simulation-Extrapolation Bayesian Logistic Regression
SO APPLIED MEASUREMENT IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
ID LIKELIHOOD ESTIMATION; MAXIMUM-LIKELIHOOD; ABILITY
AB Calibrating pretest items in multistage adaptive testing (MST) remains challenging, particularly under conditions of sparse response data, limited item exposure, and the need to preserve scale stability. To address these challenges, this study proposes a Simulation-Extrapolation Bayesian Logistic Regression (SBLR) approach and evaluates its performance relative to established methods, including test characteristic curve, information-weighted characteristic curve, fixed item parameter calibration, and Bayesian logistic regression. Using simulated MST data under varying ability distributions and sample sizes, performance was assessed using multiple item parameter recovery indices. Results indicate that SBLR - implemented via maximum a posteriori estimation with informative priors - consistently achieves higher precision and lower bias than alternative methods, particularly under sparse data conditions. These findings suggest that SBLR provides a robust and efficient solution for MST programs by reducing scale drift, improving calibration accuracy, and supporting long-term score comparability. Implications for future research and operational practice are discussed.

AB This paper examines the cultural, ecological and political dimensions of the contemporary water crisis through a curatorial and environmental humanities lens. Through the watery conceptual epoch of the Hydrocene, it highlights the work of artists and interdisciplinary practitioners whose hydro-artistic methods propose ways to realign human-water relations. TI Integrating Entomology into Formal and Non-formal Education to Improve
   Adolescent Attitudes and Knowledge: A Case Study from Southern Mexico
SO AUSTRALIAN JOURNAL OF ENVIRONMENTAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE environmental education; diseases; insects; Oaxaca coast; secondary
   school
ID WILDLIFE
AB Insects are increasingly used in environmental education (EE) due to their high diversity, ecological relevance, and presence in urban environments. This study evaluates the use of insects as a pedagogical tool by implementing formal and non-formal EE activities with secondary students living in areas with a high incidence of vector-borne diseases, on the coast of Oaxaca, Mexico. A total of 118 students participated in theoretical, fieldwork, and laboratory activities, as well as a public outreach event ("Entomo-Expo"). Pre- and post-workshop questionnaires were used to assess changes in knowledge, perceptions, and attitudes. At the end of the workshop, students identified 11 insect orders. They communicated their knowledge using scientific terminology, and negative reactions toward insects decreased, particularly in reports on killing behaviour, while responses associated with observation and the release of insects increased. Participants also recognised key ecological roles of insects, especially pollination. These results are associated with improvements in students' conceptual understanding and more positive attitudes towards insects following participation in the programme. However, given the pre-post-design without a control group, these findings should be interpreted as changes over time rather than causal effects. To address the persistence of negative behaviours in older students, EE should employ both formal and non-formal teaching strategies to support a sense of responsibility and encourage a cognitive shift toward sustainable development.

TI Mapping spatial reasoning profiles using two-tier VR-Assisted questions:
   a cognitive visualization approach
SO CHEMISTRY TEACHER INTERNATIONAL
LA English
DT Article
DE Virtual Reality; two-tier assessment; diagnostic assessment; learning
   analytics; PCA
ID GENERAL-CHEMISTRY; EDUCATION; CURRICULUM
AB The rapid advancement of immersive technologies, such as Virtual Reality (VR), presents new opportunities to enhance chemistry education by linking abstract concepts to interactive, three-dimensional representations. This study investigates the application of a VR-enhanced two-tier diagnostic assessment to assess high school students' integrated conceptual and representational reasoning in molecular geometry and intermolecular forces. The instrument comprises seven items that combine interactive 3D molecular visualizations with paired multiple-choice questions targeting answer accuracy and underlying reasoning. Data from students in Sukoharjo, Indonesia, were scored using a balanced accuracy-reasoning rubric and analyzed with Principal Component Analysis (PCA), k-means clustering, trajectory plots, and t-SNE-based response density maps to characterize patterns of performance across items. The results indicate that many students can correctly identify molecular shapes in VR yet struggle to provide theory-based explanations grounded in VSEPR and intermolecular interactions, revealing frequent misalignment between spatial recognition and conceptual justification. Three broad performance profiles were identified, ranging from low accuracy and weak reasoning to high accuracy and high consistency patterns, highlighting the value of going beyond correctness alone to capture the depth and coherence of reasoning. These findings suggest that VR-enhanced two-tier instruments can serve as rich diagnostic tools for revealing conceptual and representational difficulties, as well as informing targeted instructional interventions. Implications are discussed for the classroom-feasible design of VR assessments and for future AI-supported analytic systems that assist, rather than replace, teachers in interpreting students' reasoning profiles.

AB Background United Kingdom (UK) clinicians report growing demand for intellectual disability diagnostic assessment among adults from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, yet practice is variable, and evidence to guide assessment is limited. TI A Classic Experiment,Reimagined: Using Group Theoryto Assign
   Coordination Complex Geometry via IR Spectroscopy
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Inorganic Chemistry;

   Compounds; Group Theory/Symmetry; IR Spectroscopy; Molecular
   Properties/Structure
ID ISOMERS; SPECTRA
AB Group theory is a foundational yet abstract component of undergraduate inorganic chemistry, and students often struggle to translate symmetry operations into experimentally observable spectroscopic outcomes. This work addresses the challenge of facilitating students' movement beyond symbolic manipulation to apply group theory in authentic chemical contexts. TI Reading and Cognitive Predictors of Reading Anxiety: An 8-Year
   Longitudinal Study
SO JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL PSYCHOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE reading development; reading anxiety; cognition
ID KINDERGARTEN; METAANALYSIS; DYSLEXIA; GROWTH; AGE
AB A growing number of empirical studies show a negative association between reading achievement and reading anxiety, but most evidence relies on cross-sectional correlational data. Importantly, there is a need for developmental studies that investigate how cognitive factors, reading development, and reading anxiety are intertwined. In this study, we aimed to close this gap by testing the extent to which intelligence quotient, working memory, initial reading skills, and reading development throughout elementary and middle school predict reading anxiety at the end of middle school on a sample of 499 children from Romania. The results indicated that initial reading skills tested in first grade, reading development in elementary school, and reading development in middle school each predicted reading anxiety in eighth grade. Neither intelligence quotient nor working memory was directly associated with reading anxiety but initial reading skills and reading development mediated the relationship between the cognitive factors and reading anxiety. The results highlight an important longitudinal relationship between reading development and reading anxiety and suggest an underlying mechanism that can be responsible for internalizing problems among adolescents.

TI Imaginal Role Interventions for Adolescent Emotional Overwhelm and
   Trauma-Related Features: A 10-Session School-Based Experience-Sampling
   Feasibility Study
SO JOURNAL OF PSYCHOLOGISTS AND COUNSELLORS IN SCHOOLS
LA English
DT Article
DE school counselling; guided imagery; imagery rescripting; identity
   development; adolescent emotional overwhelm
ID SELF-CONCEPT CLARITY; PREVENTION; MECHANISMS; IMAGES
AB This school-based feasibility study investigated a brief, structured guided imagery approach for adolescent girls struggling with emotional overwhelm, self-criticism, and difficulty asserting themselves, often linked to high levels of parental control. The intervention, a 10-session small-group study (N = 5, ages 13-16), taught students to use helpful roles (like the Protector or Boundary-Setter) to safely practice a more effective sense of self during stressful moments. We measured emotional distress and the clarity of their sense of self before and after the term. All students completed the sessions, and none required escalation to external psychiatric services. These findings support the feasibility of this brief imaginal method in school counselling and suggest that independence (home autonomy) is a crucial factor for positive outcomes.

TI The impact of introducing relational approaches into four primary
   schools
SO SUPPORT FOR LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE Boxall Profile (R); nurture groups; relational approaches; suspensions
ID NURTURE GROUPS
AB In this two-year project, four participating primary schools received training, support and investment to develop relational approaches and nurturing practices in their settings. The investment included funding for a nurture group, training for the nurture group staff and whole-school staff training in attachment theory, neuroscience and emotion coaching. The socio-emotional progress of 57 pupils attending a nurture group intervention was measured using the Boxall Profile (R) assessment instrument and staff focus group interviews reflected on any perceived changes to school ethos and practice over the course of the project. The impact of relational approaches on school suspension data was also investigated. The socio-emotional progress made by pupils attending the nurture group intervention was found to be statistically significant and this progress was confirmed by qualitative observations made by staff. The development of relational approaches in school changed the way that adults spoke to children and to each other; schools felt calmer and more nurturing; and staff well-being also improved. The impact on school suspension data was inconclusive. The findings recommend an investment in relational approaches in schools to promote positive emotional development, a calmer school atmosphere and improved staff well-being.

TI School-related needs of inclusion and multiple disabilities students via
   drawing analysis
SO SUPPORT FOR LEARNING
LA English
DT Article
DE drawing analysis; inclusion; multiple disabilities; school-related
   needs; special education classroom
ID CHILDREN; SERVICES
AB Students in inclusive education experience problems due to insufficient support services, while those with multiple disabilities face challenges due to their complex needs. This study aimed to identify the unmet school-related needs of both groups through an analysis of their drawings. The qualitative case study included 17 students aged 8-12 years, including 10 students with multiple disabilities enrolled in special education classrooms and 7 students receiving inclusive education. Data were collected through a General Information Form, 'My Dream School' drawings, and interviews, and analysed using a 12-criteria list. Students with multiple disabilities emphasized emotional security, structured environments, and family connections in their artwork. Drawing analysis has proven effective for understanding the emotional, social, and physical needs of students with special needs in school contexts. The findings show that students with special needs' requirements differ significantly from those of students in inclusive education, as do their expressions of these needs. School environments and interventions should be tailored to the distinct developmental and educational profiles of both groups.

TI Academic Freedom in the United Kingdom: a Case Study of Legislation,
   Pathology and Current Stakeholder Attitudes
SO TERTIARY EDUCATION AND MANAGEMENT
LA English
DT Article
DE Academic freedom in UK; Freedom of speech in UK; United Kingdom
   uncodified Constitution; UK woke culture and campus debates; Higher
   Education (Freedom of Speech) Act 2023; UK university governance and
   regulation
ID AUTONOMY; REFORM
AB This article examines the development, current condition, and contested meanings of academic freedom in the United Kingdom, situating recent debates within historical, legal, and socio-political contexts. Drawing on comparative data from the Academic Freedom Index, it highlights a marked decline in UK academic freedom since 2015, positioning the country below several European counterparts. Conceptually, the paper distinguishes academic freedom-centred on teaching, learning and research-from freedom of speech, while arguing that British legislation increasingly conflates the two. The analysis traces the late and politically contingent legal codification of academic freedom in the 1988 Education Reform Act, linking it to wider neoliberal reforms, reduced tenure protections, and increased state influence over universities. It then explores contemporary "pathologies" in higher education, including debates around the "woke" movement, no-platforming, and self-censorship, noting tensions between inclusion, equality law, and open debate. Although empirical evidence suggests that formal restrictions on speech are relatively rare, perceptions of a free speech crisis have driven significant policy responses. Central to the discussion is the Higher Education (Freedom of Speech) Act 2023, which imposes active duties on institutions to protect expression, alongside regulatory oversight by the Office for Students. The high-profile Kathleen Stock case at the University of Sussex illustrates the complexity of balancing legal, institutional, and cultural pressures; its eventual judicial resolution underscores concerns about regulatory overreach. The article concludes that threats to academic freedom in the UK arise from intersecting factors, including political polarisation, economic constraints, and declining public trust. While legislative measures may strengthen protection, broader societal conditions ultimately shape the viability of academic freedom.

TI A Systems-Based Mixed-Methods Approach to Identifying Work-System
   Factors Contributing to Burnout Among Internal Medicine and Internal
   Medicine Pediatrics Residents
SO INTERNATIONAL MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE resident burnout; internal medicine; mixed methods; contextual inquiry;
   systems approach; work-system factors; National Academy of Medicine;
   well-being
AB Burnout among internal medicine (IM) and internal medicine-pediatrics (Med-Peds) residents is at epidemic levels, yet few studies use systems-based methods to identify the specific work-system factors that drive it. Guided by the National Academy of Medicine (NAM) systems model of clinician burnout, we conducted a five-phase sequential mixed-methods study-survey, focus groups, contextual inquiry, affinity modeling and validation, and impact-effort prioritization-among 119 IM and Med-Peds residents at one academic medical center. Burnout (two-item Maslach Burnout Inventory [MBI]), resilience (two-item Connor-Davidson Resilience Scale), and 21 NAM-derived work-system factors were assessed, along with analyses report means, standard deviations (SD), 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and internal-consistency reliability. Among 36 respondents (30% response rate), 55.6% screened positive for burnout (95% CI 39.6-70.5%); mean emotional exhaustion was 3.78 (SD 1.12), and depersonalization was 3.17 (SD 1.38). The 21-item severity scale showed good reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.85). The highest-severity factors were interruptions/distractions, excessive workload, time pressure, and work-life integration. Focus groups (n = 30), contextual inquiries (n = 14, similar to 80 observation hours), and validation sessions (n = 8) yielded 167 breakdowns and 11 priorities. An impact-effort analysis (n = 19) identified clinic workflows and in-basket workload as high-impact/lower-effort priorities. This participatory, systems-based method yields contextually grounded, prioritized targets for reducing resident burnout that survey data alone would not surface.

AB Since the 1960s, Bioethics, Law and Deontology have become increasingly integrated into healthcare education in response to the growing ethical, legal and professional complexity of clinical practice. This national cross-sectional comparative study aimed to investigate the presence and structural characteristics of Bioethics, Law and Deontology teaching in Greek undergraduate Medical, Dental and Nursing curricula. TI A Research-Inspired Chemical Biology Laboratory Module: Synthesis and
   Evaluation of an H2S-Responsive Diselenide Theranostic
SO JOURNAL OF CHEMICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Upper-Division Undergraduate; Research-Inspired Laboratory; Authentic
   Research Experience; Chemical Biology; Medicinal Chemistry; Drug
   Discovery; Prodrug Design; Fluorescence Spectroscopy; Redox Chemistry;

ID UNDERGRADUATE RESEARCH EXPERIENCES; CYSTATHIONINE-BETA-SYNTHASE;

AB Chemical biology integrates organic synthesis, mechanistic insight, and functional evaluation of small molecules in biological contexts, yet undergraduate laboratory instruction rarely reflects this interdisciplinary workflow. Here, we describe a six-week, research-inspired laboratory module, compatible with a standard 4 h undergraduate laboratory course, in which students synthesize and evaluate a hydrogen sulfide (H2S)-responsive diselenide theranostic derived from the clinically relevant anticancer agent SN-38. TI Comparing between face-to-face and mobile learning for improving nurses'
   performance in premature infant positioning: a quasi-experimental study
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Face-to-face training; Mobile learning; Multimedia; NICU nurses;
   Positioning; Preterm infants; WhatsApp
ID OXYGEN-SATURATION; PRETERM INFANTS; EDUCATION; CARE; COMFORT
AB Background Proper positioning is widely recognized in neonatal care. Implementing evidence-based education to improve Neonatal Intensive Care Unit (NICU) nurses' competency in infant positioning performance is essential. Evidence-based educational strategies are critical to enhancing NICU nurses' competency in infant positioning. Objectives To compare the effect of face-to-face training versus mobile learning (m-learning) utilizing multimedia resources on the positioning of preterm infants among NICU nurses. Methods This quasi-experimental pretest-posttest study employed a nonequivalent control group design, with 90 convenience-selected nurses from the NICU assigned to one of three groups: control, face-to-face training, or mobile learning (m-learning). The intervention consisted of face-to-face training (30 min plus 10-15 min of bedside training over 2 weeks) and m-learning (interactive multimedia content via WhatsApp for 2 weeks). Data were collected using the Infant Positioning Assessment Tool (IPAT) at baseline (T1), one week (T2), and one month (T3) post-intervention. Results Nurses' performance of infant positioning was in a "need to change" state in three groups preintervention (p > 0.05). Post-intervention, in T2, the control group remained in a "need to change" state (IPAT score = 4.71 +/- 0.44), whereas both the face-to-face training group (IPAT score = 8.66 +/- 0.55) and the m-learning group (IPAT score = 8.57 +/- 0.40) were in an "acceptable" state. In T3, compared to T1, there was a significant difference in IPAT scores among the control, face-to-face training, and m-learning groups, respectively (IPAT scores = 4.66 +/- 0.37, 6.63 +/- 0.48, 7.88 +/- 0.65, p < 0.001). Both intervention groups showed decline from T2, but the pattern differed markedly: all nurses in the face-to-face group (100%) returned to "need to change" status, while 40% of the m-learning group maintained acceptable performance. The m-learning group demonstrated significantly higher scores and better knowledge retention at one month follow-up compared to the face-to-face group. Conclusion Face-to-face and m-learning methods significantly improved nurses' ability to position premature infants, with m-learning showing better long-term knowledge retention. These findings confirm that each approach is effective on its own, while also suggesting that their unique strengths could be combined. Therefore, we recommend future research explore the effectiveness of blended learning strategies that combine the immediate feedback and practical experience of face-to-face training with the accessibility and reinforcement of m-learning.

TI Teacher Attrition Beyond Exit: Semi-Attrition and Intra-County Mobility
   in Rural China
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE teacher attrition; semi-attrition; teacher mobility; spatial inequality;
   rural teacher retention; life-course theory; rural education;
   county-based governance
AB Teacher attrition in rural China is commonly framed as exit from schools or the profession. This framing obscures a more consequential form of mobility: the stepwise internal movement of teachers from remote village schools to township and county-seat schools within county governance systems. This study conceptualizes such patterned movement as semi-attrition and examines its mechanisms and consequences in a formerly poverty-designated county in southwest China. Drawing on semi-structured interviews with 14 participants and county-level administrative records, and integrating teacher labor market theory, spatial inequality theory, and life-course theory, we find that semi-attrition is directional, normalized, and invisible in official statistics, yet produces cumulative staffing instability in remote schools. Geographic isolation, subject mismatch, and unequal access to career advancement create structural push-pull dynamics, while marriage, childcare, and strategic title-accumulation strategies intensify individual mobility pressures. Together, these mechanisms reproduce spatial inequality through a Matthew effect: county-seat schools accumulate experienced teachers while remote schools cycle through successive early-career cohorts. We propose the County-Based Mobility Ecology Framework (CMEF) to explain how internal redistribution-rather than outright exit-drives staffing inequality in county-based governance systems. Findings call for policies that track internal mobility, address structural root causes, and equalize career advancement opportunities across school types.

TI Becoming a Recognisable Parent: Parental Voice, Migrant Positioning and
   the Politics of Belonging in Norwegian ECEC
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE politics of belonging; parental voice; parental engagement; migrant
   parents; ECEC partnerships; good parenthood; refugee parents
ID EARLY-CHILDHOOD EDUCATION; QUALITATIVE RESEARCH; SCHOOL RELATIONS;
   INVOLVEMENT; CHILDREN; CARE
AB This article examines how differently positioned migrant parents gain unequal access to voice, trust and participation in parent-ECEC collaboration in Norway. Rather than understanding parental engagement primarily as a matter of parents' willingness or interest, the article analyses how engagement is shaped by institutional expectations and by the forms of communication, trust and participation that ECEC staff recognise as legitimate. This article draws on selected material from a broader qualitative project, including interviews with refugee parents, professional interviews and focus groups with ECEC professionals, and fieldwork in four ECECs. It also includes a newly analysed interview with an American migrant father, used as a contrast to the refugee-parent material. The analysis is conducted as a theoretically informed, abductive and reflexive thematic analysis through the lens of the politics of belonging. The findings identify four forms of positioning: guarded belonging, confident belonging, normative belonging and bounded participation. The analysis shows that migrant parents are not positioned as one group. Rather, their possibilities of being recognised as legitimate co-educators are shaped by language, institutional familiarity, trust, cultural recognisability and staff expectations of "the good parent". The article contributes to parental engagement research by showing that equitable parent-ECEC partnerships require more than formal opportunities for involvement. They require institutional conditions in which different parental voices are heard as sources of legitimate knowledge about children's education, care, and belonging.

TI Assessing Multiliteracies in English Language Teacher Education: The
   Perceived Levels of Multiliteracies and the Impact of Demographic
   Factors
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE multiliteracies; demographic factors; English language teacher
   education; pre-service teachers; teaching experience
ID CRITICAL LITERACY; PEDAGOGY
AB The growing emphasis on 21st-century skills underscores the importance of multiliteracies for pre-service English language teachers in navigating diverse, digital, and multimodal classrooms. However, research on their perceived multiliteracies and associations with demographic factors remains limited. Thus, this study bridges this gap by determining how pre-service English language teachers perceived their multiliteracies using Teacher Multiliteracies Scale (TMS) encompassing four key dimensions: multimodal literacy (ML), digital literacy (DL), critical literacy (CL), socio-cultural literacy (SCL), and analyzing the variations based on demographic characteristics involving a total of 393 pre-service English language teachers. The result showed that the participants generally perceived themselves as moderately competent across all the dimensions, with DL dimension scoring the highest, followed by SCL, ML, and CL dimensions. Interestingly, no significant differences were found for gender, age, or academic level. Further regression analysis confirmed that teaching experience was modestly associated with ML, CL, and SCL dimensions, whereas DL showed no significant variations across the demographic variables among pre-service English language teachers. These findings suggest that teacher education programs may consider providing more authentic teaching experiences and practice-based learning opportunities to support multiliteracies development.

TI A Conceptual Model of Hybrid Intelligent Assessment Systems for Higher
   Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE Hybrid Intelligent Assessment Systems; generative artificial
   intelligence; self-regulated learning; AI literacy; EdTech
AB Rapidly expanding use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in higher education creates both opportunities and challenges for learning assessment. While GenAI can provide adaptive feedback and personalization, its pedagogical integration remains underdeveloped and often disconnected from established theories of learning and participatory design processes. This paper addresses this gap by proposing an integrative conceptual model of Hybrid Intelligent Assessment Systems (HIAS), which combines AI capabilities with human oversight to enable transparent, ethical, and pedagogically aligned assessment. HIAS is structured through three interdependent layers of adoption: a pedagogical layer, aligning AI-supported assessment with self-regulated learning and the development of knowledge, skills, and attitudes; a governance layer, ensuring transparency, fairness, and human-in-the-loop validation; and a technological layer, enabling scalable integration within digital learning environments. The study is situated in Estonia, a digitally advanced context with system-level AI integration through the national AI Leap initiative. To complement the conceptual model, an empirical study was conducted across three major Estonian universities, involving 66 professors and researchers and 153 students. In addition, a small-scale pilot implementation was conducted in a design thinking course to explore the practical feasibility of a course-specific HIAS-based AI assistant. The findings reveal a consistent pattern: while both groups demonstrate a broadly positive orientation toward AI, students approach AI primarily as an efficiency-driven learning tool, whereas academic staff emphasize pedagogical control, ethical considerations, and responsible use. Across both groups, AI literacy remains uneven, particularly in critical evaluation and structured application. These findings expose a critical gap between rapid AI adoption and insufficient pedagogical integration. In response, HIAS is proposed as a structured, human-centered framework that supports teachers in designing AI-enhanced learning environments and students in developing critical, self-regulated, and responsible use of AI.

TI Polish Adaptation and Psychometric Evaluation of the Self-Rated
   Creativity Scale for Online Assessment in Higher Education
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE self-rated creativity; BSRCS-6_PL; Polish validation; online assessment;
   digital assessment; educational measurement; cognitive flexibility;
   openness to experience; measurement invariance; higher education
ID COGNITIVE FLEXIBILITY; DUAL PATHWAY; OPENNESS; PERSONALITY; MODEL;
   ACHIEVEMENT; EXPERIENCE; BIG; PERCEPTIONS; ACTIVATION
AB Despite the growing use of brief self-report measures of creativity in digital higher education, no Polish adaptation of the Self-Rated Creativity Scale (SRCS) has been psychometrically evaluated. The present study translated and evaluated the Polish SRCS as an online assessment instrument for higher education. The sample comprised 406 university students studying in Poland (age range = 18-57 years; M = 22.04, SD = 4.01; 72.4% women) from artistic and non-artistic majors. The sample was randomly divided for exploratory factor analysis (EFA; n = 203) and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA; n = 203). Participants completed the Polish SRCS, the Openness subscale of the IPIP-NEO-PI-R, and the Cognitive Flexibility Scale. In the initial 12-item EFA, the six retained items had primary pattern loadings of 0.717-0.819; in the re-estimated brief solution, primary loadings ranged from 0.688 to 0.842 with negligible secondary loadings. CFA favored correlated two-factor models over one-factor models for both the full and brief versions, with excellent fit for the 6-item model (CFI = 1.000, RMSEA = 0.000, SRMR = 0.017). Internal consistency was good (Cronbach's alpha = 0.80-0.84; McDonald's omega = 0.80-0.84), scalar invariance was supported across gender and study major, and correlations with openness and cognitive flexibility ranged from r = 0.34 to 0.44 (all p < 0.001). The 6-item Brief Polish Self-Rated Creativity Scale (BSRCS-6_PL) appears to be a reliable and efficient measure of creativity-related self-beliefs for online research and group-level screening in higher education; however, its educational utility requires direct implementation and predictive validity studies.

TI Assessing Institutional Transformation in Magnet Schools in Catalonia: A
   Multidimensional Analysis and Emerging Indicators for Professional
   Development Programs
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE educational transformation; teacher professional development; school
   improvement; educational innovation; professional learning communities;
   school-based teacher education
ID IMPACT
AB Despite the growing body of research on teacher professional development, there is still limited empirical evidence on how sustained, school-based teacher education contributes to institutional transformation. This study analyses the changes observed after two years of implementation of the programme titled "Magnet: Partnerships for Educational Success", a four-year educational initiative focused on co-creation, collaboration and reflection on practice. The study adopted a longitudinal qualitative multiple-case design, gathering data from three primary schools in Catalonia through focus groups, stakeholder interviews, non-participant observations and document analysis. Findings showed that the programme acted as a catalyst for institutional change processes, particularly in enhancing the focus and consistency of the school educational project, developing more distributed leadership, consolidating collaborative work structures, improving school climate, and strengthening relationships with partners and the local ecosystem. Based on this, emerging indicators of institutional transformation were identified to guide the design and assessment of future programmes, providing specific tools for a systemic and context-sensitive approach to putting educational transformation into practice.

TI A Metacognitive Blind Spot: Student Comprehension, AI Reliance, and the
   Conceptual Difficulty Gap
SO EDUCATION SCIENCES
LA English
DT Article
DE generative AI; AI reliance; reading comprehension; readability metrics;
   illusion of knowing
AB This exploratory study investigates the relationship between student metacognition, use of artificial intelligence, and empirical performance within a multidisciplinary course on AI. Using data from a sample of college-age, full-time undergraduate students (averaging 18 participants per assessment) enrolled in an in-person junior seminar at a Midwestern U.S. university, we correlate student self-assessments with standard readability metrics (e.g., Flesch-Kincaid), L2SCA metrics, and objective assessment outcomes, analyzing how learners evaluate their own comprehension and how they deploy AI tools in response to the complexity of 21 reading assignments over 8 weeks. We find that students' perceptions of linguistic difficulty correlate with classical readability scores, but their perceptions do not predict their success nor does their engagement with assistive AI. The results suggest that students utilize generative AI tools as a habitual baseline rather than a strategic response to difficult material. We argue that while students can identify surface-level linguistic friction, they fail to recognize deep conceptual hurdles, leading to a false sense of mastery that neither their intuition nor their AI assistants appear to mitigate. We propose that a quantifiable metric, the Conceptual Difficulty Gap (CDG), may be useful for identifying a class of texts that syntactically appear to be simple, but consistently trigger performance failures. Crucially, we uncover a possible metacognitive blind spot: student self-ratings of difficulty are negatively correlated with this gap, implying that student assessments of difficulty are not based on actual conceptual difficulty. Furthermore, self-reported AI reliance shows no correlation with the gap, indicating that students may not be strategically deploying generative AI tools to mitigate conceptual difficulty.

DT Article
DE financial attitudes; financial behaviour; financial inclusion; financial
   well-being; Generation Z; university students
ID SELF-EFFICACY; SAVINGS
AB Introduction Financial inclusion has become an important policy tool for promoting financial participation and improving financial outcomes, particularly among young adults in emerging economies. However, access to financial services alone may not necessarily translate into improved financial well-being. This study examines the role of financial inclusion in shaping financial attitudes, financial behaviour, and financial well-being among Generation Z (Gen Z) university students in South Africa. Additionally, the study also investigates whether financial attitudes and financial behaviour mediate the relationship between financial inclusion and financial well-being.Methods A quantitative survey was conducted among 428 Gen Z students at a public university in South Africa. The findings imply that policymakers, universities, and financial institutions should complement financial inclusion initiatives with targeted financial education, behavioural support mechanisms, and responsible digital financial practices to enhance the financial well-being of young adults.

TI Multidimensional and multi-actor evaluation of the quality of LMS
   platforms in higher education through a mixed-methods approach
SO FRONTIERS IN EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE higher education; learning management systems (LMS); mixed methods;
   multidimensional approach; multi-stakeholder approach; quality
   evaluation
ID LEARNING ANALYTICS; SYSTEMS SUCCESS
AB The digital transformation of higher education has consolidated Learning Management System (LMS) platforms as strategic infrastructures for academic management, pedagogical mediation, and online assessment. However, most studies on LMS quality have primarily focused on the perceptions of students and faculty members, paying limited attention to the perspective of administrative and technical staff, which is essential for understanding the sustainability, security, and operational performance of these systems. The aim of this study was to evaluate the quality of an LMS platform at the Universidad T & eacute;cnica Estatal de Quevedo (Ecuador) through a multidimensional and multi-actor approach that integrated the perspectives of students, faculty members, and administrative-technical staff. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed. In the quantitative phase, 230 users (140 students, 80 faculty members, and 10 administrative-technical staff members) completed a standardized and previously validated instrument composed of four dimensions, thirteen criteria, and thirty indicators. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, confirmatory factor analysis (CFA), multigroup measurement invariance testing, and robust inferential procedures for group comparisons. In the qualitative phase, 40 semi-structured interviews were conducted and analyzed through thematic coding using ATLAS.ti. Subsequently, quantitative and qualitative findings were integrated through methodological triangulation. The results revealed that the proposed multidimensional structure, comprising the technical, pedagogical, usability, and administrative dimensions, demonstrated an acceptable structural fit for representing the perceived quality of the LMS. Significant differences were also identified among user groups, with faculty members reporting more critical evaluations than students and administrative-technical staff. The platform demonstrated strengths related to academic management, administrative efficiency, and operational stability. In addition, opportunities for improvement were identified in accessibility, pedagogical interactivity, cybersecurity training, advanced functionalities, and tools supporting formative assessment and academic integrity. The proposed analytical framework provides a comprehensive perspective for the multidimensional evaluation of LMS platforms and offers useful evidence to support continuous improvement processes and digital transformation initiatives in higher education institutions.

TI TAM analysis of interactive video acceptance and learning retention in
   higher education
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE Interactive video; Technology acceptance model (TAM); Educational
   technology; Learning retention; Instructional design
ID ONLINE; INSTRUCTION; PERCEPTIONS; MULTIMEDIA; CLASSROOM; PLATFORM;
   IMPACT; ADULTS; OLDER
AB This study addresses a critical gap in the educational technology literature by empirically comparing the effects of linear and interactive instructional videos on students' technology acceptance and learning retention in an informal learning environment. Employing a mixed-methods design, a within-subjects experiment was conducted with 55 university students who engaged with both video formats. Quantitative data, collected via a Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) questionnaire and a multiple-choice retention test, were analyzed using a paired t-test. These findings contribute to the field by providing a clear rationale for the pedagogical superiority of interactive videos and offering a practical framework for educators and designers to create more effective and engaging digital learning materials.

ID PERCEPTIONS
AB Objective: This study aimed to assess how students from 8 different educational backgrounds engage in and differ in collaborative practice; examine structural relationships among key domains, including leadership, communication, shared goals, roles understanding, member relationships, conflict management, and patient involvement; and explore perceived enablers and challenges in collaborative learning. Methods: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was used. Quantitative data were collected from 793 vocational students using the 7-factor, 48-item Collaborative Practice Assessment Tool instrument. Qualitative findings emphasized the impact of clinical exposure and structured learning, highlighting the need for clear roles, conflict management training, and community-based IPE. Conclusion: Discipline-sensitive, community-based IPE strategies, reinforced shared goals, and role clarity are essential to strengthen collaboration among health professions students.

AB This study examines how design thinking (DT) can function as a conceptual and analytical framework for supporting students' critical AI literacy practices in writing and technical communication classrooms.    generative AI in collaborative writing assignments
SO COMPUTERS AND EDUCATION OPEN

DT Article
DE Academic writing; Collaborative learning (CL); Generative artificial
   intelligence (Gen-AI); Group writing assignments; Student-Gen-AI
   interaction
AB Generative AI (Gen-AI) tools have gained immense popularity among university students, offering advantages such as reduced time for assignment preparation, enhanced product quality, and accelerated learning. When combined with the benefits of collaborative learning (CL), the group use of Gen-AI holds significant potential. The present study aims to explore how students use Gen-AI during the preparation of a group writing assignment in their academic writing course. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 10 postgraduate students majoring in AI research, and the data was analysed using thematic analysis. Two independent coders employed QDA Miner Lite software and adhered to Braun and Clarke's (2006) thematic analysis. As a result of analysis, three themes emerged: 1) group strategy: how students establish and implement strategies of collaborative work with Gen-AI application; 2) strategy characteristics: specific Gen-AI functions addressed by students; 3) strategy considerations: perceived benefits, limitations, and other factors affecting group uses of Gen-AI. The findings reveal that students employ Gen-AI either through pre-planned strategies or spontaneous, individually-driven interactions coordinated through shared documents. In both cases, Gen-AI supported not only language and ideation but also integration, helping merge parallel sections into a coherent text and underscoring the need for coordination and verification.

TI Cognitive load and interest in immersive learning: Applying the
   cognitive affective model of immersive learning
SO COMPUTERS & EDUCATION: X REALITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Immersive virtual reality; Situational interest; Cognitive load; Field
   experiment study
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY; ARCHITECTURE
AB Immersive virtual reality (IVR) is gaining popularity. However, its potential in education-especially how immersion affects the learning process-remains unclear, with theoretical accounts and empirical findings often contradicting one another. To address these gaps, an experimental randomized field study was conducted with 119 ninth graders at one German school to investigate the impact of IVR-mediated immersion on their learning. The participants were randomly divided into three groups: a non-immersive group, an augmented reality (AR) group, and an IVR group. Presence, interest, cognitive load and learning gains on the basis of declarative knowledge were measured, and the data are discussed against the background of the Cognitive Affective Model of Immersive Learning (CAMIL). The results revealed (1) that learners in the IVR group showed a greater level of situational interest and presence, and (2) that the intrinsic cognitive load (ICL) was negative, with situational interest being a positive predictor of learning gains. Finally, path modeling revealed (3) that the data only fit to the assumptions of the CAMIL when a correlation between situational interest and ICL was included. Despite the fact that this finding does not necessitate a comprehensive revision of the overall model, the study nevertheless contributes to the literature by raising the question regarding the interaction between the CAMIL variables. While the generalization of these findings should be critically evaluated, future studies are needed to gain further insight into the connections between cognitive and affective factors as well as their interaction in the learning process with immersive media.

TI Well-being of academics in the changing higher education systems of
   central and eastern Europe
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE Well-being; Job demands and resources; Academics; Central and eastern
   europe
ID UNIVERSITY TEACHERS; WORK
AB While the impact of job demands and resources on employee well-being has been well established in occupational psychology, empirical studies of this impact among academic staff in postsocialist Central and Eastern Europe remain scarce. This study examines the emotional wellbeing of academic staff in five Central and Eastern European (CEE) countries -Hungary, Slovakia, Romania, Serbia and Ukraine -within the context of rapidly evolving higher education systems. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) framework and data from a crossnational survey, the manner in which job demands (e.g. workload, emotional exhaustion, work-life conflict) and job resources (e.g. managerial support, peer collaboration, development opportunities) shape well-being outcomes was analysed. Regression results identify emotional exhaustion, workplace bullying, work-life conflict and workload as strong negative predictors of well-being. Contrary to standard JD-R assumptions, job resources did not exert a direct protective effect under conditions of elevated cumulative demands, suggesting a demand-dominated regime specific to the CEE institutional context. Significant disparities in well-being were observed by age, academic rank and national context. By applying the JD-R model to a geopolitically distinct and institutionally fluid region, this study contributes new insight into how structural and cultural factors mediate academic experiences that offer actionable directions for higher education institutions seeking to promote sustainable academic careers in post-socialist systems.

TI Preceptors' perspectives on the work readiness of newly graduated nurses
   and strategies for enhancement: A qualitative study
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Newly graduated nurses; Nursing; Work readiness; Transition programs;
   Preceptor; Qualitative
ID TRANSITION
AB Background: The transition from student to practicing nurse represents a critical and often challenging period for newly graduated nurses (NGNs). Enhancing their work readiness is essential for a successful transition. However, no consensus exists regarding the evaluation and cultivation of NGNs' work readiness. Existing research predominantly focuses on NGNs' self-assessments of work readiness and personal transitional experiences, while studies exploring preceptors' perspectives and recommendations remain scarce. Aim: To explore preceptors' perspectives on new graduate nurses' work readiness, as well as their recommendations for improving transition programs and new graduates' self-improvement. Design: A descriptive qualitative study. Participants: Fourteen preceptors from nine tertiary first-class hospitals in China. Methods: Data were collected through online semi-structured interviews. Data analysis followed Graneheim and Lundman's content analysis method. Findings: Three themes and 10 categories were identified: (1) novice phase with potential (disconnection between theory and practice, positive attitude versus limited team integration, high digital literacy versus low evidence-based practice capability, and learning potential versus barriers to knowledge internalization); (2) prepared workplace environment (comprehensive competency development supported by new technologies, tacit knowledge transmission, systematic support for preceptors, and creation of supportive learning environments); and (3) self-development strategies during transition (proactive coping with timely help-seeking and targeted reflection). Conclusion: While recognizing the shortcomings of NGNs as novices, preceptors also acknowledge the potential they possess. The study highlights the necessity of providing NGNs with a well-prepared work environment, where supportive environments hold equal importance to comprehensive skill development. For NGNs, preceptors emphasize recommendations for enhancing capability-building methods: proactive coping, timely help-seeking, and targeted reflection. This also indicates that the training strategy for NGNs should reflect a dual shift, transitioning the cultivation model from "knowledge transmission" to "facilitating competency development," while transforming the preceptor's role from "knowledge authority" to "competency development facilitator."

TI Holding presenters accountable for their posters during
   post-presentation discussions in a project-based EFL classroom
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE EFL; Project work; Post-presentation discussions; Question-answer
   sequences; Account-seeking; Account-giving; Conversation analysis
ID INTERACTIONAL COMPETENCE; DISCOURSE SOCIALIZATION; LANGUAGE; STUDENTS;
   ENGLISH; CONVERSATION; QUESTIONS
AB This study examines follow-up discussions after students' poster presentations in a project-based English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) classroom at an upper-secondary school in Sweden. As part of this project, students designed posters based on George Orwell's Animal Farm, presented them in a whole-class setting, and then engaged in post-presentation question-answer exchanges. Drawing on conversation analysis, the study shows how audience members (i.e., peers) hold presenters accountable for meeting the task expectations by prompting them to explain how their posters are grounded in the book and to justify their design choices. In doing so, peers mobilize a range of account-seeking questions, including when-type questions that ask presenters to situate their posters within the storyline, questions that embed candidate explanations of specific features of the posters, and why-interrogatives that ask presenters to account for particular design choices. The analysis of the presenters' responses shows that they consistently orient to their epistemic primacy over the design and meaning of the posters by providing accounts that explain poster-book connections and justify or defend particular design choices in response to their peers' questions. The findings demonstrate that post-presentation discussions in project-based language classrooms afford rich interactional spaces for sustained task-relevant L2 use. The study concludes by emphasizing that oral presentations, in addition to serving as an effective assessment tool, can be leveraged to develop students' questioning and responding practices through systematic engagement in post-presentation discussions.

TI Fostering ethical AI literacy and academic integrity through CEFR-based
   mediation pedagogy in secondary EFL classrooms
SO SYSTEM
LA English
DT Article
DE CEFR mediation; Ethical digital literacy; Artificial intelligence in
   education; EFL; Academic integrity; Critical posthumanist literacy; K-12
   education
ID DIGITAL LITERACIES; ENGLISH
AB The rapid integration of GenAI into educational settings has created an urgent need to redefine literacy not merely as a set of linguistic skills, but as a critical, ethical, and socially mediated practice. While the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR) offers a robust framework for mediation, there remains a significant gap in empirical research regarding how mediation pedagogy can foster ethical digital literacy in K-12 EFL contexts. This mixedmethods study investigates the impact of a mediation-based instructional intervention on 90 Turkish ninth-grade EFL learners. The study concludes that mediation-oriented pedagogy effectively positions learners as social agents and facilitates the transformation of GenAI from a compliance threat into a collaborative resource for responsible meaning-making.

AB Observing expert practice is an important aspect of Initial Teacher Education (ITE), yet creating meaningful opportunities for trainee teachers to observe strategies in real-life contexts can be challenging. TI Fluent, confident, wrong: Why LLMs' most
   underexploited pedagogical use is producing errors
SO THINKING SKILLS AND CREATIVITY
LA English
DT Article
DE Llms; Chatbots; Education; Stem; Critical thinking; Evaluative judgment;
   Error-based learning; Assessment validity
ID WORKED EXAMPLES; VALIDATION; STUDENTS
AB Artifact-based assessment assumes that the quality of a student's work reflects the student's underlying expertise. Large language models (LLMs) break this assumption by decoupling output quality from user knowledge, which renders artifact-only evaluation diagnostically unreliable. This shift also exposes a long-standing imbalance in engineering education, in which the profession has relied on both production and review, yet curricula and grading have emphasized production far more than the skills that make review effective. In engineering, review is the disciplined detection and correction of errors that can propagate into unsafe designs, incorrect calculations, or noncompliant decisions. Historically, teaching review at scale has been constrained by the scarcity of high-quality, realistic, and flawed artifacts. LLMs invert this constraint by generating plausible-but-wrong engineering work on demand, at controllable levels of subtlety and difficulty. Consequently, we argue that assessment validity can be strengthened by treating review performance in terms of error detection, diagnosis, and justification as a primary learning outcome rather than treating artifact production as the primary proxy for competence. We position review competence as a domain-specific form of critical thinking and evaluative judgment, anchored in the constraint structures that distinguish engineering verification from generic critique. Building on this perspective, we present a taxonomy of LLM-generated engineering errors, categorized by error type, severity, and detectability. We also provide templates for prompts and an accompanying LLM interface for generating on-demand, review-centered instructional activities.

TI Transesophageal Echocardiography in the Emergency Department:
   Development of a Validated Checklist for Training
SO AEM EDUCATION AND TRAINING
LA English
DT Article
ID OF-CARE ULTRASOUND; CARDIOPULMONARY-RESUSCITATION; CARDIAC-ARREST;
   SIMULATION; ACCURACY
AB Objectives: Although the use of transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) may improve cardiac arrest management, emergency physicians (EPs) may have insufficient clinical practice opportunities to become competent in TEE. Standardized checklists, such as those used in simulation-based mastery learning (SBML), improve trainee performance for rarely performed procedures. To date, there is no validated checklist for performing point-of-care (POC) TEE in the emergency department setting. The objective of this project was to develop and validate an SBML checklist containing the critical actions for performing POC TEE that can be used for procedural skills training. Methods: This was a multiphase study that began with a three-round modified Delphi to develop the checklist and ended with pre-post assessment. After checklist development, aspects of reliability were measured by piloting the checklist as part of an SBML training program. A previously validated survey was used to assess pre- and post-training confidence in using TEE. Results: The final checklist consisted of 43 items across 7 sections. The minimum passing score (MPS) was set at 83% and the panel deemed 4 actions as critical to patient safety. There was near-perfect inter-rater agreement among all raters with a Gwet's AC1 of 0.99 (95% CI 0.98-1.00) for the full checklist. All EPs that participated in training met the MPS, with a mean score of 97.0% (95% CI 95.0-100%). Median confidence using TEE improved after SBML (23 to 80, p < 0.0001). The post-training confidence for trainees who had prior TEE experience was not significantly different compared to trainees without prior TEE experience (86 vs. 75, p = 0.142). Conclusions: We have developed a novel POC TEE SBML checklist and present validity evidence for the checklist. When using the SBML checklist for TEE training, pretraining confidence was higher among participants with prior TEE experience, but post-training confidence equalized between participants with and without prior TEE experience.

TI Enhancing perceived clinical competence of nursing students in the AI
   era: the role of AI acceptance and self-directed learning
SO BMC MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Artificial intelligence; AI acceptance; Clinical competence; Digital
   literacy; Nursing education; Self-directed learning; Structural equation
   modeling; Technology acceptance
AB Background In the context of AI-driven transformation in healthcare education, preparing nursing students to effectively engage with generative artificial intelligence tools has become increasingly important. While self-directed learning (SDL) has been consistently associated with clinical competence, the role of AI acceptance in this relationship remains underexplored. Objective To examine the mediating role of AI acceptance in the relationship between self-directed learning ability and perceived clinical competence among nursing students. Methods A cross-sectional, correlational design was employed. Data were collected from 550 nursing students at Alexandria University, Egypt, using validated self-report instruments measuring self-directed learning ability, AI acceptance, and perceived clinical competence. Structural equation modeling was conducted to test the hypothesized relationships and examine the mediating effects. Results Self-directed learning ability was significantly associated with clinical competence (beta = 0.452, p < 0.001), and AI acceptance was positively associated with perceived clinical competence (beta = 0.489, p < 0.001). AI acceptance partially mediated the relationship between self-directed learning and perceived clinical competence (indirect effect: beta = 0.206, p < 0.001). The model accounted for 51.0% of the variance in clinical competence. Conclusion The findings indicate that both self-directed learning and AI acceptance are associated with perceived clinical competence, with AI acceptance acting as a mediating factor. These results highlight the relevance of integrating learner-centered approaches with supportive AI-enabled learning environments in nursing education.

TI Forging Industry 4.0 Readiness: A Quasi-Experimental Study on the Impact
   of Spreadsheet-Integrated Automation in First-Year Engineering Physics
   Labs
SO COMPUTER APPLICATIONS IN ENGINEERING EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE first-year engineering; industry readiness; outcome-based education;
   quasi-experimental; spreadsheet-integrated automation
AB The rapid global transformation catalyzed by Industry 4.0 fundamentally necessitates a reconstitution of the engineering skillset, particularly emphasizing digital tool proficiency, systematic problem formulation, and collaborative practice. A persistent and troubling skills gap remains, as traditional introductory physics laboratories, constrained by procedural compliance, routinely fail to cultivate these multidimensional professional competencies during the critical first-year stage. This study addresses this pressing curricular deficit by rigorously evaluating a novel spreadsheet-integrated automation framework (SIAF) designed for early curricular intervention. We utilized a quasi-experimental mixed-methods design involving 203 first-year engineering students. Our methodology demonstrates technical depth by integrating ubiquitous spreadsheet software with low-cost IoT microcontrollers (ESP32) for real-time data processing and acquisition, thereby simulating authentic industrial workflows. Crucially, the study deployed a validated multi-dimensional IRR, addressing a persistent methodological deficit in holistic competency assessment. Quantitative analysis confirmed the SIAF's robust efficacy, yielding statistically significant positive improvements across six competency domains. The most substantial gains were registered in domains essential for the digital workplace: spreadsheet skills (d approximate to 0.65), technical skills (d approximate to 0.45), and digital/automation literacy (d approximate to 0.43). Qualitative data revealed that automation successfully reduced extraneous cognitive load, fostering systematic troubleshooting and a strong sense of digital fluency derived from self-mastery. These results provide compelling empirical support for adopting this replicable, outcome-based education-aligned model to transform foundational physics labs. Future research must prioritize longitudinal designs to assess skill transferability.
